#1364. Imaging exoplanets below the telescope stability limit

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature volume 659, pages 58–62 (2026) Cite this article

Exoplanet imaging is the main method for detailed characterization of planets orbiting beyond 1 au (ref. 1) but it requires suppressing the bright glare of the star to see the faint planet light. As well as sophisticated instrumentation2,3, effective image processing is necessary for starlight suppression, which continues to be a substantial limitation4. Standard algorithms use reference images for starlight modelling and thus they are limited by inevitable telescope instabilities that change from reference to science observation5,6. Addressing this challenge will increase the number of planets amenable to direct imaging and will be a notable step towards imaging exo-Earths with future observatories7. Here we present a new physics-based method for starlight subtraction. Our method combines a multistep optimization with a flexible physical model to produce a starlight model, allowing modelling and compensation of instrument instabilities. We use automatic differentiation (autodiff)8 to optimize millions of model parameters. We demonstrate our method on observations from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) Near-InfraRed Camera (NIRCam)9,10,11 coronagraph instrument. We achieve sensitivity 2–15 times superior to standard techniques, including the first detection of 51 Eridani b (ref. 12) at 4.3 μm. This is the first time, to our knowledge, that such an approach has demonstrated substantially improved sensitivity on real, on-sky coronagraphic imaging. Our framework can be extended to other current and future ground-based and space-based observatories, including the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope and the Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO), potentially relaxing the unprecedented stability requirements needed to make these a success.

To detect any planetary signals by direct imaging, the glare of the star (or stellar point spread function (PSF)) must be modelled and removed from our observations. Because even the brightest young giant planets are about 105 times fainter than their host stars in the near-infrared, modelling the stellar PSF to the required precision is difficult. This is because of its strong dependence on factors such as stellar properties and instrumental aberrations. Until now, the most successful approaches build the PSF model empirically using a library of reference observations taken at other times or wavelengths or of other stars (for example, refs. 13,14).

However, these empirical approaches are fundamentally limited by various sources of instabilities (Fig. 1). In space-based observatories, these mostly include telescope pointing errors and thermal drifts6, causing differences between reference and science PSFs and reducing our sensitivity6,15. Advances in PSF modelling that do not rely as heavily on observatory stability could have transformative implications for exoplanet imaging, for both current and future observatories. For example, one of the main challenges for future missions such as the HWO, with the ambitious goal of imaging Earth analogues around Sun-like stars (1010 brightness contrast), is achieving an extreme and unprecedented stability at the picometre level (100 to 1,000 times more stable than the JWST5,16).

a, Standard starlight subtraction. b, Our method based on FLIP. The stellar PSF is shaped by inevitable and imperfectly known aberrations in the telescope (including star–coronagraph misalignment and optical phase aberrations, represented by coloured curves to the left of the diagrams). Starlight subtraction methods based on empirical reference images are limited by telescope instabilities that cause changes in these aberrations, as these result in dissimilar reference PSFs (symbolized with curves and image outlines of different colours) and thus imperfect PSF subtraction when combining them into an empirical PSF model. Our method, FLIP, pre-calibrates an instrument model on reference images to reproduce the reference PSF and then solves for small changes in telescope aberrations that better explain the science image. This is represented by the optimization loop that tunes aberration estimates with arbitrary flexibility (and thus closer to the effective aberrations that produce the science PSF, represented by the red curves), beyond the limited aberration diversity provided by imperfect reference PSFs in standard approaches. This circumvents the stability limit of the instrument and enables imaging of fainter planets.

An attractive alternative to starlight subtraction by means of empirical reference images is model-based PSF subtraction: directly modelling the physics of the instrument to reconstruct the stellar PSF. This approach has been noted for its potential to relax the stability requirements of the telescope and to reach the fundamental Poisson noise sensitivity limit7. Although promising, previous work investigating model-based PSF subtraction have noted formidable challenges given the complexity of optical systems that prevents accurate modelling17,18,19,20. Even in a stable space-based instrument such as JWST NIRCam, PSF subtraction with synthetic PSFs has only been used in extraordinary circumstances, in which empirical reference libraries are exceptionally low quality, and it has never produced sensitivity superior to standard techniques (for example, refs. 21,22).

Fortunately, nowadays, the computational challenges of model-based PSF subtraction can be mitigated with GPU-accelerated differentiable models. Differentiable models make use of autodiff8 to compute analytic derivatives even with millions of free parameters and thus greatly accelerate optimization problems. Differentiable models have been explored recently, for example, in non-coronagraphic modes of JWST23 and ground-based PSF reconstruction24. Preliminary experiments on simplified simulated coronagraphic data25 have suggested that differentiable coronagraphic models could have a large impact in exoplanet imaging.

Here we present a framework for coronagraphic exoplanet imaging that uses differentiable models for model-based PSF subtraction to deliver notable gains in exoplanet detection sensitivity. Our approach, Physics-based Learning for Imaging Planets (FLIP), incorporates a multistep optimization strategy with a flexible physical model informed by wavefront sensing data to achieve the PSF fidelity necessary for real data. We demonstrate this framework with real JWST NIRCam observations, providing the first, to our knowledge, successful application of differentiable model-based PSF subtraction on real, on-sky coronagraphic data. Our approach improves exoplanet detection limits by up to 15 times relative to published analyses that used standard pipelines. These improvements enable the recovery of planetary signals that were previously inaccessible to existing approaches. We demonstrate this by obtaining the first image of giant planet 51 Eridani b at 4.3 μm, which previously resulted in a non-detection with standard techniques26. These results show the potential of physics-based, autodiff-enabled algorithms to surpass limits set by telescope stability in current and future observatories.

FLIP (Fig. 1) applies three main methodological innovations23,24,25 to on-sky space-based coronagraphic imaging for the first time: physics-based modelling, autodiff and a multistage optimization framework. At a high level, FLIP can be summarized as follows. We use a physics-based instrument model and wavefront sensing data to generate a simulated PSF of the star. Using gradient descent, we tune the parameters in our instrument model to match the real PSF of the star as observed on real data, minimizing the difference between the simulated star PSF and the real JWST NIRCam science image. Autodiff makes optimization by gradient descent computationally efficient. In our multistage optimization, we pre-calibrate our instrument model on a reference JWST NIRCam observation before tuning it on our science observation. Pre-calibration places our model close to an accurate solution, whereas tuning on the science image overcomes the differences between reference and science images owing to instrument instabilities. To mitigate overfitting of real planet signals, we inject fake planets on the science image and track their signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) during our optimization, stopping it when the SNR reaches a maximum or plateaus.

Our physical model consists of an astrophysical scene (a point source corresponding to the host star), an optical model and a detector model. Our JWST optical models are based on the nominal models provided in the open-source software STPSF27, the de facto JWST PSF modelling tool maintained by the Space Telescope Science Institute. These models are known to be imperfect, particularly for NIRCam coronagraphy, but they represent the current best characterization available of the optics and known aberrations. We implement this physical model in PyTorch28, following ref. 25, to make it differentiable and use autodiff in our gradient descent optimization. With this model as our initial condition, we solve for wavefront aberrations, the position and flux of the star and the pixel-level response of the detector.

Our multistage optimization framework is used to overcome model mismatch between our model and the real instrument, essentially improving the initial condition for our science image optimization. For pre-calibration, we choose a reference star similar to our science observation, typically one of the empirical reference images that would be used in traditional PSF subtraction methods. During our optimization on the science image, our fake planets are injected close to the sensitivity limit or at similar separation and brightness as the known planet in the image if there is one. They also serve as injection-recovery tests to quantify signal loss and sensitivity corrections in the final PSF-subtracted image. In this stage, we also slow down our optimization (scaling down the loss, and thus the gradient, during our gradient descent) and tune only a subset of the model parameters to further reduce the risk of planet overfitting. This end-to-end optimization, tuning around 106 free model parameters with an Adam optimizer29, takes around 35 min in a normal NVIDIA A30 GPU. See Methods for details.

We show the performance of FLIP on published JWST NIRCam data and compare it with the optimal PSF subtraction obtained in those publications with standard method Karhunen–Loève image processing (KLIP)14. We analyse observations of two star systems with known planets: HIP 65426 (ref. 30), first published in ref. 31, and 51 Eridani (ref. 12), originally published in (ref. 26). We also process an observation of TYC 5899, a star from a planet search survey with no known companions and with notable aberration drifts between reference and science observations32. We choose this target to showcase the exoplanet discovery potential of FLIP even when faced with long-term observatory instabilities. For HIP 65426 and TYC 5899, we use the observations in the F444W filter with the round 335R coronagraph mask and for 51 Eridani, we process two filters, F410M and F430M, both with the bar coronagraph (in the NARROW position)33,34. This choice of experiments shows the performance of FLIP across a wide range of stellar spectral types, coronagraphs, observational filters, reference star observation strategies and levels of observatory stability. Figure 2 shows comparisons of the PSF-subtracted observations using KLIP and our method FLIP.

Top, observations reprocessed in this work with KLIP, using the same algorithm hyperparameters as in their respective publications. In all cases, our reprocessed KLIP results are comparable with the published results26,31,32. Middle, data processed with FLIP, showing the full field of view optimized over 80 × 80 pixels. Bottom, our detected companions with FLIP next to ideal simulated PSFs, to highlight the recovered morphology and to distinguish real point sources from PSF side lobes. The SNR of the detection is shown in the upper-right corner of each panel. Accounting for small sample statistics following ref. 50, the confidence of the detections from top left to bottom right correspond to 23.7σ, 5.7σ, non-detection, non-detection, 26.3σ, 8.8σ, 5.3σ and 7.7σ. The position of the star is marked with a star-shaped icon. In all panels, north is up and east is left. 51 Eridani F430M observations are convolved with a Gaussian kernel (σ = 1 pixel) to smooth out pixel-to-pixel noise (only in this panel is pixel-to-pixel noise comparable with the brightness of the companion). Scale bar, 1 arcsec.

FLIP achieves superior performance in all observations relative to KLIP, with large improvements in most cases. We obtain around 1.6 times better SNR on HIP 65426 b, 2.1 times better SNR on 51 Eridani b in F410M and a SNR = 6.3 detection of 51 Eridani b in F430M, which yielded a non-detection in the original publication (sensitivity was improved by a factor of about four at the location of the planet). For TYC 5899, we inject fake planets before PSF subtraction with both KLIP and FLIP to illustrate the sensitivity improvement. One of the injections is shown in Fig. 2, which we recover at high importance, whereas it is far from being detected with KLIP. Furthermore, there is a bright, nearby star in the TYC 5899 scene that is still visible after our PSF subtraction, but it has been distorted. See Methods for details.

Figure 3 shows marked improvement in sensitivity to exoplanet detection compared with KLIP. For example, in TYC 5899, FLIP produces roughly 15 times better sensitivity than KLIP at 0.5 arcsec and approximately five times at 1 arcsec, and in the F430M image of 51 Eridani, FLIP provides about five times better sensitivity at 0.5 arcsec and about 2.5 times better at 1 arcsec. We also estimate a fiducial stability-limited sensitivity for KLIP, for which we quantify the predicted KLIP sensitivity limit assuming realistic differences between reference and science observations owing to the changing state of the observatory and assuming no other noise sources. We simulate observations with STPSF on similar observing conditions as the data, including realistic star–coronagraph misalignments33 and optical path difference (OPD) drifts, and accounting for algorithm over-subtraction intrinsic to KLIP. Although simplified, we show that the KLIP sensitivity on real data is consistent with our estimated stability-limited KLIP performance within a factor of two. In most cases, FLIP achieves performance well below this limit.

These curves are calibrated with injection-recovery tests. Also shown is the fundamental noise-limited sensitivity for these on-sky datasets and a range of estimated stability-limited KLIP sensitivity computed using simulated data. Our method enables substantial improvements (in some cases, 4–15 times) in exoplanet detection sensitivity. For the stability limit, we simulate 50 random realizations of reference and science observations with realistic OPD drifts and star–coronagraph misalignment and we run the same KLIP on these data (shaded regions correspond to the central 68% confidence interval from these 50 random draws). For HIP 65426, we do not sample the FLIP sensitivity within 0.6 arcsec owing to contamination from the bright planet PSF lobes, whereas we do sample the KLIP reductions because they are computed after subtracting the planet with KLIP-FM (ref. 51).

These results are illustrative of the potential of FLIP to aid exoplanet discovery and characterization with the JWST. Our new SNR = 6.3 detection of 51 Eridani b in F430M is the first image of the planet at 4.3 μm, in which the absorption band of carbon dioxide is located. This is a wavelength range inaccessible to ground-based measurements owing to telluric contamination from the Earth’s atmosphere. With CO2 being a good tracer of atmospheric metallicity, future work will use this detection to measure the 4.3-μm photometry of the planet and carry out a new atmospheric characterization. This will help assess previous evidence for an elevated metallicity of about five times the stellar value26,35 and better understand the formation history of 51 Eridani b. Similarly, our images of TYC 5899 show how FLIP can enhance exoplanet discovery, overcoming even sensitivity limitations from using reference stars observed months apart from the science observation. Several current exoplanet discovery surveys are similar to the TYC 5899 dataset, with self-referenced observing strategies. These use other science targets as reference stars to increase observing efficiency, which can include data taken across many weeks and months, as opposed to dedicated, ideal contemporaneous reference stars. This observation of TYC 5899 in particular was taken four months after the reference stars observations. Even in this case, FLIP yields sensitivity gains of up to an order of magnitude. With more than 100 observations taken in similar observing programmes (for example, JWST programmes GO 5835, SURVEY 6005), the exoplanet discovery potential of using FLIP in these surveys is large.

By being insensitive to instrument instabilities in principle, model-based PSF subtraction could be capable of reaching sensitivities down to the fundamental noise limit7. FLIP, in general, achieves contrast levels much closer to the noise limit than standard method KLIP (Fig. 3), but the photon noise limit is not reached in any observation yet. Furthermore, although FLIP can effectively compensate for phase drifts and random star–coronagraph misalignments that limit KLIP, our models have not yet been systematically calibrated to retrieve accurate estimates of these instabilities with associated uncertainties. Clear avenues for improvement include a more sophisticated detector model to process deep observations of very bright stars23,36, disentangling degeneracies between different model parameters, a detailed exploration of algorithm hyperparameters37 reducing the computational cost of the method and a framework to handle large data volumes for ground-based applications. See Methods for details.

After more than 35 years of development in coronagraphic exoplanet imaging, this work is the first time to our knowledge that model-based PSF subtraction surpasses standard PSF subtraction techniques, with up to an order of magnitude improvement in sensitivity. In the short term, the demonstrated 2–15 times sensitivity improvement will be notable for exoplanet discovery and characterization with the JWST, enabling access to fainter, and thus colder, lower mass or older, giant planets in JWST NIRCam observations38,39,40. This will expand the imaged exoplanet population precisely in the region of parameter space in which the JWST is most valuable41. Furthermore, with the predicted discovery of thousands of wide-separation giant planets from the Gaia mission42,43, FLIP could be instrumental to characterizing some of these planets with the JWST. Furthermore, our framework can be extended to the JWST Mid-Infrared Instrument (MIRI), contributing to exoplanet detection and characterization in valuable wavelengths beyond 5 μm.

In the long term, these first results show the potential of physics-based image processing on other current and future telescopes, as well as the crucial role that machine-learning-based techniques can play. For ground-based telescopes, recent work24 has shown great promise in non-coronagraphic PSF calibration. FLIP could be extended to coronagraphic ground-based imaging aided by detailed wavefront sensing and adaptive optics telemetry. Although this involves distinct data volume challenges (see Supplementary Discussion in the Supplementary Information), the potential to reach the photon noise limit could be extremely valuable (especially at shorter wavelengths at which we are typically limited by contrast rather than thermal background), particularly to directly image temperate terrestrial planets around low-mass stars with the extremely large telescopes44,45. Similarly for future space-based missions, the extreme levels of stability needed to image exo-Earths with the future HWO is a substantial challenge46,47, aggressively restricting the design space for the telescope. In this work, we have shown sensitivity beyond the stability limit in JWST NIRCam. If this can be extended to HWO contrast levels, the ultrastability requirement for the system may be partially lifted, with the error budget necessary for image post-processing being reduced, and thus the design of the observatory may become more tractable. Investigating this through testing in the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope48 and the Lazuli Space Telescope49 will be critical. If successful, the goal of imaging true exo-Earths and achieving photon-noise-limited high-contrast imaging for the first time will be closer to reality.

FLIP models the stellar PSF by optimizing many of the free parameters in a physical model that influence the PSF, including the star being observed and the instrument used for the observation. We base our models on the nominal STPSF optical models, which are used to simulate PSFs in the JWST for a variety of instruments and filters. Extended Data Fig. 1 shows a schematic diagram equivalent to the physical models used to simulate observations with the JWST NIRCam coronagraphs.

Given these models, we find that four groups of free parameters are sufficient for PSF fidelity in our experiments:

The flux of the star and its precise position behind the focal plane mask of the coronagraph.

The OPD (a phase aberration) before the focal plane mask of the coronagraph.

The OPD after the focal plane mask of the coronagraph.

Physically, these parameters capture the imperfect alignment of the star with the coronagraph (telescope pointing errors), the imperfect alignment of the primary mirrors in the JWST (deformations or tilts relative to the closest-in-time OPD measurement), the imperfectly known OPD internal to specific instruments in the JWST (in our case, the coronagraphs in the NIRCam instrument) and imperfectly known detector calibrations. Although other physical mechanisms are capable of affecting the PSF (such as pupil shear, manufacturing errors in the optics or more complicated detector physics), we find that our choice of free parameters is generally capable of effectively reproducing the effects of these other systematics and produce high-quality PSF subtractions. A summary of our model parameters is shown in Extended Data Table 1.

Implementation details. Following STPSF, our model implements light propagation in the Fraunhofer approximation through Fourier optics. When modelling any specific observation, we use STPSF to calculate the nominal instrument state and produce a simulated PSF, taking into account the instrument and filter, the closest-in-time OPD measurement to the reference star observation and the spectrum of the host star. We take this instrument state and replicate it in PyTorch28. See ref. 27 for details on the STPSF model construction and Supplementary Methods in the Supplementary Information for details on our implementation.

Previous work on simulated monochromatic data25 found that, given a near perfectly accurate physical model, it is possible to optimize it directly on science observations and produce excellent PSF subtraction without overfitting planet signals. However, in our experiments with real data, we find that accidentally subtracting planet signals is indeed possible. This is probably because of STPSF models having substantial inaccuracies relative to real JWST instruments and to our model being much more flexible with more free parameters, thus making the optimization problem less straightforward.

To address this, we implement a two-stage optimization. In stage 1, we use the full flexibility of our model and calibrate it on a reference star (because, by design, it is unlikely to host any contaminants such as planets or binaries), optimizing all of the free parameters described in the ‘Model design’ section. This helps overcome inaccuracies in the optical model and sets the parameters closer to a good solution. In stage 2, we use our calibrated model and optimize only a reduced number of free parameters directly on the science observation. This accounts for different pointing errors and different OPDs between reference and science observations owing to telescope instabilities.

In both stages, we optimize different parameters in separate sub-stages. This is done to reduce degeneracies between different parameters. In stage 1, we have three sub-stages: (1) solving for star position and flux; (2) solving for both OPDs; and (3) solving for both OPDs and pixel responses. In stage 2, we have two sub-stages: (1) solving for star position and flux and (2) solving for the OPD after the focal plane mask. Although the OPD before the coronagraph mask is also expected to change owing to the JWST mirrors, we at present find the optimization to be more stable if we solve for the OPD after the mask instead (as this OPD does not need to be propagated through the coronagraph mask). These stages are summarized and illustrated in Extended Data Fig. 2, with the number of iterations dedicated for each one. On a single NVIDIA A30 GPU, stage 1 takes 10–15 min and stage 2 takes 10–30 min.

We carry out ‘leave one out’ tests to illustrate intuitively the reasons behind our contrast improvement (Extended Data Fig. 3). In the top two rows of Extended Data Fig. 3, we see that the star position has little effect on the contrast: although it is physically important (hence our inclusion), the effect is probably absorbed by other OPD terms in the model as tip-tilt phase aberrations. It is clear that OPDs strongly affect the PSF, as they are related to it directly by means of a Fourier transform. Detector responses are required to remove pixel-level errors that are not the result of and cannot be fit by OPDs. This illustrates the source of the improvements relative to approaches such as KLIP, as methods based on empirical reference images cannot account for arbitrary differences between reference and science data (stages 2.1 and 2.2). The bottom row of Extended Data Fig. 3 shows that model calibration is crucial, because removing it substantially increases the risk of planet over-subtraction. In the bottom row of Extended Data Fig. 3, we also see that a single OPD plane is not enough model flexibility: in our formulation, the interaction between both OPD planes (separated by a focal plane mask) is important. This illustrates the improvements of FLIP relative to previous autodiff-related efforts, notably ref. 25 (which used a far less flexible model and no model calibration).

Implementation details. We use the Adam optimizer29 with a cosine annealing learning rate scheduler. We use an L1 loss function for our optimization.

We select the learning rates in our model by hand, increasing it across orders of magnitude until we find one that produces a stable optimization with convergence below around 15,000 iterations. Owing to the different magnitudes of different parameters in our model, we assign a different learning rate to each family of parameters. A simple coarse search clearly shows the appropriate scale for each parameter. Extended Data Fig. 4 shows that order-unity variations to learning rates do not substantially affect our results and that increasing or decreasing them by orders of magnitude clearly shows the correct scale for stability and relatively fast convergence. A summary of the order of magnitude of these learning rates per parameter is shown in Extended Data Table 1.

Across different observations, we find that globally scaling all learning rates by some order-unity constant can help with stability and convergence speed. This is probably because of the magnitude of the loss function depending on the brightness of the stars. We find that a global scaling of four works well in all of the experiments presented here, but preliminary analysis on fainter stars showed better results by using 1 or 0.5 instead in those cases.

Similarly, during the last sub-stage of our optimization, we reduce the global scaling factor to around 1% of its original value to further reduce risk of overfitting. Our results are not strongly sensitive to the exact choice of this value but it can be tuned differently for different observations depending on the similarity between reference star and science target.

To determine a stopping point for our optimization, we inject fake planets in the science observation and track their SNR as a function of iteration number. When measuring sensitivity, we inject planets at 5–7 separations and 1–3 planets per separation. For each injection, we inject the fake planet by simulating an off-axis PSF with the nominal STPSF model at the desired location in the field of view and adding it to the science image. We inject them at 4–20 times the 5σ fundamental noise contrast limit. This number may be adjusted depending on the amount of signal loss observed. We inject each planet individually per FLIP run. We measure the SNR every approximately 300 iterations. As expected, the SNR of each injected planet increases for several iterations and then decreases owing to algorithm overfitting. Therefore we stop our optimization at the approximate iteration when the injected planets reach an SNR plateau or peak on average, which was found to be consistent for planets injected at similar separations. Extended Data Fig. 5 shows this for fake planets injected at a variety of separations. In light of this, in our experiments, for simplicity, we choose our stopping point tracking a single fake planet injection. Just as with KLIP, the optimal fake planet injection strategy depends on context. For instance, we can choose as the stopping point the iteration number with maximum average SNR across all planet injections (for example, if the goal is to maximize sensitivity across the field of view) or based on one or several injections at a specific brightness and position (for example, if the goal is to optimize the SNR of a specific planet signal). Extended Data Fig. 5 also shows that our PSF subtraction is not strongly sensitive to our specific choices of fake planet injections.

We carried out experiments on four datasets: three with known companions (HIP 65426 in the F444W filter and 51 Eridani in the F410M and F430M filters) and one with no companions, part of a planet search survey (TYC 5899) in the F444W filter. HIP 65426 and TYC 5899 are observed with the MASK335R coronagraph mask, whereas 51 Eridani is observed with the LWBAR coronagraph mask in the NARROW position offset. We selected this diverse set of data to be representative of a wide range of observations with JWST NIRCam coronagraphy. In particular, our four datasets include:

Three different physical systems (HIP 65426, 51 Eridani and TYC 5899).

Three different observational filters (F444W, F410M and F430M).

Two different coronagraphs (NIRCam 335R round coronagraph and NIRCam LWBAR bar coronagraph).

Both real planets (HIP 65416 b and 51 Eridani b) and simulated planets (TYC 5899).

Observations with a dedicated reference star with a 9-POINT-CIRCLE dither pattern (HIP 65426), with a dedicated reference star with 5-POINT-BAR dither pattern (51 Eridani) and without dedicated reference stars but with a PSF library composed from a self-referenced survey (TYC 5899). This is relevant for the KLIP performance under a variety of reference star configurations.

Observations with reference stars close in time to the science target (HIP 65426 and 51 Eridani) and far in time from the science target (TYC 5899).

Observations of host stars of various spectral types: A2V (HIP 65426), F0IV (51 Eridani) and M3 (TYC 5899).

We run standard PSF subtraction method KLIP and our technique FLIP on all four datasets and compare the performance of each, both with the SNR of the known recovered companions and with the planet detection sensitivity at several separations from the star. We perform our KLIP subtractions in accordance with the optimal set of KLIP hyperparameters described in the respective publications to replicate what the authors considered the best performance. In particular, all KLIP subtractions are done using RDI + ADI (see, for example, ref. 31) on both roll angle observations of the science targets, which we then de-rotate and mean-combine. In all cases, we obtain PSF subtractions comparable with the published works. For FLIP, for simplicity, we perform it on only one roll per dataset. Future work could explore the differences in sensitivity between using FLIP only on one roll, FLIP on both rolls and mean-combining the de-rotated images and FLIP on both rolls, using ADI on the resulting images and mean-combining the FLIP + ADI results.

For TYC 5899, the original publication32 presents two epochs: one with a single roll angle (the second failed) and one with two roll angles observed four months after the reference star sequences. We use the latter in this analysis for both KLIP and FLIP, to illustrate the gains in sensitivity when there is substantial drift between reference and science observations. Although ref. 32 used all three observations for their contrast curves and we replicate it only with the last two, we obtain comparable contrast performance: about 3 × 10−6 at 2.5 arcsec and about 4 × 10−5 at 1.0 arcsec for KLIP and FLIP and about 3 × 10−4 for KLIP and about 5 × 10−4 for FLIP at 0.5 arcsec. Because the target has no known companions, we inject planets at various separations and brightnesses to compare the performance of KLIP and FLIP in a controlled setting.

Extended Data Table 2 shows the optimization hyperparameters used during our reductions with FLIP.

The observations of HIP 65426, 51 Eridani and TYC 5899 and their reference stars were processed with the JWST pipeline (version 1.18.1) and the community-developed tool spaceKLIP (version 2.2.1). Data processing steps (which include ramp-fitting, converting from detector counts to physical flux units and bad pixel cleaning) and observation set-up are detailed in the respective papers for those observations26,31,32.

The JWST and spaceKLIP pipelines include bad pixel flagging and cleaning. However, imperfect bad pixel cleaning can cause more difficulties in our model-based PSF subtraction than in methods such as KLIP. This is because hot or dead pixels, or variations in pixel responses, cannot be ‘cancelled out’ by subtracting observations with the same pixel variations. Therefore, bad pixels that persist even after the automated cleaning routines are identified by eye and masked during our optimization process.

Both HIP 65426 and 51 Eridani were observations carried out with dedicated reference stars: a bright star with probably no planets around it, of similar spectral type to the science target, observed just before or after the science observation. For these targets, we use as our calibration star (optimization stage 1; Extended Data Fig. 2) the same reference stars used for those observations: HIP 68245 for HIP 65426 and HD 30562 for 51 Eridani. We use a single dither for model calibration with FLIP for simplicity but all dithers are used to build the principal components for KLIP. See refs. 26,31 for details.

For TYC 5899, the observation was taken as part of a self-referenced programme, in which only science observations are taken, and a large number of these are put together to be used as a reference library for every other science observation. For our KLIP subtractions, we use the full PSF library used in ref. 32 to reproduce the result in their published work. For an apples-to-apples comparison of FLIP and KLIP, we chose one of the observations in the self-referenced library as our calibration star for stage 1 of FLIP. We select the HIP 17695 observation as it has the most similar spectral type to TYC 5899 from the targets in the library. See ref. 32 for details.

The contrast curves for both KLIP and FLIP were calculated by dividing the image into small concentric annuli and computing the standard deviation within each annulus accounting for small sample statistics50 and for planet signal loss owing to both algorithm overfitting and coronagraph throughput. For reference, the signal loss from algorithm overfitting near the location of the measured planets (in the same order as in Fig. 2) for KLIP is about 5–10%, about 20–70%, about 50–80% and about 10–40% and for FLIP it is about 5–20%, about 20–40%, about 30–50% and about 40–60%. We also smooth all datasets with a Gaussian kernel (σ = 1 pixel) before computing the standard deviations, as FLIP residuals are mostly dominated by pixel-to-pixel noise. For HIP 65426, the FLIP contrast curve excludes the central 0.6 arcsec of the image given that a bright lobe of the planet PSF prevents sampling this region, whereas KLIP uses the KLIP-FM algorithm to subtract the planet before computing sensitivity. Future work incorporating planet modelling and subtraction with FLIP will overcome this limitation. See refs. 26,31,32 for details on computing and calibrating these contrast curves.

For the fundamental sensitivity curve, we use the ERR extensions of the JWST data products, which track the combined total uncertainty in each pixel value from read noise, Poisson noise and flat noise. We generate a random Gaussian sample with mean 0 and σ equal to the total noise level in each pixel. That is, when generating our noise realization, we are simulating what the image would look like after perfect PSF subtraction. We finally compute the contrast curve on this image in the same way as described above for KLIP and FLIP subtractions, assuming no planet signal loss. This assumes that the only source of fundamental noise comes from the science observation. This is essentially the case 0 presented in ref. 4. In KLIP, further noise also comes from the reference observations (see ref. 4). FLIP is model-based PSF subtraction, so our FLIP subtraction adds no extra fundamental noise. The fundamental noise curves can also be interpreted as a lower limit, or the most optimistic case, of the possible sensitivity. Because we perform FLIP on only one roll per dataset, the noise limit corresponds to the noise limit of that roll.

To supplement Fig. 2, we compute SNR maps for each PSF-subtracted image (Extended Data Fig. 6). We generate a non-coronagraphic PSF model cropped to the central 5 × 5 pixels and cross-correlate our image with the PSF model. Then we compute the SNR of each individual pixel within an annulus of width approximately 0.2 arcsec in a two-step process: we compute the noise per annulus to identify pixels with SNR > 5 as a first pass and then compute a refined noise estimate excluding those pixels. The final SNR map is simply the pixel values of the cross-correlation map divided by the refined noise estimate.

In Fig. 3, we show a fiducial stability-limited sensitivity. This limit is computed by performing KLIP on simulated data, in which we can isolate the physical factors that contribute to the KLIP performance limitations. We perform 50 realizations of each observation sequence, stochastically varying the star–coronagraph misalignment and the OPD drift consistent with empirical JWST characterization in flight5,33, as detailed below. To isolate the effects of these instabilities, we include no other source of noise (for example, photon noise, flat noise) in our simulations.

For the science target, we generate STPSF models using the spectral type of the star and scale the flux within the central 20-pixel radius to the flux of the real data. We simulate two rolls offset by 10° in position angle. For the reference stars, for HIP 65426, we simulate nine PSFs following the 9-POINT-CIRCLE dither strategy, for 51 Eridani five PSFs following the 5-POINT-BAR dither strategy (https://jwst-docs.stsci.edu/jwst-near-infrared-camera/nircam-operations/nircam-dithers-and-mosaics/nircam-subpixel-dithers/nircam-small-grid-dithers#gsc.tab=0) and for TYC 5899, we simulate the same number of reference stars that were used in the PSF library of ref. 32.

We assume that all reference stars are of identical spectral type and brightness to the science target and assume no photon, detector or flat noise. In some targets, this results in the KLIP stability limit being deeper than the fundamental noise limit at large separations from the star (Fig. 3). This is acceptable for our purposes, because at these close separations, we are generally limited by PSF subtraction inaccuracies rather than fundamental noise and we are mostly interested in improving sensitivity in the regions of the image in which we are stability-limited rather than fundamental-noise-limited.

For each observation, we simulate a target acquisition error with a random star–coronagraph misalignment drawn from \({\mathcal{N}}(\mu =0,\) \(\sigma =10)\,{\rm{mas}}\), consistent with target acquisition accuracy in flight33. We simulate the PSFs with the closest-in-time OPD measurement. We assume that there is no notable OPD drift between reference star dithers. To mimic small OPD drifts owing to telescope slews, for each observation in the real data that required a telescope slew (for example, going from reference star to the science target), we add an OPD drift term to the OPD measurement. The shape of the OPD drift is taken from subtracting the two closest-in-time OPD measurements to the observation being simulated. The root mean square (r.m.s., that is, the amplitude) of the drift term is randomly drawn from \({\mathcal{N}}(\mu =4,\sigma =1)\,{\rm{nm}}\), smaller than drifts measured over day timescales (about 7–9 nm r.m.s.) and bigger than drifts on minutes timescales (about 1–2 nm r.m.s.)5.

For HIP 65426, the bright companion has a non-negligible effect on PSF subtraction by skewing the KLIP algorithm (for example, during mean subtraction and in the calculation of Karhunen–Loève (KL) modes). We recreate this effect by injecting a fake planet in our HIP 65426 observation at the same contrast, separation and position angle as the real companion in our simulated observation.

We perform KLIP with ADI + RDI on all targets, using all KL modes for HIP 65426 and 51 Eridani and six KL modes for TYC 5899, following the respective publications. We compute our calibrated stability-limited KLIP sensitivity with injection-recovery tests, injecting planets at 3–7 separations and 2–3 position angles across the 80 × 80-pixel field of view, with the injected flux being four times the uncalibrated KLIP sensitivity at the injection separation. The central 68% range of the resulting contrast curves are plotted as shaded regions in Fig. 3.

To compare the sensitivity of FLIP and KLIP on TYC 5899, we inject fake planets with known flux across the image and assess the recovery PSF subtraction. Extended Data Figs. 7 and 8 show a range of planet injections, complementing Fig. 2. At each separation, we inject a planet with flux equal to 20 times the 5σ fundamental noise limit. For PSF subtraction, we process all observations in Extended Data Figs. 7 and 8 identically, using the same learning rates and numbers of iterations for FLIP and the same numbers of annuli and KL modes for KLIP. This is a standard method to quantify sensitivity in KLIP (for example, ref. 37): once a set of annuli and KL modes have been chosen (for example, to recover the signal in Fig. 2), we inject fake planets across the field of view while keeping the annuli and KL modes fixed. This estimates the detection sensitivity across the field of view, given a set of hyperparameters. In FLIP, we use an analogous strategy, by injecting fake planets across the field of view, while keeping the learning rates and numbers of iterations fixed.

We find that FLIP outperforms the standard method KLIP in most cases, especially at closer separations, producing higher SNR on a diverse range of possible planets. We also see that, in this particular dataset, at larger separations, FLIP produces higher signal loss than KLIP in some cases, which explains the contrast curve for KLIP being deeper than FLIP at larger separations in Fig. 3. Future work could address these differences in signal loss. Nevertheless, at these larger separations, we are often background-limited rather than contrast-limited; that is, sensitivity is mainly limited by exposure time rather than by starlight subtraction. In the interesting regime in which we are limited by telescope stability and imperfect starlight subtraction, at smaller angular separations (which also correspond to more Solar-System-like physical separations), FLIP robustly outperforms KLIP.

The JWST NIRCam data used in this paper are from JWST programmes ERS 1386 (PI: S. Hinkley), GTO 1412 (PI: M. Perrin) and GTO 1184 (PI: J. Schlieder) and are publicly available from the Mikulski Archive for Space Telescopes (MAST).

The FLIP code and an example demo with test data are available at https://github.com/rferrerc/pyflip/tree/submission (submission commit: a92e684).

This includes calibration (stage 1, top panels) on a reference star and parameter tuning (stage 2, bottom panels) on the science target of interest. For visualization purposes, we keep all panels in the detector orientation, except for the last one, in which we rotate it north up as in Fig. 2. Our full optimization is shown in the far left on 51 Eridani (F410M) for comparison. Top two rows, excluding individual stages. We skip the fit for star-mask misalignment (top) and the fits for individual OPDs and for detector effects (bottom). In all cases, we fit the flux of the star. Example FLIP runs using different learning rates while keeping the number of iterations identical. Increasing our learning rate by orders of magnitude leads to unstable optimization unable to converge (top left) or to substantial overfitting (bottom left). Lowering our learning rate by orders of magnitude increases the amount of unsubtracted starlight (bottom right) or, for this specific target, reduces the ability of our model to compensate for imperfect stellar flux estimate (stage 2.1) owing to the presence of the bright companion (top right). In each panel, all learning rates in the model are scaled by the factor indicated inside the panel.

In the left and right panels, all planets were injected at 10 and 20 times the 5σ fundamental noise contrast curve (blue curve in the HIP 65426 panel of Fig. 3) at the separation of the injected planet, respectively. The separation of each planet corresponds to the colour of each line. The top panels correspond to the number of iterations used in our experiments, with the stopping condition marked with a dashed line (11,000 iterations) and including the SNR and signal loss for 2,000 iterations beyond our stopping condition. Planets injected at most separations reach SNR plateaus at similar numbers of iterations, with no strong dependence on the brightness of the injection (left and right panels). The bottom panels show the optimization resulting from substantially increasing the number of iterations, for which we set our learning rate scheduler to have 20,000 total iterations.

Barcelona are reportedly interested in signing Arsenal defender Piero Hincapie as Deco looks to strengthen Hansi Flick’s defensive options ahead of the January transfer window.

According to a report from Sport, the Catalan giants have identified the Ecuadorian international as a potential defensive addition, with the club’s sporting director already exploring the possibility of bringing him to Camp Nou.

Barcelona are keen to add more quality and depth to their defensive unit, and Hincapie could be an attractive option for the Spanish giants. The 24-year-old has struggled to establish himself as a regular starter at Arsenal this season, which could potentially open the door for a January departure.

The Ecuadorian international has several qualities that make him an appealing target for Flick. He is naturally left-footed and comfortable operating both as a centre-back and left-back, offering the German manager valuable tactical flexibility.

Hincapie also has considerable experience at the highest level, having previously impressed during his time at Bayer Leverkusen before moving to the Premier League.

Reports suggest Deco and Flick have received positive assessments of the defender, with the Barcelona sporting director reportedly making initial contact with his representatives to understand his willingness to consider a move.

Want more CaughtOffside coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust.

However, convincing Arsenal to part ways with Hincapie mid-campaign could prove challenging for Barcelona.

Mikel Arteta remains reluctant to weaken his squad during the January transfer window, particularly with the Gunners competing across multiple competitions. Despite the defender’s limited involvement this season, the Spanish manager may be unwilling to sanction his departure.

Barcelona will therefore need to assess their options carefully before making a formal approach. Hincapie’s versatility and potential make him an interesting addition, but Arsenal’s stance could ultimately determine whether the Catalan giants can turn their reported interest into a concrete transfer.

Real Madrid have also been linked with Hincapie.

#1362. Martin O'Neill's greatest mistake was staying after winning the league

By CALUM CROWE, SCOTTISH DEPUTY CHIEF SPORTS WRITER

Published: 12:24 EDT, 3 November 2026 | Updated: 14:51 EDT, 3 November 2026

Winning the league title in such dramatic fashion on the final day of last season, Martin O’Neill should have recognised the moment for what it was. The End.

In a chaotic season where he had rescued Celtic from oblivion not once but twice, that was the moment when the credits should have rolled.

The blockbuster Hollywood finale. The perfect opportunity to go out in a blaze of glory and sail off into the sunset, his legacy not only secure but further enhanced.

His decision to stay on as manager this season has proven to be a mistake. In his heart of hearts, O’Neill must realise this. The whole thing is done. Finished. Finito. Terminado, as one of his predecessors would have said.

On the back of the 2-0 defeat to Falkirk last weekend, it has now reached the point where O’Neill’s continued presence at the club is damaging his legacy.

The fans are turning on him. They don’t care what he did for the club 20-odd years ago. They aren’t interested in his wisecracks. They don’t want to hear nostalgic tales of old about how things used to be.

They care only about the here and now and about what they are watching on the pitch. Now mired in a run of three wins in their last ten matches, O’Neill’s side are, if anything, actually getting worse.

O’Neill’s argument about still being top of the league is one of deflection, denial and delusion. Complete and utter claptrap. It is an insult to the intelligence of Celtic supporters.

Martin O'Neill's Celtic team lead the table but have struggled to convince

This is the problem. If there is solid evidence to support the claims that he has lost the faith of the players, then he is also rapidly losing the faith of the fans.

In a way, it is sad that it should come to this. The man is 74 years old. He didn’t ask to be thrust back into the spotlight. At least, not initially.

On two occasions, he answered an SOS call from Dermot Desmond last season. He came back and he did exactly what was asked of him.

If Celtic had any sort of competent succession plan in place, there wouldn’t even have been a conversation around O’Neill’s future towards the end of last season.

It would have been a case of shaking his hand, thanking him enormously for a heroic contribution, before being serenaded by supporters one last time after winning a league and cup double.

Yet, going back to those final few weeks of last season, it was clear O’Neill had the bug for it once again. He was never going to walk away, and nor were the board ever going to turn him down.

In the end, the situation needed one of two things to happen. It either needed O’Neill to save himself from his own desires, and have some sense and foresight about how the club was being run, or it needed Celtic to show some vision and make a proper long-term appointment.

In the absence of both, it was the blind leading the blind. O’Neill hung around primarily to have another crack at Europe, the Celtic board thought they had a bulletproof shield by retaining the services of a club icon.

The argument that kept on being trotted out at the time centred on how winning the league title meant that O’Neill had earned the right to stay on.

But that fundamentally missed the point. Of course he had earned the right. He’s Martin O’Neill. Only Jock Stein stands above him in the pantheon of the club’s all-time greatest managers.

Fans adored him (yes, past tense). But just because he had earned the right doesn’t mean it was the right thing to do. That’s the key difference.

Celtic manager Martin O'Neill lifts the league trophy back in May

Whenever Manchester United inevitably sack Michael Carrick, let’s suppose for a second that Sir Alex Ferguson comes in and takes charge for a few games.

Everything goes well, the team start winning games again, everyone starts getting those old feelings coming back.

But would it mean that the right thing to do is to hand Sir Alex the job for another season? Of course it wouldn’t.

The failure to separate that nostalgia and love for O’Neill from what was required moving into this season was a catastrophic error of judgment on Celtic’s part.

The club had absolutely no idea how to move forward in the summer – just like they would have absolutely no idea who to appoint now if O’Neill was to be relieved of his duties.

In the past, Celtic sacked Tommy Burns. They sacked Billy McNeill. The belief that O’Neill could not suffer a similar fate is hugely naive.

Right now, a growing section of the fanbase view him as little more than an extension of Desmond. His status as a club icon is fading.

Over the weekend, a couple of articles surfaced from a few years ago when O’Neill was sacked as Nottingham Forest manager in 2019.

They spoke of how O’Neill eventually lost the dressing room and of how the players were left bemused by his lack of detail on the tactical side of the game.

Some Celtic fans view O'Neill as little more than an extension of major shareholder Dermot Desmond

The parallels with this current Celtic side are obvious. Just look at the comments from Callum McGregor and Cameron Carter-Vickers over recent weeks.

They are a team with absolutely no tactical identity – and it’s difficult to see how this gets any better for as long as O’Neill, along with coaches Shaun Maloney and Mark Fotheringham, remain at the helm.

O’Neill attended a Q&A session at a supporter’s club in Greenock on Monday night, along with chief executive Michael Nicholson and chairman Brian Wilson.

A bizarre announcement from Celtic yesterday claimed that the questioning had been ‘hard but fair’ as supporters voiced their concerns about the current malaise.

The one man who continues to dodge the Paxman treatment is, of course, Desmond himself, the club’s largest shareholder who operates as the commander-in-chief.

And the one question which is now becoming painfully unavoidable is this: what grounds are there for Martin O’Neill to continue as Celtic manager?

Liverpool teenager Trey Nyoni marked his first senior goal for the club with a sublime first-time volley from the edge of the box during Wednesday’s UEFA Champions League clash against Fenerbahçe.

The 19-year-old midfielder broke the deadlock in Istanbul with a moment of pure technical brilliance in the 25th minute.

The attack opened when fellow teenager Rio Ngumoha skipped past a sequence of challenges to carve his way into the penalty area.

After Ngumoha’s initial shot was blocked, Szoboszlai put in a teasing cross in and Fenerbahçe failed to clear the danger, heading the ball out to the edge of the penalty box.

Nyoni met the dropping ball on the full volley, sending a struck effort past Ederson, wrong-footing the goalkeeper via a minor deflection, to net his landmark first goal in red.

The young Liverpool midfielder scores his first professional goal, and he does it on the Champions League stage ?

? Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB pic.twitter.com/Vtj4Yd3tnn

— Football on TNT Sports (@footballontnt) November 4, 2026

Nyoni’s strike highlights the continued faith manager Andoni Iraola has placed in Liverpool’s academy talents during their European campaign.

18-year-old winger Rio Ngumoha was once again extremely threatening down the left flank, continually unpicking the Fenerbahçe defense with his direct dribbling and pace.

Under Iraola’s high-tempo tactical setup, Liverpool’s next generation is proving capable of producing game-defining moments on the highest stage.

Liverpool’s lead proved short-lived, however, as the host side responded quickly in front of a boisterous Istanbul crowd.

Just four minutes after Nyoni’s opener, Fenerbahçe won a set-piece outside the area. Mason Greenwood stepped up to take the free-kick, seeing his effort take a cruel deflection off the Liverpool wall to wrong-foot Alisson Becker and restore parity for the Turkish side.

#1360. A spatiotemporal cancer cell trajectory underlies glioblastoma heterogeneity

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Cancer cells show highly heterogeneous and plastic states in glioblastoma, an incurable brain tumour1,2,3,4,5. However, how these malignant states arise and whether they follow defined cellular trajectories across tumours is poorly understood. Here we generated a deep single-cell and spatial multi-omic atlas of human glioblastoma that pairs transcriptomic, epigenomic and genomic profiling of 12 tumours across many regions. We identify that glioblastoma heterogeneity is driven by spatially patterned transitions of cancer cells from developmental-like states towards those defined by a glial injury response and hypoxia. This cellular trajectory regionalizes tumours into distinct tissue microenvironments and manifests in a molecularly conserved manner across tumours as well as genetically distinct tumour subclones. Consistently, using a new deep-learning framework to map cancer cell states jointly with clones in situ, we show that tumour subclones are finely spatially intermixed through glioblastoma tissue microenvironments. We validate this cellular trajectory by using somatic mutation-based hierarchies in vivo and an experimental patient-derived organoid model ex vivo. Finally, we show that this cancer cell trajectory is intimately linked to myeloid heterogeneity and unfolds across regionalized myeloid signalling environments. Our findings define a stereotyped trajectory of cancer cells in glioblastoma and unify glioblastoma tumour heterogeneity into a tractable cellular and tissue framework.

The extensive tumour heterogeneity of glioblastoma (GB), an incurable adult brain cancer, presents a major obstacle to treatment. Nearly two decades of molecular profiling has found that malignant cells exist across a spectrum of cellular states within each tumour, resembling developmental neural progenitors as well as mesenchymal-like and injury response states1,2,3,4,5. These states are suggested to vary in abundance across tumours and stratify GBs into subtypes1,2. Furthermore, patient-derived xenografts have shown that malignant cells can transition across cellular states, indicating their plasticity2,6. Despite these extensive efforts, we still do not understand how cancer cells diversify into distinct states and give rise to GB heterogeneity. In particular, whether malignant cells follow stereotyped or variable cellular trajectories across GB tumours is unknown. A cancer cell trajectory that is conserved and tractable across GBs would present a highly attractive therapeutic target.

Single-cell, bulk and spatial genomics have revealed stereotypical aspects of GBs. Several malignant cell states can be detected within each tumour2,5,7 and their single-cell transcriptional profiles can be mapped onto an axis between developmental-like (dev-like) and injury response-associated gene expression programs4,8. Genetic heterogeneity1,2 and tumour microenvironment (TME) signals9 also influence malignant cell state identity. Furthermore, these states show a recurrent spatial organization across tumours5,10. Yet, these observations have not been linked together to resolve malignant cellular trajectories in GB, in part due to the lack of multimodal profiling efforts that can integrate insights from various cell and tissue atlassing technologies. Here we address this challenge by means of deep single-cell and spatial multi-omic profiling of human GBs and identify that a stereotyped spatiotemporal trajectory of cancer cells gives rise to GB heterogeneity.

To comprehensively profile GB heterogeneity, we generated a single-cell and spatial multi-omic atlas of 12 isocitrate dehydrogenase wild-type (IDH-wt) primary GB tumours (Fig. 1a and Supplementary Table 1), combining three main approaches. First, we profiled each tumour across many sites, ranging from 4 sites (roughly 1.25 cm3 each) for most cases to 15 sites effectively covering one whole tumour (Extended Data Fig. 1a and Supplementary Fig. 1), spanning 57 tumour sites in total. Second, we generated paired single-nuclei and spatial omic data from each sampling site, profiling consecutive tissue sections with single-nuclei joint transcriptome sequencing and chromatin accessibility sequencing (‘multiome’ snRNA + ATAC-seq) and Visium spatial transcriptomics (ST) (Fig. 1a). Select sites were assayed with orthogonal Xenium ST and immunohistochemistry, as well as whole-genome sequencing (WGS) of tumour microbiopsies (Supplementary Fig. 1). Third, we profiled large numbers of nuclei (more than 1 million) and spatial tissue sections (more than 0.3 million spatial transcriptomes across 97 Visium sections) (Supplementary Table 2). The resulting ‘GBM-space’ dataset, accessible on a user-friendly interactive webportal11 (www.gbmspace.org/), enables comprehensive multimodal characterization of GB and presents a unique holistic tumour atlas for cancer research.

To examine GB heterogeneity, we first annotated malignant and TME cell states in our multiome data. After standard data processing workflows, we filtered nuclei on the basis of quality of both RNA and ATAC profiles, resulting in 1,025,329 nuclei with more than 85,000 nuclei per tumour on average (Methods, Fig. 1a and Extended Data Fig. 1b,c). We then annotated transcriptomic cell states in snRNA-seq data and examined ATAC data in a companion study to map GB gene regulatory networks12.

We integrated snRNA-seq data using scVI13 to account for batch variations, then distinguished malignant clusters on the basis of inferred copy number (CN) gain of chromosome (chr.) 7 and loss of chr. 10, as well as enrichment of known GB expression programs2 (Fig. 1b and Supplementary Figs. 2 and 3). Subclustering yielded 28 malignant clusters, including 10 highly common clusters present across 50% of the tumours, as well as 71 TME clusters (Fig. 1c and Supplementary Fig. 4).

We annotated malignant clusters by relating them to GB cell state gene programs described in ref. 2 and developing human brain single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) data14 as well as gene-set enrichment analysis (Methods and Supplementary Fig. 5a,b). As a result, we hierarchically grouped malignant clusters into four main classes and nine subclasses of GB cell states that were each observed across several tumours (Fig. 1c,d, Supplementary Fig. 4a and Supplementary Table 4).

Two main classes of GB cell states resembled distinct developmental progenitors: neural progenitor-like and oligodendrocyte progenitor-like (NPC-OPC-like) and neuronal progenitor-like and neuronal-like (NPC-neuronal-like) cells. These two dev-like states matched those previously described in ref. 2 and expressed respective developmental markers of oligodendrocyte (PDGFRA, OLIG1) and neuronal lineages (MYT1L, STMN2) (Fig. 1c and Supplementary Note 1).

The third main GB cell state showed a transcriptomic spectrum from astrocyte progenitor (AC-prog)-like to gliosis-like (that is, glial injury response) and hypoxic states, broadly expressing core astrocyte markers (SLC1A3, GFAP) (Fig. 1c). Whereas AC-prog-like cells showed Neftel ‘AC-like’ signatures and resembled developmental glioblasts, AC-gliosis and gliosis-like cells expressed genes related to wound healing and injury response (VIM, SERPINE1) and angiogenesis (VEGFA) and the remaining cells were defined by hypoxia (HILPDA) (Fig. 1c). The gliosis-hypoxic cells were initially described as mesenchymal-like states1,2 defined by Neftel ‘MES1-2’ programs. Recently, they were reinterpreted as more similar to reactive astrocytes responding to injury4 and glial wound healing states4,8. Here we adopted the latter nomenclature that better reflected malignant cellular trajectories in our atlas (sections below). The final main malignant state represented proliferative cells. Although dominated by G2M and S phase gene expression, we resolved that these cells represent actively cycling analogues of main GB cell states (Fig. 1c, Supplementary Fig. 6a and Supplementary Note 1).

GB cell states showed substantial inter-tumour and intra-tumour heterogeneity. Most tumours showed a dominant GB cell state among the main classes (for example, NPC-OPC-like for AT5 and 9) (Fig. 1d, left). However, despite their stratification, each tumour contained substantial fractions of both dev-like and AC-gliosis-hypoxia cells. Two tumours (AT4 and 10) showed near equal proportions of both classes, whereas in others, the minority states represented 5–21% of all malignant cells (Fig. 1d and Supplementary Table 4). Individual sampling sites also contained a mixture of GB states broadly reflecting the parent tumour (Supplementary Fig. 8b,c). Yet, we could often identify at least one site per tumour with a unique cell state composition. In a striking example, tumour AT10 showed distinct dominant GB cell states at each site (Fig. 1d, right). Consistent with other studies5,7,15, these observations show that single biopsies can be confounded to stratify GB tumour phenotypes.

We also captured all main cell lineages in the GB TME (Supplementary Figs. 4b and 7). Although OPCs, mature oligodendrocytes and myeloid cells were the most abundant, we also annotated fine-grained neurons, astrocytes, lymphocytes and vasculature (Supplementary Note 1). Taken together, our single-nuclei transcriptomic atlas presents a deep, fine-grained cellular census of malignant and TME states in GB.

Next, we examined the spatial organization of GB cell states. To resolve fine GB states in Visium ST data, we mapped malignant and TME clusters from each patient’s snRNA-seq profile to their matched Visium data using cell2location16 (Fig. 2a). Whereas integrating paired snRNA-seq and ST accounted for inter-tumour heterogeneity, it also enabled us to link GB spatial organization to malignant cell trajectories, subclonal organization and TME signalling that we subsequently inferred from snRNA-seq.

a, Workflow for identification of GB spatial TMs that recur across tumours. b, Distinct cellular compositions of recurrent GB TMs. The heatmap depicts the proportion of cell state abundance associated with a given tumour-specific NMF factor. Factors (columns) are ordered by their corresponding spatial microenvironment clusters (top colour bar). The most frequently observed cell states for each microenvironment are shown per row, in which black and blue text represents TME and malignant cells, respectively. c, TM abundances for several Visium ST sections showing key microenvironment distribution patterns in an intratumoural context (AT15) and across different tumours. d, Network diagram illustrating spatial proximity between recurrent TMs. Edge width and colour represent the mean pairwise Euclidean distance between microenvironment spots. e, Xenium sections depicting spatial maps of main cell states in tumour AT10.

GB cell states showed striking segregation across all tumours. In particular, gliosis and hypoxia cell states segregated from dev-like states (Extended Data Fig. 2), consistent with previous surveys10,15. GB states also showed regional heterogeneity across tumour sampling sites (Extended Data Fig. 2 and Supplementary Fig. 8c). We also observed concordant spatial mapping results between cell2location and alternative computational methods, especially for highly abundant GB cell states (Methods and Supplementary Fig. 10a–c).

We then asked whether GBs have a conserved spatial architecture. To determine whether malignant and TME cells assemble into stereotyped tissue microenvironments (TMs), we first identified spatially colocalized cell states (that is, microenvironments) per tumour by means of non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) of cell2location results16 (Fig. 2a and Methods). This resulted in 192 factors across our cohort (Supplementary Table 7 and Supplementary Fig. 11a), which we then clustered by their cell state similarity to identify 16 TMs that recurrently appear across tumours (Fig. 2b).

We annotated the recurrent GB TMs on the basis of their cellular composition and anatomical location (Fig. 2b,c and Supplementary Note 2). ‘Tumour’ TMs represented malignant, immune and vasculature states in the tumour core, whereas ‘infiltrated’ TMs spanned non-malignant neurons and glia in the surrounding infiltrated regions (Fig. 2b,c). Most tumour TMs were defined by their distinct GB cell state composition and appeared across many tumours (Extended Data Fig. 3). Core malignant TMs such as Dev-like (OPC), Dev-like (AC), Proliferative, Gliosis transition, Gliosis and Hypoxic 1 were detected in more than 50% of tumours, whereas others such as Dev-like (Neuron) and Hypoxic 2 were rare. Crucially, 8 out of 12 tumours (for example, AT3, AT10) showed nearly the full complement of core TMs (Extended Data Fig. 3a), suggesting these features are fundamental to GB organization. Finally, we recapitulated these TMs with cell2location alternatives on our GB atlas and on public GB Visium ST datasets10,15 (Methods and Supplementary Fig. 12).

Previous ST studies have mapped hypoxic ‘mesenchymal’-like states at the necrotic core and dev-like states at the infiltrating edge of tumours10,15. Correlating GB TMs with tumour anatomy showed Dev-like TMs occurred in the cellular tumour compartment bordering the infiltrating tumour and leading edge. By contrast, Gliosis and Hypoxia TMs were localized further from the infiltrating regions, forming layered zones around perinecrotic and necrotic areas (Fig. 2c, Extended Data Fig. 3a and Supplementary Note 2).

To quantify their precise spatial arrangement, we calculated the pairwise spatial proximities of GB TMs across all tumours (n = 97 Visium sections) into a network graph (Methods). This showed that GB TMs are ordered along a main anatomical axis between the infiltrating tumour edge and the necrotic tumour core (Fig. 2d). Dev-like (OPC) was found closest to infiltrated white matter. Dev-like (AC) spatially overlapped with the Dev-like (OPC), yet extended deeper into the tumour towards successive layers of Gliosis transition, Gliosis and Hypoxia (Fig. 2d). Dev-like (Neuron) was similarly positioned near the infiltrated regions when present (Fig. 2c). In tumour AT15 that we profiled in whole, these gradual transitions from dev-like TMs to gliosis and hypoxia were observed across each sampling site (Supplementary Fig. 13a,b).

We validated these observations with orthogonal 315-plex Xenium ST data (n = 17 sections from 8 tumours) annotated at the single-cell level by means of snRNA-seq integration (Methods). This validated malignant cell state zonation, in which dev-like states bordered infiltrated regions marked by neurons, contrasting with the gliosis and hypoxia states situated further around necrosis (Fig. 2e and Supplementary Fig. 13c). Profiling centimetre-scale tumour sections revealed this pattern at each sampling site (Fig. 2e), indicating stereotyped spatial organization throughout each tumour. Xenium also enabled us to validate the accuracy of cell2location predictions on GB data (Methods and Supplementary Fig. 14).

GB TMs also reflected TME organization. ‘Vasculature’ captured pericytes, VLMCs and endothelial cells, anatomically correlated with microvascular proliferation and hyperplastic blood vessels, and was found in close proximity to Dev-like (AC) and (OPC), Gliosis transition and Proliferative malignant TMs (Fig. 2b,d and Extended Data Fig. 3a). Two ‘Immune’ TMs captured distinct myeloid cell compartments (last section). Among infiltrated regions, ‘White matter’ was found in close proximity to tumour leading edge (Fig. 2c,d), consistent with being a main GB invasion route17,18,19.

Taken together, we reveal stereotyped stepwise spatial transitions of malignant cells from dev-like to gliosis and hypoxia states in GB.

We proposed that the stereotyped spatial transitions of GB states relates to their cellular trajectories. Specifically, we proposed that as GB tumours expand at their leading edge into normal brain tissue, the dev-like malignant cells progressively transition towards gliosis and hypoxia states. To test this, we first examined putative malignant trajectories related to gliosis and hypoxia.

In the snRNA-seq data, we observed an expression gradient of astrocyte, injury response and hypoxia-related genes through AC-gliosis-hypoxia states (Fig. 3a). The AC-prog-like states showed the highest levels of developmental and homeostatic astrocyte gene expression (EGFR, SLC1A3, AQP4, ALDH1L1). These were downregulated in AC-gliosis-like cells and replaced by a transcriptomic program resembling astrogliosis, including genes from the integrin–N-cadherin pathway (ITGAV, ITGB1, CDH2) associated with glial scar formation20. This program expanded in gliosis-like cells to genes associated with JAK–STAT signalling (JAK2, STAT3, SMARC4), wound healing (ANXA2, ANXA5, YAP1, F1, AKAP12), cytokine production (IFI16, IL6R, IL1R1) and coagulation (SERPINE1), as well as angiogenesis and hypoxia (VEGFA)21,22,23. This trajectory terminated in hypoxia (HILPDA, BNIP3L, VEGFA) and stress-response gene expression (JUN, FOS, HSPA1B) (Fig. 3a and Extended Data Fig. 4a). Transcriptome-wide pseudotime analysis produced consistent results (Methods and Supplementary Fig. 15).

Whereas they were previously thought to resemble mesenchymal cells2, we observed negligible and non-specific expression of key epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition regulators (for example, SNAI1/2, TWIST1/2, ZEB1/2) in gliosis-hypoxia states24,25 (Extended Data Fig. 4a). Hence, our nomenclature places these states in the more specific biological context of glial injury response and hypoxia, putatively stemming from developmental astrocyte-like malignant cells.

The molecular trajectory was correspondingly patterned in space, manifesting as concentric segregation of AC-gliosis-hypoxia states in ST data (Fig. 3b,c and Extended Data Fig. 4c). AC-prog-like cells resided in the non-necrotic cellular tumour in the Dev-like (AC) microenvironment. AC-gliosis-like and gliosis-like cells formed Gliosis transition and Gliosis microenvironments, respectively, that spatially intermixed to varying degrees. In tumours such as AT10, AC-gliosis-like was located at the margin of the cellular tumour and gradually transitioned into gliosis-like within the perinecrotic zone. Hypoxic cells were located either within or adjacent to the tumour necrotic core. The marker genes of these states showed consistent zonated expression with ST and immunohistochemistry (Fig. 3b and Extended Data Fig. 4b).

Taken together, we identify putative GB cellular transitions from developmental astrocyte-like to gliosis then hypoxia states, unfolding across an anatomical axis from tumour expansion towards hypoxia and necrosis (Fig. 3d).

To explore GB cellular transitions, we then asked whether dev-like and gliosis-hypoxic states could emerge within the same tumour subclones (that is, genetically related malignant sublineages). Initially, we performed copy number aberration (CNA) inference to our multiome data, jointly calling clones from tumour snRNA-seq and snATAC-seq profiles (Fig. 4a and Supplementary Note 3). Distinguished by chr. 7 and chr. 10 CNs, most tumour subclones contained both dev-like and gliosis-hypoxic cells (Fig. 4b and Supplementary Fig. 16b,c), with the minority states making up an average of 15% (ranging from 3% to 49%) of each clone. Whereas subclones tended to show similar GB state compositions, three tumours contained individual subclones with divergent states. For example, tumour AT10 clone 0 was marked by chr. 17p loss and chr. 17q gain and was preferentially enriched for NPC-neuronal-like states, whereas AT10 clone 1 was enriched for AC-gliosis-hypoxia (Fig. 4b).
