a, Total number of species detected with SNVs in each cohort before filtering. b, Total number of gut microbial SNVs detected in each cohort before filtering. c, Distributions of detected SNV numbers of each species in each cohort before filtering. d, Proportion of detected SNVs in the core region of each species in each cohort before filtering. e, Number of common SNVs in the core region of each species in each cohort before filtering. The distributions of common SNV numbers exhibit two peaks separated by approximately 1,000 SNVs (dashed horizontal line). For c–e, each data point represents one microbial species (n = 881 for all datasets combined, n = 879 for DMP, n = 879 for LLD1, n = 878 for LLD2-APK, n = 874 for LLD2-FSK, n = 878 for 500FG-APK, n = 875 for 500FG-FSK, n = 878 for 300OB, n = 880 for IBD, and n = 875 for 300TZFG). f, Numbers of gut microbial species with at least 1,000 common SNVs in each cohort after filtering. g, Total numbers of common gut microbial SNVs kept for each cohort after filtering. h, Distributions of common SNV numbers of each species in each cohort after filtering. i, Proportion of common SNVs in the core region of each species in each cohort after filtering. For h and i, each data point represents one microbial species (n = 433 for all datasets combined, n = 247 for DMP, n = 207 for LLD1, n = 240 for LLD2-APK, n = 248 for LLD2-FSK, n = 200 for 500FG-APK, n = 256 for 500FG-FSK, n = 243 for 300OB, n = 154 for IBD, and n = 327 for 300TZFG). The inner boxplots in c, d, e, h, and i show the summary statistics: the centre line represents the median, the box hinges represent the lower and upper quartiles of the distribution, whiskers extend no further than 1.5× interquartile range from the hinges, and data beyond the end of the whiskers are outliers plotted as individual points.

Proportion of SNV impact classes in each species (see key for impacts). Species are sorted by the total proportion of synonymous variants and non-protein-coding region variants.

Per-cohort linear mixed model association results were combined by meta-analysis, with study-wide significance defined as P < 5.42×10−11. Robust associations required nominal significance (Ppermutation <0.05) in two or more cohorts with consistent effect direction and confirmation by permutation testing (Ppermutation <0.05 in ≥ 2 cohorts). Linked SNVs (r² > 0.01 within 10 Mb) were grouped to yield independent signals. Numbers in blue indicate counts after each filtering step.

The bar plot shows the ratio of SNV impact category in the associated SNVs of each phenotype (number of associated SNVs >10), all phenotypes, and all common SNVs (background). Phenotypes are sorted by the ratio of start/stop codon variants and missense variants. The horizontal dashed red line is the reference line indicating the ratio of start/stop codon variants and missense variants in the background (0.176). The red “+” and blue “-” indicate significant enrichment and depletion, respectively, of start/stop codon variants and missense variants compared to the background SNVs (Two-sided Chi-squared test, P < 0.05). Significant enrichment was observed for Lifelines protein diet score (P = 2.01 × 10−4), on-a-diet behaviour during the past month (P = 1.09 × 10−10), thrombocyte count (P = 2.92 × 10−4), waist circumference (P = 0.0366), beta blocker intake (P = 0.0193), and sex (P = 0.0211). Significant depletion was observed for BMI (P = 0.0104), DBP (P = 0.0376), HbA1c (P = 0.0467), lymphocyte count (P = 0.00281), SBP (P = 0.00360), and body weight (P = 0.0357). P values were not adjusted for multiple comparisons.

The heatmap shows the phenotype and species pairs with SNV-level associations supported by at least one Dutch cohort and the Tanzanian cohort.

a, Number of significantly associated phenotype−species pairs at the different gut microbiome feature categories. b, Number of significantly associated species at the different gut microbiome feature categories for each phenotype.

Observed versus expected −log10(P) values for the association between age and microbial SNVs in F. prausnitzii_I (species ID: 102274). P values were obtained from two-sided linear mixed-model tests in each cohort followed by sample-size-weighted meta-analysis and are shown without multiple-testing adjustment. The shaded region indicates the 95% confidence interval expected under the null hypothesis. The genomic inflation factor (λ) is shown.

a, Distribution of the SNV 102274_1617247 genotype in the phylogenetic tree of F. prausnitzii_I across all samples. b, Heatmap shows the Spearman’s correlation coefficients between age-associated SNVs and SVs of F. prausnitzii_I (FDR < 0.05). c, Heatmap shows the P-values of association between SNVs and host age after adjusting for the associated SVs in each cohort (Ppermutation <0.05). P values were obtained using two-sided permutation-based linear mixed-model tests with 999 permutations; no multiple-testing adjustment was applied (Ppermutation <0.05).

a, Frequency of the alternative alleles for five age-associated SNVs in F. prausnitzii_I (species ID: 102274) across the six cohorts. b, Mean host age (years) across the six cohorts.

ΔG predictions (Kcal/mol) from the in silico docking analysis are shown for the wild-type (WT) protein and the age-associated mutant (MUT). Reference ligands: KAK, KWK, KKK, AAA, GFG, GAG, DED, and EEE. For each protein–ligand combination, n = 4 docked poses were analyzed. Horizontal and vertical dashes indicate the mean and standard deviation (SD), respectively.

Liverpool have been handed a major setback in their pursuit of Trent Alexander-Arnold, with Real Madrid reportedly determined to keep the England international beyond the January transfer window.

The former Liverpool defender has struggled to establish himself as a regular starter at the Spanish club, raising questions about his long-term future at the Santiago Bernabeu.

According to a report from Football Insider, Real Madrid have no intention of selling the 28-year-old despite growing speculation about a possible return to Anfield.

Alexander-Arnold has shown glimpses of his quality since leaving Liverpool in 2025, but he has struggled to reproduce the performances that made him one of Europe’s most creative defenders.

Manager Jose Mourinho has preferred Federico Valverde and Denzel Dumfries at right-back on several occasions this season, restricting the Englishman’s opportunities.

However, Mourinho is reportedly keen to retain the defender and believes he can still play an important role in the squad.

Alexander-Arnold is also determined to establish himself at the Spanish club after a difficult start to his career in Madrid. His recent return to the starting lineup against Racing Santander could help him build momentum.

This development will make it considerably harder for Liverpool to secure his signature in January.

The Reds have been linked with a reunion as they look to strengthen their right-back options. Jeremie Frimpong has struggled to convince, while Conor Bradley is recovering from a serious knee injury.

However, former Liverpool defender Glen Johnson has questioned whether bringing Alexander-Arnold back would be the right decision, suggesting that another disappointing spell could damage his legacy at Anfield.

It remains to be seen whether Liverpool will revisit the possibility next summer, but for now, a January reunion looks unlikely.

#1352. Pocognoli backs returning star McTominay to lead Scotland into new era

Published: 15:09 EDT, 3 November 2026 | Updated: 15:55 EDT, 3 November 2026

Scotland boss Sebastien Pocognoli has welcomed Scott McTominay back into the fold after heart surgery and revealed he’s banking on him to help kickstart a new era for the national team.

McTominay went through a minor operation to address mild benign arrhythmia in September and missed Pocognoli’s first Nations League camp as head coach.

However, having scored four times after returning to action at Italian outfit Napoli, the 29-year-old midfielder is back in the squad for this month’s double-header against North Macedonia and Switzerland.

Torino striker Che Adams, absent last time out due to a muscle strain, is also back in the fold while there is a first call-up for left-back James Penrice, currently on loan at Rangers from Greek side AEK Athens.

Celtic left-back Kieran Tierney returns after withdrawing from Pocognoli’s first squad while centre-back Scott McKenna misses out after reportedly picking up a back strain playing for Dinamo Zagreb. Josh Doig, Colby Donovan, James Wilson and Lennon Miller also drop out from Pocognoli’s debut matches.

Scott McTominay is fit and available for Scotland after minor heart surgery

Speaking while naming his squad at Hampden Park, Pocognoli emphasised the role McTominay will play – along with other senior stars – in helping bring through a new generation of stars under his guidance.

‘I have been in contact with Scott from the first day. He missed the first camp with some physical problem,’ stated the Belgian.

‘We were still in contact during the rehabilitation, when he came back on the pitch. He’s one of the captains, so there’s a special contact with them, but he’s looking forward to come, to play for us, to play in a different way, on the pitch and he is very positive, so that’s important.

‘There is plenty of experience back in the squad. With Scott, with Che, with Kieran. He’s also back, so, if you accumulate the caps, we have some experience that will be useful for this camp and to also embrace the young lads - because we still have a young squad with many players who don’t have a lot of caps.

‘I’m sure the mix will be good and these (experienced) players will also show the way for them.’

Sebastien Pocognoli has picked his squad to face North Macedonia and Switzerland

Scotland are third in Group B1 with four points from four games, three points behind Slovenia and eight behind runaway leaders Switzerland. The Scots host North Macedonia at Hampden on November 13 with a trip to Switzerland three days later.

With one eye on the forthcoming 2028 European Championship qualifying campaign, Pocognoli said: ‘I’m looking forward to working with everybody, but, for sure, we want to see most of the players just to have as much information as possible to start the qualification for the Euros.

‘All I want to do now is to get the most out of this, to know my squad as deeply as possible, to see the body language, the attitude of the players in some situations, and to have most of the information to start the big job.’

On the issue of a first call-up for 27-year-old former Hearts defender Penrice, Pocognoli said: ‘Like I said in the first camp, we have a list of players that we select regarding the performance at their clubs, but also the style of play or the way that we want to play.

‘We have some missing players around the left side, so, combined with his quality and what we are looking for on the pitch, it’s a logical choice for me. It can be very useful for the system that we want to play and also I think he deserves it.’

Arsenal are reportedly interested in signing Rangers youngster Kai Urban as Mikel Arteta’s side continues to strengthen their academy ranks with some of the most promising young talents in British football.

According to a report from Football Insider, the Gunners are keen on securing a deal for the 15-year-old right-back, who has impressed with his performances at youth level for the Scottish giants.

The North London outfit have made youth recruitment an important part of their long-term strategy, and Urban has now emerged as a potential addition to their Hale End academy.

#1350. Pierre Sage fears for his Crystal Palace future after Brighton humiliation

Pierre Sage has admitted that he fears for his future at Crystal Palace, adding that he felt “shame” after his side slumped to their joint-heaviest defeat by rivals Brighton and Hove Albion.

Sage replaced Oliver Glasner as manager in June but since then Palace have won just two league matches with him in at the helm. The south London club have taken seven points from seven Premier League games and have already conceded 17 goals, the most of any team in the league.

“I don’t know,” Sage said when asked if he will get enough time to rectify Palace’s slump. He admitted that his shame was about how Palace were overwhelmed, leaking three goals within the first nine minutes of the game before eventually losing 5-0.

“We are not at the level we expected, and I’m really sorry for that,” the 47-year-old said. “I just want to apologise to the fans because it’s not normal to show this face.”

The Frenchman said that he took full responsibility for the 5-0 defeat, and understood why hundreds of Palace fans left well before the final whistle.

“I cannot blame anybody because we didn’t do the job in a good way,” he said. “I’m responsible for this team, and when the team play as today, it’s not normal. It’s my fault. I understand them.

“Another feeling is about shame because that’s my feeling after the game and from the beginning. It’s not normal to not respect the necessary of this kind of game.”

Sage admitted that he will be assessing how Palace need to rethink their approach in the coming fixtures, beginning with Thursday’s trip to Besiktas in the Europa League.

“The first work to do is on me,” he said. “I’m responsible for what’s happened on the pitch, and I have a lot of work to do because I have to change this kind of thing.

“It’s maybe in the preparation, in the way we give them the motivation to start the game just before in the locker room in the warm-up. We have to analyse that because it’s not normal. And today it was really at the highest level we cannot expect, and that’s the moment to change the thing.”

For all the scrutiny on his back three, Sage urged his entire side to take greater defensive responsibility, highlighting how the team were too passive in pressing Brighton. Palace have struggled to regain the solidity that long characterised the side since the departures of Marc Guéhi in January and Maxence Lacroix this summer.

“The way of defending is not only on the back three; it is for every player, and there are some things to do collectively, too,” Sage said. “When we defend low we struggle a lot.”

Sage joined Palace after a fine campaign with Lens. He led the club to second place in Ligue 1, just six points off Paris St-Germain, and victory in the Coupe de France. Yet, despite Sage’s reputation when he moved to Selhurst Park, his suitability for the Palace job is increasingly being questioned.

Three years ago, Patrick Vieira lost his job after a defeat by Brighton. Now, Sage could suffer the same fate, with doubts growing that he will still be in charge for Thursday’s trip to Besiktas.

“It’s not my decision,” Sage said. “I don’t want to accept the level of the moment if we are able to do better. And today the work is really important to do, and I will do it. It’s my job, and I’d like to change this.”

With only Manchester City and Arsenal above them, Brighton and Hove Albion are entitled to dream of making history. Yet, whatever happens between now and May, one accolade is already surely their own: the goal of the season award.

Diego Gómez’s 56-yard strike will instantly become the stuff of Brighton lore. The Paraguayan’s audacity will be even more cherished for coming against Crystal Palace, who were pummelled 5-0 in the M23 derby.

All Premier League defeats are equal but some are more equal than others. Three years ago, Patrick Vieira lost his job after a defeat by Brighton. Now, Pierre Sage is at grave risk of suffering the same fate. Naturally, Brighton fans revelled in reminding him of this threat as the final whistle approached.Palace were so ragged that their performance felt like a defeat that marks the end of a managerial reign. Even stand-in captain Adam Wharton was guilty of dawdling and losing the ball in possession. Hundreds of away supporters left well before the full-time whistle and those who remained booed all players bar Jefferson Lerma.

With less venom in attack, especially with Ismaïla Sarr being an unused substitute, Palace’s sole chance lay in counter-attacking. This strategy disintegrated in the fourth minute, when Jaydee Canvot headed Pascal Gross’s free-kick into his own net.

Jaydee Canvot glances the ball into his own net and Brighton lead! 🔵 https://t.co/subm9ggwId

But the hint of self-immolation in Palace’s display should not obscure the swagger of Brighton’s performance. Despite losing Danny Welbeck, last year’s top scorer, Brighton have scored 23 goals already this Premier League campaign, the most in the league. This tally includes one of the most extraordinary goals in Premier League history.

Most simply, Gómez’s goal, which put Brighton 2-0 up in the seventh minute, was a triumph of the imagination. Receiving a short pass from Olivier Boscagli just inside his own half, Gómez could have sought to pick out a team-mate. Instead, his scanning of the pitch before receiving the ball had revealed that goalkeeper Walter Benítez was off his line and Brighton’s attacking players were being tightly guarded by defenders. And so, just as he entered the centre circle in the opposition half, Gómez attempted the absurd.

"Would you look at that!" DIEGO GOMEZ SCORES FROM THE HALFWAY LINE! 🤯 https://t.co/qmagVbGEb4

“I’m not training with Diego Gómez shooting from 50 metres in training,” head coach Fabian Hürzeler said while breaking into a smile. “It’s just about making the players quick in their minds.

“In these moments it’s about being very precise with his long kick. The perception to recognise the keeper and being quick to go to the action was impressive.”

The presence of mind to attempt something outlandish was one thing; the execution was quite another. With Benítez vulnerable, Gómez took just one touch with his right foot before taking his shot, not giving the keeper enough time to scramble back to cover his line. As he looked up to confirm the opportunity, the 23-year-old struck the ball over Benítez with such venom that it did not even bounce until it reached the goal.

All that remained was for the Paraguayan international to hurtle towards the corner flag, engulfed by his ecstatic team-mates. For the Brighton fans, soaked by showers at the Amex, rain can never have felt so sweet.

Gómez’s goal will earn comparisons with David Beckham’s lob from the halfway line at Wimbledon. The advancements in pressing and conditioning in the 30 years since, with space ever more congested, makes such a strike even harder today. Not since Wayne Rooney in 2017 has a player scored a Premier League goal from further out than Gómez’s 56 yards.

Gómez may well attempt an encore. He shot from even further out at the Stadium of Light a week ago. When October ends, three of the last four Premier League goal-of-the-month winners will be Brighton players. Alongside his meticulous emphasis on set-pieces, Hürzeler empowers flair in open play.

Brighton only need three-and-a-half minutes to get their opener: a Pascal Gross free-kick from the left-hand side, headed into his own net by Palace centre-half Jaydee Canvot. Just the tonic for the thousands of Brighton fans being soaked.

Jaydee Canvot glances the ball into his own net and Brighton lead! 🔵 https://t.co/subm9ggwId

Kadioglu sets the tone early on, snapping in to cut off a loose pass out from the back by Palace. The ball is eventually worked up to Kostoulas, but he cannot bring it under his spell.

The heavens have opened up at the Amex, but that has not dampened the stadium announcer’s enthusiasm. He announces each player to the fans, with Pascal “the Goat” Gross’ name receiving an especially hearty cheer from the crowd.

The players (all 22 starters, it seems) take a knee before Brighton get us started.

The clouds have come in and the rain has started at the Amex as kick-off approaches. A raucous atmosphere, as you’d expect for the M23 derby, with plenty of Brighton fans relishing singing anti-Crystal Palace songs on the way to the ground. Should Brighton win - as they will expect to - they will move second, at least until Arsenal play later.

Kick-off is almost upon us. There’s just about enough time to make a brew before the action begins...

Eighteen-year-old defender Honest Ahanor starts in Palace’s back three alongside Jaydee Canvot, 20, and Chris Richards, 26. This afternoon will be a decent examination of their credentials as a unit. The Italy defender is on loan from Atalanta and will join Chelsea next summer.

The police-to-fan ratio looks fairly healthy here...

Palace fans head to #Brighton Station more on @brightonargus https://t.co/LQ9MKobmFH

Brighton’s form is all the more impressive given that Hurzeler has not had recourse to key men in Yankuba Minteh, Kaoru Mitoma and Mats Wieffer.

Femi Azeez, signed from Millwall in the summer for £15m, has only featured in a friendly match during the international break and remains sidelined with a muscle issue.

These missing men are nearing returns, and it makes you wonder whether Brighton can reach even further heights.

There will be supporters of both sides who are not particularly moved by this match-up. Some Crystal Palace fans may argue that their rivalry with Nottingham Forest has been more intense in recent years.

When asked about the rivalry, Sage said: “I know that the fans don’t like this name [the M23 derby] because it is too far to name it this. We know it is a big game for the club and the fans, and we have to show our better phases, like the second halves of our last two games.”

Interestingly, the categories in which Brighton have excelled marry up almost perfectly with Crystal Palace’s weakest areas. Here are their numbers in the same/reciprocal departments:

Brighton’s fast start to the season has been evidenced by league-leading numbers in key departments, particularly in the attacking third.

"I have to give a lot of credit to my players" Fabian Hürzeler discusses Brighton's blistering start to the season 👏 https://t.co/o92tBqBO9i

So the video below, released on Thursday, has caused quite a stir on social media, generating in excess of 10 million views.

What is it? Well, I have been reliably advised that this is a take on a social media trend where implausible, dystopian AI videos are set to the song Storm II by GENER8ION featuring Yung Lean (don’t worry, me neither).

While some may argue that Palace’s roller-coaster 2025-26 season was at times dystopian (just ask Marc Guéhi or Oliver Glasner), the Europa League trophy is very much real. No AI needed here.

Crystal Palace. 26/27 squad. https://t.co/1SkWVPxyK1

Crystal PalaceSept 12: Crystal Palace 2 Ipswich Town 3Sept 17: Crystal Palace 4 Lech Poznan 0 (Europa League) Sept 20: Leeds United 0 Crystal Palace 0Oct 11: Crystal Palace 3 Nottingham Forest 1Oct 15: Lyon 3 Crystal Palace 2 (Europa League)

Pascal previews today's test... 💬 https://t.co/Cgj4APvfi4

"We have to play with passion and energy" Régis Le Bris speaks ahead of Sunderland's visit to Bournemouth 🎙️ https://t.co/KgWfOi4Pt5

Palace have conceded in the first 20 minutes of three of their six league games this season, and within the first 10 minutes in their last two outings.

It is a concern Sage acknowledged in his pre-match press conference: “It’s difficult to explain… We just have to put altogether the conditions to start well to make a good game in the whole of this one [against Brighton]. I think we are able to do it, we did it in Leeds, now we are in this situation.

“We are aware of what’s happened in these two games [against Forest and Lyon], one was a good result, one was a bad result, but in each game, when we are 100 per cent on what we have to do in our gameplan, I think we are able to do really wonderful things. When we are not like this, it is another story.”

Brighton have played against 10 men twice this season but were consigned to that very fate last weekend at the Stadium of Light.

Having gone ahead through De Cuyper, Struijk was given his marching orders (a decision that has since been overturned on appeal) and the visitors were made to show a different side to their character, battling in a deep block and frustrating Sunderland before adding a second.

"Today it's up to us" Marco Rose is hoping for Bournemouth's first league win of the season 🍒 https://t.co/VoNR9VfCOd

Pascal Gross may be 35 years old, but he is enjoying one of the finest seasons of his career, creating the most chances in the Premier League. Of his midfield talisman, Hurzeler said: “It started in pre-season. During pre-season he’s never the person who can lay on the beach for several hours doing nothing…

“He really suffered in pre-season. In pre-season you really build a foundation for the whole season, you build a physical foundation, a resilience, you build also the mindset… How he came back after this break was impressive. He looked so fit, so sharp, so ready… We saw a different face from him already and then it’s just a progression for him on the pitch…

“Of course no one expected it would be that good, but shows that he still has all this capacity in his body.”

Neither Brobbey nor Isidor make the match-day squad, so it will be up to 21-year-old Tutyerov to lead the line for Sunderland.

Sunderland: Roefs; Mukiele, Danso, Alderete, Reinildo; Xhaka, Sadiki; Hume, Rigg, Le Fee; Tutierov

Sage also makes one tweak to his starting complement, replacing Lerma with Ahanor.

Sarr, who returned against Lyon in midweek, makes the bench. Henderson remains sidelined.

Your Palace this afternoon! ❤️💙 https://t.co/53K9Kk0Cvb

Just the one change to the XI that started at Sunderland as Dunk replaces Struijk at the heart of Brighton’s defence.

TEAM NEWS! 🚨 How we start 🆚 Palace... ✊ https://t.co/5rhqp66u4S

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of the M23 derby – or El Gatwicko, as the kids call it these days – as high-flying Brighton and Hove Albion host Crystal Palace at the Amex Stadium. Being frank, this is neither the fiercest nor the most storied Premier League rivalry, but few would have imagined when these sides faced off in the Third Division in the mid-1970s that this would ever become a top-flight match-up sandwiched between European games.

Brighton have been outstanding this season and took their league form into the Conference League, thrashing Lithuanian champions Kauno Zalgiris on Thursday night. Fabian Hürzeler was delighted by his fringe players’ performances on Thursday night and may have some selection questions to answer with Jack Hinshelwood and Georginio Rutter finding the net. Brighton are third in the Premier League and were the division’s heaviest scorers after the last round of matches.

Yet the Palace nut has been a tough one to crack for Hürzeler, having not yet registered a win in four attempts. When asked what he enjoyed most about the rivalry, the German said: “Nothing yet, because I didn’t win any games so far. Hopefully on Sunday this changes… I like these games because they’re derbies, more emotions, it’s a rivalry, it’s [us] against Crystal Palace.”

In his pre-match interview Hürzeler admitted to being an admirer of Pierre Sage, and while the Frenchman’s side have failed to match Brighton’s fast start, they rallied impressively to defeat rivals Nottingham Forest last weekend and fought back valiantly away at Lyon, albeit in a losing effort, in midweek. The return of Ismaïla Sarr from injury is a significant boost.

Elsewhere Bournemouth host Sunderland hoping to secure their first Premier League victory of the season. Marco Rose’s side and Tottenham are the only teams still without a win, but Bournemouth have been perfect in the Europa League and will look to transfer some of that momentum into the league. Sunderland scored late to win away at Portuguese side Torreense.

You can also follow the latest updates from Manchester United’s crucial trip to Elland Road in our sister blog here.

#1349. A conserved flowering-time module underlies double-season cropping

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Adapting crops to intensive cultivation systems under climate change requires varieties that combine yield potential with optimized flowering and maturation1,2. In central and eastern China, barley has long been cultivated in a double-season cropping system, in which early flowering and maturation are critical for escaping presummer terminal heat stress and enabling flexible rotation with summer crops3,4. Here we trace the genomic footprints of 80 years of modern breeding in China using 505 representative cultivars and identify a flowering-time module defined by a single amino acid substitution in PHYTOCHROME C in combination with a winter-type VERNALIZATION 1 haplotype that underpins this adaptation. The derived allele accelerates heading and maturity, and its frequency has risen sharply in modern autumn-sown varieties. Using base editing in barley and wheat, we confirm causality and demonstrate that this flowering-time combination module, PhyC–VRN1, is functionally conserved across Triticeae. Our results identify and experimentally validate a breeding-relevant flowering-time module that has been selected during modern breeding to enable intensive crop rotations, as well as demonstrate how precision genome editing can be used to reconstruct such adaptive modules for climate-resilient crop design.

The photoreceptor PhyC functions as an upstream flowering regulator in grass species, promoting the expression of the photoperiodic responser PHOTOPERIODIC 1 (PPD1) and the flowering inducer FT1 (VERNALIZATION 3)21,22,23. The ancient haplotype PhyC-l, in combination with the winter-type vrn-H1 allele that requires vernalization, delays the transition from vegetative to reproductive growth, thereby preventing flowering (2nd panel, blue). In contrast, the spring-type Vrn-H1 variant, which carries a truncation in the first intron of VRN-H1 and eliminates the need of vernalization, enable flowering without cold exposure (1st panel, yellow). This allele in conjugation with PhyC-l is commonly adapted to spring-sown regimes in high-latitude or high-altitude regions. The East Asian-specific PhyC-e variant, which carries an F380S substitution at the PhyC locus and is consistently associated with winter-type vrn-H1 allele, promotes early flowering and supports adequate biomass accumulation (3rd panel, pink). The PhyC-e + vrn-H1 module allows barley to escape terminal heat stress, safeguard final yield, and fit to double-season cropping systems by leaving sufficient time for subsequent crops. This module has been widely selected in China’s Yangtze River basin. Notably, the haplotype combination PhyC-e + Vrn-H1 was not detected in barley natural germplasm (4th panel, dashed line). In this study, this novel module was generated either by base editing or by linkage breaking in the near-isogenic lines (NILs). It resulted in extremely early flowering and maturity, significantly reduced biomass, and undetected grain yield. This module holds potential for application in regions with extremely short growing seasons, such as those at very high latitudes or altitudes and at subtropical zones.

#1348. Mikel Arteta reveals Arsenal have a 'massive library' of videos showing rivals pulling shirts - as he hits back after Alexander Isak controversy

Published: 15:50 EDT, 3 November 2026 | Updated: 16:22 EDT, 3 November 2026

Mikel Arteta has revealed he has a ‘massive library’ of video footage showing other teams pulling shirts - having last month disclosed he is keeping a similar dossier of other Premier League managers leaving their technical area.

Arsenal defender Jurrien Timber escaped punishment for making contact with Alexander Isak in Arsenal’s 1-0 victory over Liverpool on Sunday.

Timber tugged Isak’s shirt as the striker went to head the ball towards goal, but referee Andy Madley did not award a foul and VAR decided against recommending an on-field review. The decision has since been widely scrutinised.

When asked if there is now a danger referees will change tack and give penalties for and free-kicks for the offence, Arteta said: ‘Yeah, I have a lot of clips about shirt pulls and grabs.

‘I have a massive library that we can talk about. I have a massive library that we can (put out) there to remind everybody what every team is going through.’

Liverpool boss Andoni Iraola and captain Virgil van Dijk were outraged when they weren't awarded a penalty after Jurrien Timber pulled back Alexander Isak

Now Mikel Arteta has claimed he is keeping a dossier of similar incidents of shirt pulling which has gone unpunished

Last month Arteta claimed his touchline behaviour is punished far more harshly than that of other Premier League managers and said he had clips of his counterparts breaching their own technical areas as evidence.

‘I do have to be careful, and we need to have good sensors there,’ Arteta said after being booked during Arsenal's 2-0 win over Everton.

‘There are managers that have the record in the league - 36 times in 10 minutes leaving the touchline, no yellows.

‘So I'm clipping all of that. I have a massive storage of images. So if somebody is going to say, “I'm not in the record yet, somebody else has the record”, then it's 36 yellow cards in 10 minutes for the (other) manager.

Arteta also revealed William Saliba is ready to make his first appearance since sustaining a back injury in July as he pushes to feature against Slavia Prague on Wednesday.

Saliba played 45 minutes in behind-closed-doors friendly last week and was part of Arsenal’s travelling squad for their Champions League fixture in Prague.

The 25-year-old also took part in full training this morning for the first time since picking up a back injury in France's World Cup semi-final loss to Spain in July.

Arsenal have coped well without him, with summer signing Ezri Konsa forming an impressive partnership with Gabriel. The Gunners have conceded only five goals in nine Premier League games, which is the best defensive record in the division.

William Saliba is back in contention for the Gunners after missing the start of the season with a back injury sustained at the World Cup

Arteta said: ‘He's in a really good place. I think the timings and the manner that the injury has been dealt with, and especially the feelings that Willy has been having along the way, have been very, very positive.

‘He feels very comfortable, he played 45 minutes behind closed doors last week and he feels ready to go. So whether we use him or not now is a matter of what the team needs.

‘All the preparation has been done to measure all the loads and minimise the risk. Now he's in a really good place, he's built the capacity that we needed and now it's about giving him minutes.’

On how eager Saliba is to play, he added: ‘I think he's very desperate and very loved, because William is somebody that is admired and very liked around the team.

‘Every time he's around, he creates something special. That's William, that's his nature. He's around the team now, and we need to give him the right moment, the right amount of minutes, and hopefully that's going to be very soon.’

Everton are reportedly interested in signing Minnesota United striker Kelvin Yeboah during the January transfer window as David Moyes looks to strengthen his attacking options.

The Toffees have identified the Italian forward as a potential addition, with his impressive performances in Major League Soccer attracting attention from several European clubs.

According to a report from Football Insider, Everton are prepared to make a move for the 26-year-old, with sources describing a deal as realistic. The Merseyside club believe Yeboah could represent a relatively affordable option compared to other attacking targets in the European market.

Yeboah has been in excellent form for Minnesota United, scoring 18 goals and providing four assists in 32 MLS appearances this season. His goalscoring record has understandably attracted interest, and a return to European football could be an attractive opportunity for the striker.

#1346. Slow and dull Man Utd are just not good enough

Manchester United are like John Toshack’s duvet. You fix one problem – being far too vulnerable to conceding goals – only to create another – lacking the threat to score. It is all very Meh United not Man United. The indisputable fact is they are just not very entertaining to watch. They are slow and dull.

In the end it also points to another thing. The thing highlighted in midweek by Lisandro Martínez after the Champions League defeat at Atlético Madrid: they do not have the strength in depth to compete.

What they do have appears to not be fit for purpose. Certainly Michael Carrick, the under-pressure manager, is struggling to get the best out of the resources he has.

“It’s like a duvet,” Toshack, the former Real Madrid and Wales manager, famously said of football. “If you pull it up, your feet get cold. If you pull it down, your shoulders get cold.”

There will have been times in the last few days, with the intense criticism and scrutiny over his future, when Carrick will have simply felt like dragging that duvet up over his head and keeping it there.

Defeat by Leeds United would have been unthinkable. It would have put Carrick under potentially intolerable pressure in what appears to be a pivotal week, with Como away in the Champions League and a home Premier League fixture against Bournemouth in the coming days.

Was this a lifeline or the tightening of the noose for Carrick? Time will soon tell. The relief of avoiding defeat was tempered by the reality of it now being just one win in their opening seven league games – at home to newly promoted Ipswich Town – and they are down in 13th place. It is six games without a win in all competitions.

That is unacceptable and is their fewest number of league victories in a top-flight campaign since 1986-87. Back then they sacked their manager in November and brought in a certain Alex Ferguson.

The hard truth is Carrick needs to start collecting some “Ws” in those results columns. United are already 14 points behind leaders Manchester City and five outside the probable Champions League places. Qualifying again for that tournament must be the minimum expectation.

Ruben Amorim, Carrick’s predecessor, lost his job within 24 hours of the same 1-1 scoreline at Elland Road last season – dismissed after Martínez-like explosive comments again aimed at director of football Jason Wilcox. Carrick will not suffer the same fate after this, but the ice is becoming increasingly thin.

We have seen this movie before at United. A slow start to the season, a period of drift, falling out of contention, no reaction on the pitch, backing from the hierarchy that becomes increasingly unconvincing. And then a change.

Can Carrick, who genuinely does still retain support at the highest level, alter that pattern? Does he have it in him? Is he too passive like his team? Carrick said this draw felt like a “fresh start”, but on this evidence that comment can be classified as wildly optimistic.

Having directed his criticism at the United hierarchy, and specifically Wilcox, the former Leeds winger who was here, over a lack of summer signings, Martínez apologised and was named in the starting XI. But the Argentine only lasted to half-time, withdrawn injured with a tight thigh, and sat watching the second half with his hood up over his head.

What United did sign in the last window was three midfielders – at a cost of £155m – and all three started: Carlos Baleba alongside Andrey Santos with Youri Tielemans in the No 10 role, which meant Bruno Fernandes was pushed out to the left, from where he constantly wanted to come in-field, with Amad Diallo on the right.

Carrick talked of having a “fresh spine” as well as that fresh start. But it did not make for a potent combination even if, further forward, Bryan Mbeumo played through the middle and scored one. He should have scored another.

Bryan Mbeumo finds the net this time to put Manchester United 1-0 up at Leeds! 🔴 https://t.co/NKDIhlUND1

But beyond that United created little. “It was a dominant performance against Man United,” Daniel Farke, the Leeds manager, claimed. He was right. If one team deserved to win it was his. They had the chances but snatched at them with Anton Stach, in injury time, having a weak shot cleared off the line by Martínez’s replacement Noussair Mazraoui after a mistake by goalkeeper Senne Lammens. Stach had to score.

United were ahead at half-time. Mbeumo had headed wastefully wide when unmarked but did well to force his way past James Justin and meet a low cross from Tielemans to poke the ball home. The way the usually undemonstrative Carrick punched the air in his technical area showed the pressure he felt. It was something to build on. To gain control.

Leeds had started well but did not really pose much of a threat – beyond forcing Lammens to save well from Nico Elvedi’s downward header – and maybe the earlier kick-off subdued the crowd. This was far from a bear pit.

But after the break, Leeds were comfortably the better side. The nature of their equalising goal, with Dominic Calvert-Lewin too strong and alert for first Baleba and then Mbeumo to fire in from a corner, exposed the enduring softness at the heart of United.

Dominic Calvert-Lewin equalises for Leeds against Manchester United 👊 https://t.co/mnpyxZJKbm

And that must be addressed by Carrick, especially as he appeared to sacrifice attacking intent by shoring up defensively. But that duvet is looking far too inadequate right now. Or Carrick is making it appear so.

Michael Carrick says he has put on “the headphones” this week in an effort to drown out the noise, but admitted Manchester United have to stop their struggles from snowballing.

United sit just two points above the relegation zone after a 1-1 draw at Leeds left them with just one win from their opening seven Premier League matches.

Carrick claimed the result felt like a “fresh start” after a week in which Lisandro Martínez publicly apologised for criticising Jason Wilcox, the United director of football, and the Old Trafford board.

But the United manager acknowledged their position “doesn’t look too good” and that they must start winning soon to stop the club from entering another doom cycle.

“Listen, we’re not accepting it as everything’s great by any stretch, so I’m realistic with that,” said the United manager, who claimed “the headphones have been on this week”.

“But sometimes you do struggle, sometimes there’s a bit of it where you have to find a way through it. We haven’t really had to go through that yet [before now] and we have to find a way through it.

“There has been a cycle at times here over a period of time when it can go in different directions. We’ve got to be stable enough to keep doing the right things for the right reasons as a group, and we’re more than capable of winning football matches.

“I understand the situation doesn’t look too good if you look at it from a certain way, but I’ve no doubts we can go on a good run.”

United face Como in the Champions League in Italy on Wednesday before Bournemouth visit Old Trafford four days later.

Carrick said he remains convinced United can still have a strong campaign, despite their worst start to a season for 40 years. I know what we’ve got in the changing room, where we want to get to, how we want to get there,” he said. “We know we can do it.

“We’ve done it for some time, and we feel we’re a better group now, and I do feel that. Sometimes it doesn’t always show, but you get a feeling and I’m encouraged by a lot of things. And if we keep doing the right things, I think we can still have a really good season.”

Asked if he would be putting the headphones back on this week ahead of two more pivotal games, Carrick added: “Nah, it’s always quiet for me.”

Martínez was substituted at half-time at Elland Road with a tight thigh just days after his tirade at club executives and Marcus Rashford was left out for “purely tactical” reasons. “Nothing personal, the front players were doing a good job on and off the ball,” Carrick said. “Everyone is ready for Wednesday.”

The Leeds boss told Sky Sports: “We are slightly disappointed it is just a point. Overall, I felt it was not necessary to be losing at half time but it is still Manchester United. Second half, we got the equaliser, we should have kept up the dominance, too many strikes went over the crossbar but it was overall a solid performance. We should have won the game but we move on.

“We took it as a compliment that we have done many things right over the last month if we were seen as favourites against Manchester Untiedbut we have earned this. We wanted to prove the comments right.

“We were the dominant side but we couldn’t capitalise as we lacked quality in and around the box.

“It says a lot about how much respect we have earned. Overall, this is where we are at the moment and overall, it is a good place to be.

“It is still difficult in this league to win points. You have to be clinical and be very, very effective but we have to keep going.”

Speaking to Sky Sports, he said: “I think we could’ve played with a bit more quality in the final third, particularly in the first half. We were getting good quality in the box but just not enough numbers.

“We made sure in the second half we came out with more confidence going forward. I think we were unlucky not to win the game.

“They tried to [match us up formation-wise]. Not surprised given what happened last season. They were probably looking at our physical output and the way we liked to play and tried to go man-for-man.

“It took us a little bit to adjust to it, but I don’t think it was too difficult to adjust. It was more down to us and maybe a lack of quality in the final third.”

Brighton & Hove Albion 5 Crystal Palace 0

It’s all over at Elland Road, with Leeds and Man Utd playing out a competitive draw. Mbeumo’s opener was cancelled out by Calvert-Lewin’s equaliser in a game that was low on attacking quality and chances. Ultimately, a draw was a very fair reflection of the match. Man Utd are 14th and winless in six games across all competitions, while Leeds move into the top seven.

FULL-TIME: Dominic Calvert-Lewin earns a point for Leeds against Manchester United 💪 https://t.co/yDzLRE3Ir5

There are two yellow cards in quick succession as Ampadu is cautioned for a late tackle on Amad. Andrey Santos runs over and barges into the Leeds captain to earn himself a booking. The referee quickly calms then drama down.

Unconvincing goalkeeping from Lammens as he only punches Ampadu’s cross as far as Stach, whose tame shot squeezes through the Belgian’s legs. However, it’s blocked by the Man Utd defence and Lammens eventually gathers the ball.

There will be four minutes of added time. Can either side snatch a late victory?

Three times now United have looked like they’re about to get away down the flanks in the last few minutes and each time they’ve been flagged offside (Amad twice, Mbeumo once) and each occasion the player was able to look across the line. Carrick looked to the heavens. And he’s right to be frustrated. So avoidable.

Nmecha and Maguire challenge for the ball in the air, with the Man Utd defender bumping into the back of the Leeds substitute’s head. The crowd half-heartedly appeal for a penalty, but it’s quickly checked and cleared by VAR.

Carrick responds with a positive, attacking switch as Tielemans departs for Cunha.

Farke makes another change for Leeds as Longstaff replaces Tanaka in midfield.

Excellently goalkeeping from Trafford, who dashes out of his six-yard box to collect Andrey Santos’ pass and keep the ball in his grasp while staying in his box under the watchful eye of Mbeumo.

Dalot drives forward and leads a counter-attack. He passes to Amad, who forces a corner as Leeds get back well and recover. Man Utd take a clever short corner routine, but it ends with Mount scuffing an effort wide.

Gudmundsson’s searching cross can’t quite find Calvert-Lewin as Man Utd scramble it clear. The away side’s backline has three defenders playing out of position, and they’ve been made to pay by Leeds’ leveller.

Passionately speak about what someone else at your football club is doing wrong – particularly the unloved executives – and cast yourself as a whistleblower, selflessly exposing the truth that the long-suffering supporters deserve.

Such internal fights make for great drama, unless your own club is caught in the middle of it.

That’s why in the immediate aftermath of Martínez’s scathing comments about Jason Wilcox following the Champions League defeat by Atlético Madrid, there was a division between those who celebrated the Argentine speaking out and those who felt it was self-serving, a convenient deflection by an out-of-form player in the final year of his contract.

The narrative is completely dominated by the drama around Man Utd, which should suit Leeds perfectly. All eyes and pressure is on their opponents, and they have every reason to feel confident ahead of this huge clash at Elland Road.

Just 10 months on from Ruben Amorim’s final game in charge of Manchester United, the club return to Elland Road on Sunday afternoon with another manager under pressure and the director of football again in the spotlight.

The difference is Michael Carrick still has a chance to determine the course of his United future whereas Amorim had already sealed his fate after a furious bust-up with Jason Wilcox 48 hours before his last game ended in a 1-1 draw with Leeds and post-match fireworks.

But even for a club never far from a crisis, it seems remarkable to think they are back in a tailspin so soon after Amorim’s sacking in early January.

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of this mouthwatering Premier League fixture between Manchester United and Leeds United at Elland Road.

Quiet week in the world of Man Utd? Don’t be silly. Following a 2-0 defeat in the Champions League against Atlético Madrid in Spain on Wednesday, defender Lisandro Martinez launched an extraordinary attack on Man Utd’s director of football Jason Wilcox and the club’s hierarchy because of a dreadful start to the campaign, which has yielded two victories in nine games across all competitions.

The Argentine criticised Man Utd’s recruitment and said he expected more, but didn’t suggest Carrick was to blame. Martinez has since apologised for his outburst and met with Wilcox, Man Utd chief executive Omar Berrada and Michael Carrick, with Telegraph Sport understanding that he’s free to play today, although his role remains unclear as we all eagerly await the team news.

Carrick is under immense pressure to get a result here in Yorkshire, with last weekend’s 1-1 draw with 10-man Tottenham at Old Trafford condemning Man Utd to their worst league start for 40 years.

With all eyes on the visitors, Leeds will be licking their lips at the prospect of piling further misery on their beleaguered opponents. Daniel Farke’s side suffered their first Premier League loss last weekend, falling 2-1 to Arsenal at the Emirates after going a goal up, but the mood remains positive after a solid start to the campaign.

Leeds are eighth and the club will be harbouring ambitions of a top-half finish in the Premier League for the first time since the 2019/20 season, with the prospect of qualifying for European football not out of the realm of possibility.

Unlike Man Utd, Leeds have a settled, reliable system that clearly suits their current squad. Elland Road will also be a cauldron of hostility and noise, given the fierce backdrop between these two bitter rivals.

This has all the ingredients to be a thrilling and fascinating watch as we bring you the latest updates, information and drama. Kick-off is at 14:00, with team news coming shortly.

#1345. Oxlade-Chamberlain isn't the first big name to flop in Scotland... Five superstars who failed to make their mark in the Scottish top-flight

Published: 15:47 EDT, 3 November 2026 | Updated: 16:34 EDT, 3 November 2026

Alex Oxlade-Chamberlain's inability to nail down a starting slot in a struggling Celtic side has reinforced the theory that the hard and physical Scottish Premiership is not exactly a place for former English Premier League stars to head to in their twilight years with a view to coasting through to retirement.

Oxlade-Chamberlain arrived at Parkhead back in January with a sparkling CV that boasted a full house of domestic trophies in England plus a Champions League win and 35 international caps from spells at Southampton, Arsenal and Liverpool.

The 33-year-old has been unable to nail down a regular spot at Celtic Park, though, and was given a rare start at the weekend in the champions’ 2-0 loss away to Falkirk.

Here, in a Daily Mail Sport special, we look at five other big-name stars who have failed in Scotland in the wake of enjoying successful careers south of the border.

Arsenal legend Wright’s best days were long behind him when then Celtic manager John Barnes brought him in as a replacement for the injured Henrik Larsson up front during the 1999-2000 season.

Wright had been a sensation during his seven years at the Gunners, winning a full house of domestic trophies plus a European Cup-Winners’ Cup, but he’d been on loan at Nottingham Forest from West Ham before heading for Glasgow and was clearly over the hill at the age of 35.

He made 10 appearances in total during a short-lived spell that involved a 4-2 Old Firm loss and that infamous 3-1 Scottish Cup loss to Inverness Caledonian Thistle that led to Barnes’ departure.

Wright also left soon after for Burnley and admitted the entire affair left a mark.

He told the BBC: ‘I felt I was caught up in a war crisis in Kosovo not involved in a football result that wrecked John Barnes' career as Celtic manager.

'Some so-called fans, a few morons who know nothing better, covered my car in spit. They were shouting obscenities at myself and Regi Blinker.’

The former England midfielder had carved his reputation in the English Premier League during stays at Manchester City, Newcastle United and Queens Park Rangers and arrived at Rangers in September 2016 on a two-year deal after inspiring Burnley to promotion from the Championship.

His time in Glasgow, however, proved to be a short-lived train wreck. He left in the wake of having his contract cancelled after eight games and 133 days.

English midfielder Joey Barton did not impress in his short spell at Rangers

Barton arrived, aged 34, blowing his own trumpet and aiming verbal volleys at then Celtic’s Scott Brown, but his stay very quickly unravelled and involved a 5-1 Old Firm humbling in the east end of Glasgow in which he was targeted by the Parkhead midfielder.

In the aftermath, a training-ground bust-up involving Andy Halliday saw Barton told to stay away from Rangers by manager Mark Warburton and later hit with a three-week suspension.

It was the beginning of the end. His contract was cancelled in November.

The controversial Dane had earned a move to Spanish giants Real Madrid following five great years at Everton and arrived at Celtic from the Bernabeu on a three-year contract in August 2006 on a fee said to be in the region of £2million.

Gravesen did score a couple of goals against Rangers during his time in Glasgow, but never delivered the kind of performances required and failed to hold down a regular spot in the side by the end.

Thomas Gravesen was unimpressive at Celtic and clashed with manager Gordon Strachan

He played just 22 times before returning to Everton on a loan deal in August 2007. When the Goodison outfit refused to extend that arrangement, an agreement was struck to release him from his deal at Parkhead and he duly retired from playing.

Gravesen was hugely critical of then manager Gordon Strachan in later interviews.

‘Unfortunately, I ran into an opposition to myself in the form of a coach called Gordon Strachan. It did not work between him and me,’ he said.

‘Gordon was a defensively-minded coach of a world famous club. I could not understand why he did as he did at Celtic because we were so much better than the other teams. He was nervous about losing.’

The Welshman had won three FA Cups during a spell at Arsenal in addition to a Serie A title with Juventus when arriving on loan at Rangers from the Italian outfit in January 2022.

Rangers’ then sporting director Ross Wilson was quick to publicise his role in pulling the deal together and insisted it had sent a ripple of excitement through the dressing room at the Ibrox outfit.

However, Ramsey was unable to live up to expectations during the 13 appearances he made and was often battling fitness issues. He will be forever remembered for missing the decisive penalty-kick in the Europa League final shoot-out against Germans Eintracht Frankfurt in Seville after being sent on as a substitute by boss Giovanni van Bronckhorst late in extra-time.

Ramsey missed a penalty in Europa League final

Ramsey later told Four Four Two magazine: ‘I just wish that I’d played longer in the final. I felt I could have brought something different to the table had I come on a bit earlier.

‘I was essentially brought on solely to take a penalty in the shoot-out, which I’m not sure is the best idea. That played on my mind as I went to take it, instead of being clear about where I wanted to put it. I’m still gutted that I missed that penalty and gutted for the fans that we couldn’t lift the trophy for them.

'I was really excited to go to Rangers. I had a couple of injuries during my time there, which made it difficult to get into any kind of rhythm. I [also] had a horrible case of Covid shortly before I signed, which meant I didn’t arrive in the best shape and it was no surprise that my body broke down.’

The little midfielder had won the World Cup with Brazil before arriving at Celtic in 2004. He had become a legend at Middlesbrough, where he had three spells as a player.

He’d been the subject of a £13million move to Atletico Madrid following his first spell in England and there remains a theory that he never quite recovered from a broken leg suffered in Spain in a match against Celta Vigo.

Juninho actually started well at Parkhead by stepping into the heat of an Old Firm derby and delivering a fine display as Martin O’Neill’s side recorded a one-goal win.

Celtic fans did not see the best of Juninho

However, it quickly became clear he was a shadow of his former self and quickly slid onto the substitutes’ bench under O’Neill. By January, it had become clear he just wasn’t settling in and an agreement was made to release him from his contract after seven months and just 14 starts.

‘It was an awkward situation, and an especially frustrating one for me,’ recalled Juninho in later years.

‘I ended up in Scotland, but things didn’t really work out for me. I had this issue with Martin O’Neill and his tactics. I still can’t understand why he wanted me at Celtic. He used to play with a 4-4-2 and he asked me to play out wide with defensive responsibilities, but this was never my style. It didn’t suit me and he knew it.

‘Maybe inside his head, he wasn’t looking for the Juninho of the 90s and maybe I’m to blame for that, but a manager should know a player’s style.’

#1344. Synergy in viral–bacterial co-infection expedites algal bloom demise

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Algal bloom demise, often caused by viruses, is a major driver of carbon cycling in the surface ocean1,2. However, although blooms collapse synchronously, fewer than 30% of algal cells are actively infected by viruses3, indicating the involvement of additional mortality agents. Here we quantified tripartite interactions within a synthetic community composed of the abundant coccolithophore Gephyrocapsa huxleyi, bacteria and viruses isolated during a bloom. We found that bacteria significantly enhanced virus-induced algal mortality in G. huxleyi as well as in three other globally widespread microalgae. We quantified this interaction using two new metrics: the synergy index, which measures viral–bacterial interaction strength, and the benefit index, which assesses changes in bacterial fitness. We identified Alteromonas bacteria as drivers of viral–bacterial co-infection, with consistently high synergy index and benefit index. We found that during algal blooms, Alteromonas displayed high chemoattraction towards infected cell extracts, accumulated in aggregates derived from bloom demise, and increased in abundance during oceanic bloom collapse. Viral–bacterial synergy represents a previously unrecognized mortality agent that controls bloom termination, modulating the balance between the carbon-recycling viral shunt and the carbon-exporting viral shuttle pathways, which influence global carbon cycling4,5,6.

About 50 gigatons of carbon are fixed annually by marine phototrophs, feeding the entire microbial food web7,8,9. A substantial portion of this carbon fixation occurs during large-scale algal blooms1,10. Therefore, microbial processes that control cell fate in these blooms can have profound effects on marine carbon cycling11. Algal blooms are hotspots for diverse interactions and metabolic exchange with grazers, bacteria, fungi and viruses12,13. Marine viruses, the most abundant biological entities in the ocean, are major mortality agents, driving nutrient cycling globally and significantly impacting algal bloom demise2,14,15.

Viruses regulate the fate of carbon and other nutrients16 through two distinct ecosystem processes: the viral shunt4,5, which fuels the microbial food web by catalysing nutrient recycling in the surface ocean; and the viral shuttle5,6, which facilitates carbon export through enhanced aggregation of lysed cells and sinking of particulate organic matter in the oligotrophic ocean17 and during algal blooms18. Viral lysis of algal populations creates a distinct metabolic footprint19,20,21, which can promote the growth of adapted heterotrophs22, thereby altering microbial biodiversity23,24. Yet, how virus-induced shifts in microbial community composition influence algal cell fate—and thus global carbon cycling—remains poorly understood.

We selected G. huxleyi (previously known as Emiliania huxleyi) to study algae–virus–bacteria interactions owing to its ecological significance in marine ecosystems. This cosmopolitan unicellular eukaryotic alga forms extensive blooms, covering thousands of square kilometers25. It has a crucial role in global carbon and sulfur biogeochemical cycles due to its carbon fixation, its calcite exoskeleton production, and the release of sulfur volatiles such as dimethyl sulfide25,26,27. These blooms are often terminated following infection by a giant double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) virus, the Emiliania huxleyi virus (EhV)28. Despite the observed synchronized collapse of entire blooms29, quantification of active viral infection using single-cell approaches revealed a discrepancy: fewer than 30% of algal cells were infected by the virus during the bloom’s demise3,30. This suggests that additional mortality agents may act together with viral infection. Inspired by findings from the biomedical field demonstrating that viral–bacterial co-infections synergistically increase mortality31,32, we investigated the interplay between bacteria and viruses during algal bloom demise. Using a bacterial consortium isolated from natural algal blooms (Extended Data Fig. 1), we showed that bacteria can exacerbate virus-induced algal mortality, revealing a previously unrecognized tripartite interaction with potentially important implications for global biogeochemical cycles.

We sought to determine the role of bacteria as additional mortality agents during virus-induced algal bloom demise. We hypothesized that if bacteria that are naturally associated with an alga contribute to its mortality, then an antibiotic treatment would reduce the overall death rate during viral infection. To test this idea, we cultured a xenic strain of G. huxleyi isolated from a bloom induced during a mesocosm experiment near Bergen, Norway24. In the absence of viral infection, the xenic cultures subjected to the antibiotic treatment showed up to 1.2-fold higher algal growth (linear mixed-effects model, P < 10−4; Fig. 1a and Extended Data Fig. 2a), indicating that under normal growth conditions, bacteria naturally associated with G. huxleyi maintain a competitive relationship. Infection with EhV induced algal population decline from day 1 (Fig. 1a). However, when antibiotics were administered to reduce the abundance of the algal microbiome (Extended Data Fig. 2a), we observed reduced algal mortality, up to 19-fold, compared with cultures that were not treated with antibiotics (linear mixed-effects model, P < 0.05 from day 2; Fig. 1a). This difference suggests that the bacterial community may contribute significantly to algal mortality during viral infection, indicating a potential synergistic pathogenic interaction between viruses and bacteria. Analysis of bacterial abundance revealed that bacteria grew to 1.5-fold higher abundance in the virus-infected cultures compared with the uninfected condition (linear mixed-effects model, P < 10−4 from day 4; Fig. 1b). The differences in viral production between antibiotic-treated and untreated algal cultures were significant during the days of viral release, but the abundances leveled off resulting in similar total abundances (linear mixed-effects model, P > 0.05 on day 4 and day 6; Fig. 1c).

Dynamics of xenic alga–virus interactions for G. huxleyi (Gh) (a–c), P. globosa (Pg) (d), M. commoda (Mc) (e) and O. tauri (Ot) (f). a,d–f, Growth curves of uninfected and virus-infected xenic algal cultures with or without antibiotic (Ab) treatment. b, Bacterial abundances in uninfected and virus-infected G. huxleyi cultures. c, Viral abundances in antibiotics-treated and untreated G. huxleyi cultures. Statistical significance determined by a two-sided linear mixed-effects model, followed by Holm-adjusted pairwise comparisons per time point. Data are mean ± s.d. (n = 4 independent cultures for G. huxleyi and n = 3 for all other species). *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ***P < 0.001, ****P < 0.0001; NS, not significant (P ≥ 0.05). Exact P values are provided in the Source data.

To determine the generality of our findings, we assessed whether such synergistic pathogenic interactions occur for other marine microalgae whose bloom demise is controlled by viral infections, namely Phaeocystis globosa, Micromonas commoda and Ostreococcus tauri33,34,35. The mortality of all three algae was significantly attenuated when treating virus-infected, xenic algal cultures with antibiotics (linear mixed-effects model, P < 10−4; Fig. 1d–f). These results demonstrate that viral–bacterial synergy leading to algal mortality is a widespread phenomenon among key marine algal species. Notably, antibiotic treatment did not reduce the mortality of O. tauri upon infection with a specialist virus (linear mixed-effects model, P > 0.05; Extended Data Fig. 2e), possibly owing to the rapid recovery of a resistant population. This exemplifies that the extent of viral–bacterial synergy may depend on various factors such as host susceptibility, viral infectivity and microbiome composition. We propose that bacteria and viruses kill synergistically, whereby viral infection creates favourable conditions for bacterial pathogenicity, accelerating algal mortality and fuelling bacterial growth. Thus, bacteria naturally associated with G. huxleyi and other cosmopolitan microalgae can expedite their bloom demise during viral infection.

We sought to disentangle the interactions between algae, viruses and bacteria during algal bloom demise. To this end, we developed a tripartite laboratory model system using algal, viral and bacterial strains that were isolated from an algal bloom (Extended Data Fig. 1). We isolated the bloom-associated microbiome (BAM) from the demise phase and determined its effect on G. huxleyi during viral infection.

We next reconstituted the tripartite system by exposing axenic G. huxleyi cultures to EhV with and without the BAM community, and observed an enhancement of algal mortality in the presence of bacteria (Fig. 2a). Although viral infection alone significantly reduced algal abundance compared with uninfected cultures, the addition of the BAM accelerated this decline, resulting in approximately fourfold lower algal cell densities after 7 days (linear mixed-effects model, P < 10−4; Fig. 2a). This recapitulated our observations in xenic G. huxleyi cultures (Fig. 1a), confirming that bacterial presence synergistically enhances virus-induced algal mortality.

a, Growth curves of axenic G. huxleyi under four conditions: uninfected, with BAM only, with EhV only and with both BAM and EhV. b, Bacterial abundances in cultures with and without viral infection. c, Viral production in axenic and BAM-inoculated cultures. d, Bacterial community composition of the inoculum (In.) and over time in uninfected (bottom blue line) and EhV-infected (bottom yellow line) cultures. Data are mean ± s.d. (n = 5 independent cultures). Exact P values are provided in the Source data. Statistical significance determined by a two-sided linear mixed-effects model, followed by Holm-adjusted pairwise comparisons per day.

Bacterial population dynamics revealed significant proliferation in the tripartite system compared with the bacteria-only treatment (Fig. 2b). Similar to xenic G. huxleyi cultures (Fig. 1b), bacterial abundances in the virus-infected cultures were more than threefold higher than in the uninfected cultures 7 days post-infection (linear mixed-effects model, P < 10−4 from day 2), suggesting that bacterial communities exploit metabolites that are released during viral infection.

By contrast, viral production remained similar between axenic and BAM-supplemented cultures (linear mixed-effects model, P > 0.05; Fig. 2c). Additionally, we quantified the effect of BAM supplementation on the fraction of virus-infected algal cells (Extended Data Fig. 3), enumerated at the single-cell level using single-molecule fluorescence in situ hybridization (smFISH)3, based on the expression of the viral major capsid protein (mcp) gene. During the lytic phase, up to 70% of algal cells were virus-infected independent of the presence or absence of BAM (linear mixed-effects model, P > 0.05; Extended Data Fig. 3d), proportions consistent with previous work with infected G. huxleyi cultures3. These findings suggest that the bacterial consortium augments algal death without affecting viral infection.

To identify whether specific bacteria are driving the synergy of this tripartite interaction, we characterized changes in microbial community composition during viral infection using 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing (Fig. 2d). The bacterial community changed reproducibly in all replicates during viral infection. Whereas the uninfected cultures maintained a stable community dominated by Marinomonas, a pronounced shift occurred in the virus-infected cultures by day 4, coinciding with algal decline. Notably, the relative abundances of Alteromonas and Olleya increased in the infected cultures, from approximately 2.1 ± 0.3% and 0.01 ± 0.01%, respectively, at the beginning of the experiment (day 1), to 20.2 ± 2.7% and 32.9 ± 4.4% by day 7, thereby dominating the bacterial community (Fig. 2d). Concurrently, Pseudoalteromonas and Yoonia-Loktanella increased in their relative abundances, whereas Marinomonas declined. These findings suggest that viral infection creates a distinct metabolic niche that selectively promotes specific bacterial taxa that are capable of exploiting virus-induced changes in algal metabolism or cell lysis products, as previously shown24,36.

To disentangle the microbial dynamics governing algal bloom demise, we developed two quantitative metrics that assess the contribution of individual bacterial taxa to virus-induced algal mortality, and the effect of viral infection of algal cells on bacterial fitness. The synergy index (SI) quantifies the decrease in the algal population during viral infection in the presence of bacteria compared to viral infection alone. The benefit index (BI) measures the growth advantage that bacteria gain during viral infection compared to their growth with uninfected algae.

To calculate the SI, we use the area under the algal growth curve during viral infection alone (AUCvirus) and during viral–bacterial co-infection (AUCtripartite). We selected area under the curve (AUC) as our metric because it provides a biologically meaningful measure of cumulative biomass change that captures complete temporal dynamics rather than single time points and offers robustness through multiple daily measurements. We calculated the difference between AUCvirus and AUCtripartite and normalized this value using AUCvirus, which is represented mathematically as SI (%) = (AUCvirus − AUCtripartite)/AUCvirus × 100% (Fig. 3a and Methods). Normalizing the differences in the AUC creates a dimensionless metric, enabling direct comparison across bacterial strains and experimental conditions regardless of baseline differences. A positive SI indicates that the bacterial presence reduces algal populations beyond the reduction caused by viruses alone, with higher values reflecting stronger effects (for example, SI = 10.0% means a 10% increase in tripartite-induced algal decline compared to mortality induced by viruses alone). The BAM had an SI of 22.2 ± 2.3%, which confirms the substantial effect of this bacterial community on the virus-induced demise of G. huxleyi (Fig. 3b).
