A. stellipolaris (Ast) MB63 exhibits high (SI = 20.2 ± 2.7%) (c) whereas S. pontiacus (Sp) MB3 exhibits low (SI = 7.8 ± 2.7%) (d) synergistic killing. e, Illustration of the BI calculation, comparing bacterial growth curves in the presence of virus-infected or uninfected alga. f, Application of BI to the entire BAM community (BI = 259.8 ± 17.0%), indicating a substantial growth advantage during viral infection of G. huxleyi. g,h, Bacterial growth curves showing contrasting BI values. A. stellipolaris MB63 derives large benefit (BI = 112.4 ± 1.0%) from co-infection (g), whereas S. pontiacus MB3 shows no advantage (BI = −17.2 ± 3.0%) (h). Dashed lines mark limits for the area integration, excluding the first day which is below detection levels. i, SI and BI values for bacteria isolated directly from the BAM community (black outline) or a G. huxleyi bloom (no outline), revealing diverse ecological strategies. Asp, Alteromonas sp.; Hs, Hyphomonas sp.; Ms, Marinomonas sp.; Os, Olleya sp.; Rm, Roseovarius mucosus; Ss, Sulfitobacter sp. j, Classification of bacterial ecological strategies based on SI and BI values, identifying opportunistic pathogens, killers, consumers and agnostic bacteria (log10(BI) > 0). Data are mean ± s.e.m. (n = 3 independent cultures). Asterisks indicate P values for differences in the growth dynamics as obtained by repeated-measures two-way ANOVA (b–d,f–h); exact P values are provided in the Source data.

The BI quantifies the growth advantage bacteria derive from viral infection, calculated as BI (%) = (AUCtripartite − AUCbacteria)/AUCbacteria × 100%, where AUCbacteria represents the area under the bacterial growth curve with uninfected algae (Fig. 3e). The BAM community exhibited a high BI (259.8 ± 17.0%), indicating that viral infection of G. huxleyi creates a metabolically accessible niche that enhances bacterial proliferation almost fourfold (Fig. 3f).

To identify key contributors to this synergistic interaction, we examined the SI and BI for individual bacteria isolated from the BAM (Supplementary Data 1). Alteromonas stellipolaris MB63 exhibited a high SI (20.2 ± 2.7%), indicating that this species enhanced virus-induced algal population decline by about 20% (Fig. 3c). By contrast, Sulfitobacter pontiacus MB3 had a low, non-significant SI (7.8 ± 2.7%), suggesting that this species is not affecting algal death during viral infection (Fig. 3d). Correspondingly, A. stellipolaris MB63 exhibited a high BI (112.4 ± 1.0%), reflecting more than twofold growth enhancement during viral infection (Fig. 3g), whereas S. pontiacus MB3 showed a slight growth deficit during virus infection (BI = −17.2 ± 3.0%; Fig. 3h).

To expand the taxonomic range of our analysis, we tested a total of 12 bacteria isolated either directly from the BAM community or from the G. huxleyi bloom (Supplementary Data 1), and observed high variability in both metrics (SI range from 5.4% to 23.2% and BI range from −17.2% to 451.0%; Extended Data Figs. 4 and 5). The three Alteromonas strains tested (MB63, MB67 and MB68) consistently exhibited a large effect on algal population decline (SI range from 18.6% to 21.7%; Fig. 3i), while simultaneously deriving growth benefits from viral infection (BI range from 18.5% to 112.4%; Fig. 3i).

By mapping all bacterial isolates onto a coordinate system defined by their SI and BI values (the SI–BI phase space), we observed distinct phenotypes (Fig. 3j) and propose a framework comprising four ecological strategies: ‘opportunistic pathogens’ (high SI, high BI), exemplified by Alteromonas species, which both accelerate algal mortality and efficiently exploit the resulting metabolic niche; ‘consumers’ (low SI, high BI), such as Olleya sp. MB6, which derive substantial growth benefits from viral infection without contributing significantly to algal mortality; ‘killers’ (high SI, low BI), including Sulfitobacter sp. MB51, which enhance algal mortality but gain no growth advantage; and ‘agnostics’ (low SI, low BI), such as S. pontiacus MB3, which neither increase algal mortality nor derive substantial growth benefits from viral infection.

To determine whether synergistic bacteria directly affect the mortality of algal cells, we quantified the fraction of dying algal cells during tripartite interaction (Fig. 4a,b and Extended Data Fig. 3). Dying algal cells were identified as cells with compromised membranes using the DNA stain SYTOX Green (Fig. 4a), and were further differentiated by their chlorophyll autofluorescence as metabolically active (high chlorophyll autofluorescence) or metabolically impaired (low chlorophyll autofluorescence) cells (Fig. 4b). During viral infection, there was an accumulation of dying (SYTOX+) cells reaching up to 76.9 ± 2.4% of the algal population (on day 4; Fig. 4a). The addition of bacteria significantly reduced the percentage of dying algal cells (linear mixed-effects model, P < 10−4) reaching 21.0 ± 1.5% (on day 3; Fig. 4a), suggesting that bacteria selectively remove dying algae during viral infection. Bacteria selectively cleared low-chlorophyll cells versus high-chlorophyll cells. In the presence of bacteria, the percentage of SYTOX+ cells among all low-chlorophyll cells decreased from 54.0 ± 4.1% to 30.3 ± 3.0% on day 2 (linear mixed-effects model, P < 10−4; Fig. 4b), whereas the percentage of SYTOX+ cells among high-chlorophyll cells remained similar (linear mixed-effects model, P > 0.05; Fig. 4b). These findings show that bacteria preferentially remove metabolically impaired dying cells during virus-induced algal demise.

a, Total abundance (grey) and fraction (yellow or red) of membrane-compromised (SYTOX+) algal cells in axenic G. huxleyi cultures inoculated with EhV only (light grey, red) and with both EhV and the BAM community (dark grey, yellow). b, Fraction of SYTOX+ cells that are still metabolically active (high chlorophyll autofluorescence) or dead (low chlorophyll autofluorescence). Statistical significance determined by a two-sided linear mixed-effects model, followed by Holm-adjusted pairwise comparisons per time point. Exact P values are provided in the Source data. Data are mean ± s.d. (n = 4 independent cultures).

We sought to determine the metabolic basis for viral–bacterial synergy in algal killing. We focused on lipid metabolism since EhV infection profoundly remodels the lipidome of G. huxleyi, inducing triacylglycerol (TAG) production and accumulation of intracellular lipid bodies37. We thus sequenced and annotated the genomes of all bacterial isolates and correlated the SI of each one with the completeness (per cent of genes encoded in the KEGG pathway) of its fatty acid degradation (FAD) pathway. We found a significant positive correlation between SI and the FAD pathway completeness (Spearman’s ρ = 0.669, P = 0.017; Extended Data Fig. 6a and Supplementary Data 2). Detailed examination revealed that within the BAM consortium, the species with the highest SI values, all belonging to the genus Alteromonas, also encode the complete enzymatic machinery for TAG hydrolysis and subsequent fatty acid transmembranal transport and β-oxidation, including TAG lipase, fadL, fadD, fadE, fadB and fadA and their homologues (Extended Data Fig. 6b). By contrast, species with low SI values (for example, S. pontiacus MB3) showed several missing enzymes in the FAD pathway. Among bloom-associated bacterial isolates, only Alteromonas and Marinobacter strains encode these metabolic genes (Supplementary Data 2). Although this may be a phylogenetic trait that is not causally related to SI or BI, these genera were recently shown to selectively degrade algal lipids38. Most importantly, Alteromonas encodes a TAG lipase, an enzyme that releases free fatty acids from TAGs for cellular metabolism. This feature may be particularly advantageous during viral infection of G. huxleyi as EhV infection induces the release of extracellular vesicles that are enriched in TAGs39.

Having identified Alteromonas as having key roles in the viral–bacterial synergy during algal demise, we investigated the ecological importance of this genus during natural bloom succession. To this end, we tracked algal, viral and bacterial dynamics in a natural environment, measured daily during G. huxleyi bloom succession in a mesocosm experiment24. Following six days at low abundance (less than 5 × 105 cells per ml; pre-bloom phase), G. huxleyi showed a steady increase in cell numbers (days 7–14; bloom phase) and, upon viral infection (days 15–23; infection phase), its population collapsed (Fig. 5a).

We used 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing to track bacterial abundance in two size fractions to distinguish between planktonic (0.2–2 μm) and particle-attached (20–200 μm) populations (Fig. 5b and Extended Data Fig. 7). We observed significantly higher relative abundance of particle-attached Alteromonadaceae in all bloom phases (Kruskal–Wallis test, P < 0.05; Extended Data Fig. 8a). During the onset of viral infection and subsequent bloom demise (days 15–23), Alteromonadaceae became on average sixfold enriched in the particle-attached fraction (Welch’s t-test; P = 0.088; Extended Data Fig. 8b) compared with the uninfected bloom phase, suggesting that Alteromonadaceae specifically colonize algal aggregates generated during infection. Viral infection of G. huxleyi blooms enhances the production of transparent exopolymer particles up to 4.5-fold (ref. 24), which catalyse aggregate formation18,40 and are likely to provide a unique ecological niche for colonizing bacteria.

The dynamics of other bacterial families were markedly different from Alteromonadaceae during the G. huxleyi bloom (Fig. 5b). Rhodobacteraceae were more abundant in the planktonic fraction than in the particle-attached fraction during the pre-bloom and bloom phases (Kruskal–Wallis test; P < 0.05; Extended Data Fig. 8c), with an increase in the particle-attached fraction throughout the phytoplankton bloom succession (Extended Data Fig. 8d). Pseudoalteromonadaceae exhibited an increase in relative abundance in both planktonic and particle-attached fractions during the pre-bloom phase followed by a decrease during the bloom phase (Fig. 5b), suggesting that these bacteria inhabit a different ecological niche.

To further investigate whether Alteromonadaceae actively seek out virus-infected cells during the bloom and demise of G. huxleyi (Fig. 5c), we deployed the in situ chemotaxis assay (ISCA)41,42 at multiple times during bloom succession. The ISCA is a microfluidic device containing an array of micro-wells that are filled with different chemicals. Here we loaded the ISCA wells with cell extracts from virus-infected or uninfected laboratory G. huxleyi cultures, as well as filtered seawater from the mesocosm acting as a reference. We then deployed the ISCAs in the mesocosm water, allowing the chemical extracts to diffuse out of the wells, which generate concentration gradients that can attract chemotactic bloom-associated bacteria into the wells. We then characterized the composition of the chemotactic bacterial communities in the ISCAs using 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing (Fig. 5d).

Alteromonadaceae were enriched in ISCA wells containing extracts from both infected and control G. huxleyi during the peak of viral infection in the demise phase of the bloom (days 18 and 20), accounting for nearly half (45.3 ± 6.3%) of all chemotactic bacteria in the infected wells on day 18 (Fig. 5d). Notably, Alteromonadaceae, including Alteromonas (Extended Data Fig. 9), were significantly enriched in the ISCA wells containing virus-infected G. huxleyi cell extract compared with a seawater reference (day 18; Welch’s ANOVA, P = 0.008; Fig. 5d), suggesting they are attracted by the algal metabolites. On average, Alteromonadaceae were 19-fold enriched in infected ISCA wells (13.1 ± 19.6%) compared to their planktonic abundance across the bloom succession (0.7 ± 0.7%). This pattern contrasts with other bacterial families, including those whose abundance in the bloom was higher. For example, Rhodobacteraceae accounted for 18.3 ± 4.8% of planktonic bacteria, which is 26 times higher than the proportion of Alteromonadaceae during the overall bloom succession (Fig. 5b) but had a 20 times lower relative abundance in the infected ISCA wells (0.9 ± 1.0%; Fig. 5d). Pseudoalteromonadaceae were also enriched in ISCA wells containing G. huxleyi extracts but primarily during the pre-bloom and bloom phases (days 3, 9 and 12), accounting for up to 44.9 ± 31.4%, rather than during the viral infection phase at which Pseudoalteromonadaceae accounted for only 5.2 ± 6.6% in control and 3.6 ± 1.3% in infected ISCA wells (days 18 and 20; Fig. 5d), which is consistent with their higher relative abundance during these early bloom phases (Fig. 5b).

We next isolated seven Alteromonas strains directly from the ISCA wells (Supplementary Data 1) to quantify their selective chemoattraction to infected algae under controlled laboratory conditions (Extended Data Fig. 10). Five out of the seven Alteromonas isolates showed a significantly stronger chemoattraction towards virus-infected cell extracts versus extracts from uninfected cells (Welch’s t-test, P < 0.05; Fig. 5e and Extended Data Fig. 10). One of the two strains that were isolated from ISCA wells containing uninfected G. huxleyi extracts, namely Marinomonas sp. 3g5, showed a preference for the uninfected extract.

To determine whether Alteromonas are also enriched during natural bloom demise, we analysed data collected from two cruises in the North Atlantic that examined the ecological and biogeochemical effects of viral infections on coccolithophore blooms. These blooms were sampled during the NA-VICE cruise in 2012, with large spatial coverage18, and the Tara Breizh cruise in 2019, with high temporal resolution43 (Extended Data Fig. 11). We found a significant enrichment of Alteromonas relative abundance in the NA-VICE cruise blooms compared with its abundance across global Tara Oceans data44 (two-sided Mann–Whitney U test, P < 10−4). We next examined the data from the Tara Breizh cruise (Fig. 5f), which tracked natural bloom dynamics over five consecutive days. These data only allowed us to resolve taxa to the family level, and we used it to establish whether Alteromonadaceae increases in abundance in virus-infected blooms. Using data on calcified G. huxleyi cells and intracellular EhV abundance, as well as remote-sensing data, we established that the sampling occurred during early bloom demise21. During these 5 days, we found a more than 100-fold increase in relative abundance of Alteromonadaceae (Fig. 5g). By contrast, Rhodobacteraceae, although higher in relative abundance, did not increase during bloom demise (Fig. 5g). Pseudoalteromonadaceae had a higher relative abundance compared with Tara Oceans data, but increased only slightly in abundance during bloom demise (Fig. 5g). Together, these results show that Alteromonadaceae and Alteromonas inhabit the ecological niche of virus-infected, demising coccolithophore blooms.

The viral shunt is a key ecological process that recycles photosynthetic biomass generated in the sunlit surface ocean, providing nutrients and metabolites that fuel the marine microbiome. Our findings demonstrate that this process can selectively reshape the bloom microbiome and thereby expedite bloom demise. This viral–bacterial synergy helps to explain why entire G. huxleyi blooms collapse synchronously despite fewer than 30% of the cells being actively infected by EhV3,30. Viral infection may therefore be a trigger for additional pathogens expediting bloom demise.

Here we introduced a new experimental framework for studying complex microbial interactions. By generating synthetic communities composed of algae, bacteria and viruses isolated from algal blooms, we experimentally quantified their tripartite interaction dynamics. To this end, we developed two novel quantitative indices: the SI, measuring killing interaction strength, and the BI, assessing bacterial fitness gain. We measured more than 20% increase in virus-induced algal mortality in the presence of the BAM compared with viral infection alone, and an increase of more than 250% in bacterial benefit (Fig. 3).

This quantitative approach enabled us to disentangle these complex natural microbial communities in the laboratory and identify key players in algal bloom demise. We identified Alteromonas as major drivers of this globally important process. This cosmopolitan genus exhibits remarkable lifestyle plasticity45, including pathogenicity46,47 and chemoattraction towards photosynthetic microorganisms48. Using our quantitative framework, we showed that these bacteria become opportunistic pathogens during viral infection of G. huxleyi, exhibiting high killing interaction strength (SI; Fig. 3) and fitness gain (BI; Fig. 3). In addition, Alteromonas were chemoattracted towards infected cell extracts, accumulated in particles derived from bloom demise, and increased in abundance during coccolithophore bloom demise in the open ocean (Fig. 5). Thus, Alteromonas, despite its low abundance in healthy algal-associated populations, is a keystone bacterial genus adapted to virus-induced algal bloom demise.

Viral infection of G. huxleyi rewires its metabolism49 characterized by specific halogenated metabolites20 and lipids50,51 and enrichment—for example, in TAGs37 that may be consumed by Alteromonas (Extended Data Fig. 6b). We propose that the ephemeral nature of the release of such unique and nutritious metabolites during virus-induced bloom demise selectively recruits bacterial taxa adapted to consume these metabolites (as was shown in other algal–bacterial interactions52). Viral infection also stimulates the production of transparent exopolymer particles, which increases cell stickiness and facilitates bacterial adherence18,24,40. We showed that Alteromonas is significantly enriched in particle-associated microbial communities during algal bloom demise (Fig. 5b), highlighting its specialization in the viral shunt niche.

We complemented the laboratory model for viral–bacterial synergy with an ISCA, which enabled us to quantify bacterial behaviour directly in the environment at different phases of bloom succession. We tailored this experiment specifically to detect, isolate and characterize bacteria that were attracted to virus-infected G. huxleyi cell extracts. During bloom demise, Alteromonas was attracted towards the chemicals released by infected G. huxleyi cells (Fig. 5d), which probably led to the concomitant increase in particle association (Fig. 5b). Indeed, Alteromonas were previously shown to exploit adhesive algal surfaces for colonization53.

Our results demonstrate viral–bacterial synergy at the community level, raising questions regarding the specific cellular mechanisms that drive both the synergistic killing (SI) and the associated bacterial fitness benefits (BI). We propose four non-mutually exclusive scenarios that may mediate this phenomenon. First, viral infection may trigger the release of infochemicals that induce bacterial pathogenicity towards both infected and uninfected algal cells, thereby increasing mortality beyond the virus-infected population. Second, bacterial metabolites or signalling molecules produced during viral infection may interfere with algal cell division, reducing population growth rates even in the absence of direct cell lysis. Third, bacteria that proliferate by exploiting viral lysate may competitively exclude algal cells for essential nutrients, creating resource limitations that reduce algal growth. Fourth, bacteria may accelerate the death of virus-infected algae by efficiently metabolizing essential cellular components such as membrane lipids and sugars, thereby compromising cellular integrity. In support of this fourth scenario, we showed that bacteria selectively remove dying algal cells thereby accelerating their demise (Fig. 4). Future mechanistic studies will be essential to distinguish between these scenarios and identify the precise molecular drivers of this ecologically significant tripartite interaction.

To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of how co-infection by two agents—viruses and bacteria—can act in synergy in algal bloom demise, akin to co-infections that are major mortality agents in human diseases31,32. Although bacterial benefits resulting from viral infection of marine bloom-forming algae have been reported previously36,54,55, there is a lack of observations of viral infection-induced bacterial pathogenicity. Bacterial pathogenicity has been shown to depend on contextual parameters such as temperature56 and the growth phase of the algal host57,58. Specifically, aged and senescent algal cells can induce bacterial pathogens46,59 via the release of specific algal metabolites and reactive oxygen species60,61, thereby accelerating death in the algal population.

Here we introduce viral infection as a major environmental factor that may be the trigger of bacterial pathogenicity driving bloom demise. We show that these algal–viral–bacterial interactions occur across four cosmopolitan algal species (Fig. 1). For G. huxleyi, we provided insights into cellular mechanisms (Fig. 4), revealed chemotaxis as an important bacterial trait and found evidence in an oceanic bloom (Fig. 5). For the three additional algal species, further studies are required to assess the effect of algal–viral–bacterial interactions on their bloom termination, and to resolve the mechanism underlying these viral–bacterial co-infections. We thus propose that these tripartite interactions have profound biogeochemical implications. Viral–bacterial synergy (SI) expedites bloom demise, which is likely to reduce the amount of carbon that is fixed during algal blooms. Bacterial growth due to algal bloom demise (BI) can affect the balance between the viral shunt (increasing the recycling of carbon in the ocean surface, reflected in a high BI) and the viral shuttle (exporting carbon to ocean depths via sinking particles). Deciphering the nature of alga–virus–bacteria interactions is critical given the role of large-scale oceanic blooms in carbon and sulfur cycling as well as climate regulation.

G. huxleyi strain RCC6946, the virus EhV-M1 and the BAM were isolated from an induced G. huxleyi bloom during the AQUACOSM VIMS-Ehux mesocosm experiment conducted near Bergen, Norway, in 201824. For algal isolation, a water sample collected from mesocosm bag 4 during the bloom phase (day 13, 6 June 2018) was used for single-cell isolation within two weeks of sample collection at the Roscoff Culture Collection (RCC). The BAM was isolated from mesocosm bag 7, which exhibited the highest increase in viral abundance during G. huxleyi bloom demise. A water sample was collected during the demise phase (day 23, 16 June 2018), filtered through GF/F glass microfibre filters (~0.7 µm nominal pore size), and the filtrate cryopreserved with glycerol (15% final concentration). The lytic virus EhV-M1 was isolated from the same mesocosm experiment using G. huxleyi CCMP 374 as a susceptible host, and its genome was sequenced62.

The G. huxleyi strain RCC6946 was maintained in batch cultures at 18 °C with a 16 h:8 h light:dark cycle. Light was provided at 100 μmol photons m−2 s−1 using cool white LEDs. The medium was composed of autoclaved filtered seawater (FSW) adjusted to 35‰ and supplemented with modified K/2 medium63, modified as described in Supplementary Data 3. In parallel to the xenic culture, an axenic culture was derived by adding the antibiotics ampicillin and kanamycin at final concentrations of 100 μg ml−1 and 50 μg ml−1, respectively. The absence of bacteria was verified periodically by plating 100 μl on Difco Marine Agar 2216 (MA; BD Diagnostics) and enumerating bacteria using flow cytometry (Extended Data Fig. 12e). Dilutions with fresh medium were performed to maintain the algal cultures in exponential growth.

For viral infections, 20 ml of exponentially growing, axenic algal cultures at about 8 × 105 cells per ml were infected with EhV-M1 (freshly propagated on RCC6946, concentrated on 100 kDa Amicon filters) at a multiplicity of particles (MOP) of 1:2 of alga:virus. For testing the effect of antibiotics on algal mortality, ampicillin and kanamycin were added to xenic RCC6946 cultures at final concentrations of 100 μg ml−1 and 50 μg ml−1, respectively, simultaneously with viral co-infection at an MOP of 1:5. The experiment was performed in biological quadruplicate and repeated independently twice with similar results. Statistical significance was assessed for the log10-transformed data by using a two-sided linear mixed-effects model, followed by Holm-adjusted pairwise comparisons between treatments at each time point using lmerTest (v3.2-1) and emmeans (v2.0.3) in R (v4.5.1).

Xenic strains of the haptophyte P. globosa G(A), and the green algae M. commoda LAC38, and O. tauri RCC4221 were cultured and used for propagation of the respective viruses Phaeocystis globosa virus (PgV-07T), Micromonas commoda virus (McV-BIO217) and two Ostreococcus tauri viruses (specialist virus OtV5 and generalist virus OtV06-12), as described above, with some modifications to slow down the temporal dynamics of the viral infection and allow for bacterial synergy. Specifically, P. globosa was grown in f/2 medium64 and infected at 5 × 105 cells per ml with PgV-07T (filtered at 0.22 μm) at an MOP of 1:0.1. M. commoda was grown in FSW adjusted to 27‰ and supplemented with f/2 medium, and infected at 106 cells per ml with McV-BIO217 (filtered at 0.45 μm) at an MOP of 1:1. O. tauri was grown in K/2 medium at 50 μmol photons m−2 s−1, and infected: (1) at 107 cells per ml with OtV5 (filtered at 0.45 μm and concentrated on 100 kDa) at an MOP of 1:0.001; and (2) at 106 cells per ml with OtV06-12 (filtered at 0.22 μm and concentrated on 100 kDa) at an MOP of 1:0.1. To test the effect of antibiotics, ampicillin and kanamycin were added at 100 μg ml−1 and 50 μg ml−1 at day −1 (P. globosa), day 0 (O. tauri with OtV5), or at days 1 and 2 (M. commoda and O. tauri with OtV06-12) depending on the microbiome response. All experiments were performed in biological triplicate and repeated independently twice with similar results. Statistical significance was assessed for the log10-transformed data by using a two-sided linear mixed-effects model, followed by Holm-adjusted pairwise comparisons between treatments at each time point.

To enrich the BAM on G. huxleyi, the cryopreserved BAM was grown on diverse media containing organic material derived through exudation, mechanical lysis (sonication) and viral lysis of algal cells. To collect exponential conditioned media (Exp. CM) and sonication lysates (SL), algal cultures were grown to their exponential phase at about 8 × 105 cells per ml and centrifuged at 600g for 5 min. The supernatant was filtered through 0.22-μm PES filters and used as ‘Exp. CM’. The cell pellet was resuspended in 0.3 ml K/2 medium, physically disrupted through probe sonication (5 cycles of 30 s followed by 30 s rest). Once sonicated, the lysate was resuspended in 500 mL K/2 medium, filtered through 0.22-μm PES filters and used as ‘SL’. To collect viral free lysate (VFL), algal cultures were infected with EhV-M1 as described bove. After four days, the lysed cultures were filtered sequentially through 2-μm cellulose membrane filters, 0.22-μm PES filters and 100 kDa centrifugal filters, and used as ‘VFL’. All three filtrates were kept at 4 °C and used within 24 h. The BAM glycerol stock was directly inoculated into 30 ml of each filtrate in triplicate and incubated for 3 days in an orbital shaker at 18 °C. Triplicates were combined, and aliquots of 9 ml per medium were mixed and cryopreserved with glycerol (15% final concentration).

Algal cultures were infected with EhV-M1, as described above, and co-inoculated with an overnight culture of BAM. BAM was inoculated from a glycerol stock into Difco Marine Broth 2216 (MB; BD Diagnostics) and incubated overnight at 28 °C with agitation (160 rpm). The overnight culture was washed three times with 0.2-µm-filtered FSW by centrifugation (13,800g, 1 min), enumerated using flow cytometry, and inoculated at 104 bacterial cells per ml into the virus-infected algal cultures. The experiment was performed in n = 5 biological replicates and repeated independently at least twice with similar results. Statistical significance was assessed for the log10-transformed data by using a two-sided linear mixed-effects model, followed by Holm-adjusted pairwise comparisons between treatments at each time point.

Flow cytometry analyses were performed using a CytoFLEX S flow cytometer (Beckman Coulter). Algal cells were identified as high forward scatter (FSC) and high chlorophyll population by plotting FSC (excitation: 488 nm, height threshold = 4 × 104 a.u.) versus chlorophyll autofluorescence (excitation: 561 nm, emission: 665–715 nm). Only cells with a high chlorophyll autofluorescence >4 × 104 a.u. were counted (Extended Data Fig. 12a,b). For bacteria and virus counts, samples were fixed with glutaraldehyde (0.5% final concentration) for at least 30 min at 4 °C, then snap-frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80 °C until analysis. After thawing, samples were stained with SYBR Gold (Invitrogen; diluted 1:104 in Tris-EDTA buffer) for 20 min at 80 °C and analysed by flow cytometry by plotting violet side scatter (vSSC; excitation: 405 nm, area threshold = 1 × 103 a.u.) versus SYBR fluorescence (excitation: 488 nm, emission: 500-550 nm, area threshold = 1 × 103 a.u.; Extended Data Fig. 12c–f). All flow cytometry data were inspected and processed in CytExpert v2.4 (Beckman Coulter), technical outliers (due to unstable timelines or shifts in signal intensity) removed, and statistical analyses were conducted in GraphPad Prism (v11.0.2) and R (v4.5.1).

Alga–virus–bacteria interaction experiments were performed as described above, with 500 ml per replicate. Cultures were sampled daily for: (1) quantification of algae, bacteria and viruses via flow cytometry as described above; and (2) smFISH analysis, as previously described3. In brief, at each time point, 25–30 ml of culture was fixed with paraformaldehyde (1% final concentration), incubated for 1 h, and centrifuged for 3 min at 3,000g. The cell pellet was incubated with a cryopreservation solution for 1 h, centrifuged for 3 min at 3,000g, and stored at −80 °C. For hybridization, chlorophyll was removed by two sequential washes with 70% and 100% ethanol, enzymes were degraded with proteinase K (10 μg ml−1 final concentration) in 2× sodium chloride-sodium citrate (SSC), and the cells incubated overnight with hybridization buffer (17.5% formamide in 2× SSC) containing probes for the viral mcp transcript conjugated with the fluorophore tetramethylrhodamine (TMR; 0.1 ng ml−1 final concentration). Finally, cells were washed (17.5% formamide in 2× SSC), resuspended in buffer (10 mM Tris at pH 8.0 in 2× SSC), and analysed by flow cytometry (FSC area threshold = 4 × 103 a.u., >1,000 total events in the target gate at 30 μl min−1, abort rate <7%) using the viral probe’s fluorescence (excitation: 561 nm, emission: 564–606 nm). Cells with a signal area greater than 1 × 103 a.u. TMR were enumerated as mcp positive (mcp+), virus-infected cells (Extended Data Fig. 12g). Unstained samples were used as a reference for background fluorescence. The experiment was performed in biological quadruplicate and repeated independently twice with similar results. Statistical significance was assessed using a two-sided linear mixed-effects model, followed by Holm-adjusted pairwise comparisons per time point.

Alga–virus–bacteria interaction experiments were set up in five replicates at 400 ml. Aliquots of 40 ml were filtered by gravity through autoclaved GF/C filters (47 mm; Whatman), and the filtrate was collected on autoclaved 0.22–µm PVDF filters (47 mm; Durapore, Millipore). The filters were transferred directly to the lysis buffer of DNeasy PowerWater Kit (Qiagen), frozen in liquid nitrogen, and stored at −20 °C. DNA extraction was performed according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The 16S rRNA gene was amplified using the primers 515 F (GTGYCAGCMGCCGCGGTAA65) and 806 R (GGACTACNVGGGTWTCTAAT66) targeting the V4 region, under the following PCR conditions: initial denaturation at 94 °C for 3 min, followed by 35 cycles of denaturation at 94 °C for 45 s, annealing at 50 °C for 1 min, and elongation at 72 °C for 1 min and 30 s. A final elongation step was performed at 72 °C for 10 min to ensure complete extension of the amplified products. Sequencing was performed using a paired-end 2× 250 bp Illumina MiSeq platform at the RUSH Genomics and Microbiome Core Facility.

The 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing data were processed using the DADA2 pipeline67 (v1.28.0) in R (v4.3.2) to perform quality filtering, error correction, and amplicon sequence variant (ASV) inference. Raw sequencing reads were quality-checked using the plotQualityProfile function, and low-quality bases were trimmed using the filterAndTrim function with truncation parameters set based on quality score distributions. Error rates were learned from the dataset using the learnErrors function, and sequences were dereplicated using derepFastq. ASVs were inferred using the dada function, followed by chimera removal with removeBimeraDenovo. Taxonomic classification was performed using the SILVA_nr99 reference database68 (v138.1), and ASV tables were generated for downstream analyses. The average sequencing depth per sample was 67,413 ± 26,969 (minimum 24,150 and maximum 132,743 reads). Chloroplast reads accounting for 28 ± 23% (maximum 73%) were removed. The processed data were then analysed using the Phyloseq package69 (v1.44.0) in R to visualize microbial community composition. The nine most abundant genera are shown individually, while all remaining genera (<5%) were summed as ‘Others’.

SI was calculated by comparing the AUC of virus-infected G. huxleyi growth in the presence and absence of bacteria (the entire growth curves were used). We chose to focus on AUC for four main reasons: First, it is biologically meaningful and captures the cumulative biomass change that would occur in natural bloom systems, reflecting the total ‘ecological impact’ (for example, the total amount of carbon fixed). Second, it captures complete temporal dynamics rather than relying on a single time point or summary statistic that would miss critical dynamics. Third, it is more robust against experimental variability, as it takes into account three measurements from each experiment day. Finally, normalizing AUC difference by another AUC creates a dimensionless metric that allows direct comparison across different bacterial strains and experimental conditions even if their baseline levels are different. SI was expressed as a percentage and calculated as:

where: AUCvirus represents the algal population dynamics under viral infection alone, and AUCtripartite represents the algal population dynamics under co-infection with both viruses and bacteria.

We computed the AUC of the algal abundance for each replicate and treatment using GraphPad Prism (v11.0.2). Then, the mean AUC of each treatment (n = 3) was used to compute the SI as described above. The standard error (SE) of the SI was estimated as \({\rm{S}}{\rm{E}}\,({\rm{ \% }})=\frac{\sqrt{{\rm{V}}{\rm{a}}{\rm{r}}({\rm{S}}{\rm{I}})}}{\sqrt{{n}}}\times 100\) using analytical error propagation via the delta method, whereby the variance of the SI was determined as \(\mathrm{Var}(\mathrm{SI})=\frac{1}{{{\mathrm{AUC}}_{\mathrm{virus}}}^{2}}\,\times \) \({\rm{V}}{\rm{a}}{\rm{r}}({{\rm{A}}{\rm{U}}{\rm{C}}}_{{\rm{t}}{\rm{r}}{\rm{i}}{\rm{p}}{\rm{a}}{\rm{r}}{\rm{t}}{\rm{i}}{\rm{t}}{\rm{e}}})+(\frac{{{\rm{A}}{\rm{U}}{\rm{C}}}_{{\rm{t}}{\rm{r}}{\rm{i}}{\rm{p}}{\rm{a}}{\rm{r}}{\rm{t}}{\rm{i}}{\rm{t}}{\rm{e}}}}{{{{\rm{A}}{\rm{U}}{\rm{C}}}_{{\rm{v}}{\rm{i}}{\rm{r}}{\rm{u}}{\rm{s}}}}^{2}}{)}^{2}\times {\rm{V}}{\rm{a}}{\rm{r}}({{\rm{A}}{\rm{U}}{\rm{C}}}_{{\rm{v}}{\rm{i}}{\rm{r}}{\rm{u}}{\rm{s}}})\). To test for a significant treatment difference between the tripartite and virus-infected demise dynamics and to label the SI values accordingly, a repeated-measures two-way ANOVA was performed at a two-tailed significance level of α = 0.05 to evaluate the effects of time and the bacterial strain on algal abundance. To account for cell calcification and thus sedimentation, the raw data were detrended with a linear mixed-effects model (fixed slope, random intercept per day) using the robustlmm package (v3.4-3) in R (v4.5.1). Results are reported as SI ± SE.

BI quantifies bacterial growth differences over time by comparing the AUC in tripartite conditions versus bacterial growth alone. BI was expressed as a percentage and calculated as:

where AUCtripartite represents the bacterial growth over time when co-cultured with virus-infected G. huxleyi, and AUCbacteria represents bacterial growth over time in the presence of G. huxleyi but without viral infection.

We first computed the AUC of the bacterial abundance for each replicate and treatment between day 1 and day 6 (at day 0, bacterial inoculation density was below the detection limit of the flow cytometry acquisition settings). Then, the mean AUC of each treatment (n = 3) was used to compute the BI as described above. The SE of the BI was estimated as \(\mathrm{SE}\,( \% )=\frac{\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(\mathrm{BI})}}{\sqrt{n}}\times 100\) using analytical error propagation via the delta method, whereby the variance of the BI was determined as \(\mathrm{Var}(\mathrm{BI})=\frac{1}{{{\mathrm{AUC}}_{\mathrm{bacteria}}}^{2}}\times \mathrm{Var}({\mathrm{AUC}}_{\mathrm{tripartite}})+{\left(\frac{{\mathrm{AUC}}_{\mathrm{tripartite}}}{{{\mathrm{AUC}}_{\mathrm{bacteria}}}^{2}}\right)}^{2}\times \) \(\mathrm{Var}({\mathrm{AUC}}_{\mathrm{bacteria}})\). To test for significant differences between tripartite and bacterial growth dynamics and to label the BI values accordingly, a repeated-measures two-way ANOVA was performed at a two-tailed significance level of α = 0.05 to evaluate the effects of time and the bacterial strain on bacterial abundance (in case of missing values, a mixed-effects model was fitted). Results are reported as BI ± SE.

For bacterial isolation, glycerol stocks were sampled on different days of the induced G. huxleyi blooms and following various enrichments (Supplementary Data 1). In brief, seawater samples (filtered using 10 µm and GF/F filters) were collected during the bloom (day 13) and demise (day 21 and day 23) phases and cryopreserved as glycerol stocks at a final concentration of 15%, snap-frozen in liquid nitrogen, and stored at −80 °C. The BAM glycerol stock was prepared as described above. To enrich alga- and viral infection-associated taxa, the mesocosm and BAM glycerol stocks were inoculated into uninfected and virus-infected cultures of G. huxleyi before isolation. To enrich G. huxleyi-associated taxa, xenic cultures of RCC6946, which contain bacteria that were co-isolated with the algal cell from the mesocosm bloom, were infected with EhV-M1 before isolation. From overnight cultures of the glycerol stocks and enrichment cultures, 100 µl were plated at 100×, 1,000×, and 10,000× dilution on MA plates and incubated at 28 °C, allowing for single-colony isolation. Selected colonies were streaked onto fresh MA three times or until a uniform colony morphology was observed, ensuring bacterial isolate purity. Colonies were inoculated in 3 ml MB medium, grown overnight at 28 °C with agitation (160 rpm), and cryopreserved as glycerol stocks. Tripartite alga–virus–bacteria experiments were performed as described above in biological triplicate and repeated independently twice with similar results.

For sequencing the complete 16S rRNA gene, cells from pure colonies were lysed using a buffer containing TE and 0.1% Triton-X100, followed by heating at 95 °C for 5 min. Cell lysates were centrifuged at 13,300 rpm for 10 min, and 2 µl of the supernatant was used as a DNA template for PCR amplification. The 16S rRNA gene was amplified using the universal primers 16S-27F (AGAGTTTGATCMTGGCTCAG)70 and 16S-1492R (CGGTTACCTTGTTACGACTT)71. The PCR reaction was carried out in 20 µl using 2× HY-Taq (HyLabs) or REDTaq (Sigma) Ready Mix. PCR amplification was performed using the following conditions: initial denaturation at 94 °C for 3 min, followed by 25–35 cycles of denaturation at 94 °C for 30 s, annealing at 57 °C for 30 s, and elongation at 72 °C. A final elongation step was conducted at 72 °C for 10 min, followed by a hold at 12 °C. PCR products were visualized in 1% w/v agarose gel with ethidium bromide. Amplicons were purified with the illustra ExoProStar 1-Step enzymatic cleanup kit (GE Healthcare Life Sciences) using a 5 µl aliquot of the PCR reaction and incubated at 37 °C for 15 min, followed by enzyme inactivation at 80 °C for 15 min. For Sanger sequencing, 1–2 µl of the purified amplicons were analysed by the Life Sciences Core Facilities at the Weizmann Institute of Science. All 16S rRNA gene sequences were classified at the genus level using the SINA classifier tool72 (v1.2.12) within the SILVA rRNA database (Supplementary Data 1).

Alga–virus–bacteria interaction experiments were performed as described above. Cultures were sampled daily for: (1) enumeration of algae, bacteria and viruses via flow cytometry as described above; and (2) quantification of dying (membrane-permeable cells) using the DNA-intercalating stain SYTOX Green (Invitrogen). Samples were stained with a final concentration of 1 μM SYTOX Green, incubated for at least 20 min in the dark at room temperature, and analysed by flow cytometry (FSC height threshold = 2.5 × 104 a.u., vSSC area threshold = 1 × 103 a.u.) using the SYTOX Green fluorescence (excitation: 488 nm; emission: 505–545 nm). For samples with ≥400 cells (parent gate), cells with a signal area >1 × 105 a.u. SYTOX Green (Extended Data Fig. 12h) were counted as SYTOX+, membrane-permeable cells. Cells with a chlorophyll autofluorescence >2 × 105 a.u. were enumerated as high-chlorophyll cells. Unstained samples were used as a reference for background fluorescence. The experiment was performed in biological quadruplicate and repeated independently twice with similar results. Statistical significance was assessed using a two-sided linear mixed-effects model, followed by Holm-adjusted pairwise comparisons per time point.

Bacterial isolates (Supplementary Data 1) were inoculated from glycerol stocks in MB medium and grown overnight at 28 °C with agitation (160 rpm). Cultures were centrifuged at 12,000 rpm at room temperature for 1 min, the cell pellet was washed 3× with FSW, and frozen in liquid nitrogen. Genomic DNA was extracted following a modified version73 of a previously described protocol74. High molecular weight of the genomic DNA was verified by gel electrophoresis or Genomic DNA ScreenTape Analysis using TapeStation 4150 (Agilent Technologies), while DNA concentration and purity were validated using a Qubit fluorometer with the dsDNA HS Assay Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and NanoDrop ND-1000 spectrophotometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific), respectively. If necessary, samples were concentrated using the NEBNext Ultra II FS DNA Library Prep Kit (New England Biolabs) or AMPure XP beads (Beckman Coulter).

For Illumina short-read sequencing, shotgun metagenome libraries were prepared using the NEBNext Ultra II FS DNA Library Prep Kit for Illumina (New England Biolabs) with enzymatic shearing, according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The final size-selected pool was sequenced on an Illumina NovaSeq 6000 instrument with an S2 flow cell, utilizing 2× 150 base reads. Short reads were quality trimmed using Trimmomatic (v0.39) with the following parameters: ILLUMINACLIP:TruSeq3-PE-2.fa:2:30:10, LEADING:10, TRAILING:10, SLIDINGWINDOW:4:15, MINLEN:50. Reads that passed quality trimming were used for assembly construction with SPAdes (v3.13.0), using default k-mer sizes (21 bp, 33 bp, 55 bp and 77 bp). Contigs were filtered based on mean coverage (≥3×) and length (≥300 bp) and clustered into bins using MaxBin2 (v2.2.7) with the default parameters. Assembly quality was assessed using CheckM2 (v1.0.2) with default parameters. Multiple bins of the same isolate were concatenated into single genomes if they complemented one another based on completeness and had similar taxonomic annotation. Genes were predicted from the genomes using Prodigal (v2.6.3) in metagenomic mode. Predicted genes were filtered based on length (≥300 bp), the presence of a start codon at the first trimer, and the absence of a premature stop codon. Genes that passed filtration were clustered using MMseqs2 (v13.45111) with the following parameters: coverage mode 0, minimum coverage 0.8, and minimum sequence identity 0.9. Representative genes were annotated using eggNOG-mapper (v2.1.3) and used for downstream analysis. For PacBio long-read sequencing, multiplexed microbial libraries were prepared, using SMRTBell Express Prep Kit 2.0 (Pacific Biosciences). A single PacBio sequencing library was constructed that was used for SMRTbell template preparation as described in the protocol (Pacific Biosciences). The resulting SMRTbell template was annealed to the sequencing polymerase, using a Sequel binding kit 2.0. Sequencing was conducted with a 12pM on-plate concentration using a Sequel I System in CLR mode and a single SMRT Cell (1M; PacBio) at the WIS Genomics Unit. PacBio raw reads (polymerase reads) were processed using the SMRT Link software (v8.0). Genomes were assembled using Trycycler (v0.5.5) and Flye (v2.9.6) with default parameters. Assembly quality was assessed using CheckM2, and genes were predicted, filtered, clustered, and representative genes annotated, as described above. Nanopore sequencing was performed by Plasmidsaurus following their standard bacterial genome sequencing service using the Oxford Nanopore Technology with custom analysis and annotation. All assembled genome sequences were classified at the species level using the GTDB-Tk software toolkit (v2.4.1) with GTDB database75 v220 (Supplementary Data 1). The genome of Sulfitobacter sp. D7 was sequenced as previously described76.

To assess the relationship between bacterial metabolic pathways and bacterial synergy, all KEGG pathways and their constituent KEGG orthologues were retrieved via KEGG API. Using the eggNOG-based genome annotations for each taxon, pathway coverage (%) was calculated as the proportion of KEGG orthologues present in a strain relative to the total KEGG orthologues in that pathway. Pathway coverage for the FAD pathway was then correlated with the SI using a Spearman’s rank correlation, and the correlation coefficient ρ with the respective P value determined.

The abundance of G. huxleyi and intracellular EhV throughout the succession of the induced G. huxleyi bloom in mesocosm bag 7 were enumerated as previously described24. In brief, for the enumeration of G. huxleyi cells, water samples were pre-filtered using 40-µm cell strainers and immediately analysed with an Eclipse iCyt flow cytometer using ec800 software v1.3.7 (Sony Biotechnology). Calcified G. huxleyi cells were identified as a population of cells with high SSC and high chlorophyll (excitation: 488 nm, emission: 663–737 nm). For the enumeration of intracellular EhV, water samples were pre-filtered through 20-µm filters, and DNA was extracted from 2-µm filters. EhV abundance was determined by quantitative PCR using the major capsid protein (mcp) gene. Absolute abundances were calculated using a calibration curve of DNA at known concentrations.

Planktonic (>0.2 µm and <2 µm) and particle-attached (>20 µm and <200 µm) fractions of the bacterial community were assessed throughout the succession of the induced G. huxleyi bloom in mesocosm bag 7 using 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing, as previously described24. In brief, water samples were pre-filtered through 200 µm, sequentially filtered through 20-µm, 2-µm and 0.22-µm polycarbonate filters (Isopore, 47 mm; Merck Millipore), and immediately frozen in liquid nitrogen. DNA extraction of the 20-µm and 0.22-µm filters was performed with the DNeasy PowerWater kit (Qiagen), and sequenced following the EMP 16S amplicon protocol targeting the V4 region of the 16S gene using the 515F-806R primers77 including degeneracy to reduce bias towards Thaumarchaeota and SAR1165,66. The particle-attached fraction was sequenced using a paired-end 2× 153 bp Illumina MiniSeq platform at the RUSH Genomics and Microbiome Core Facility. Data analysis for planktonic bacteria was performed using the DADA2 pipeline and ASVs annotated with the RDP classifier. The average sequencing depth per sample and chloroplast read proportion for the planktonic community was previously reported24. Data analysis for particle-attached bacteria was performed using the DADA2 pipeline (setting ‘justConcatenate = TRUE’ to merge the forward and reverse reads introducing 10x ‘N’ in the middle) and ASVs annotated with the SILVA_nr99 reference database. The average sequencing depth for the particle-attached size fraction in bag 7 was 20,734 ± 6,517 (minimum 8,057 and maximum 29,629) reads per sample. Chloroplast reads accounting for 7 ± 8% (minimum 1% and maximum 36%) in the particle-attached fraction were removed. Kruskal–Wallis tests were performed to compare planktonic and particle-attached bacterial fractions for each family and bloom phase (pre-bloom, days 1–6; bloom, days 7–14; and viral infection phase, days 15–23). Pairwise Welch’s t-tests with the Holm–Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons were performed comparing the log2-transformed fold change of particle-attached planktonic bacterial fractions between the bloom phases. For missing samples (day 2 of the planktonic and day 1 of the particle-attached size fraction), the relative abundances were interpolated. Absence of Pseudoalteromonadaceae in some planktonic samples prevented log2 fold change computation.

To prepare cell extracts as chemoattractants, G. huxleyi CCMP 2090 was grown in 19 l modified K/2 medium in 2 carboys with stirring and aeration. One exponentially growing culture (1.2 × 106 cells per ml) was infected with EhV 201 at an MOP of 1:1 while the other culture served as an uninfected control. The viruses were propagated on CCMP 2090, washed and concentrated on 100 kDa Amicon-ultra filters (EMD Millipore), and stored at 4 °C until use within two months. Cells were counted daily using a Multisizer 4 Coulter Counter (Beckman Coulter). After 48 h, the uninfected (4.4 × 106 cells per ml) and infected (0.9 × 106 cells per ml) cultures were filtered onto pre-combusted GF/C filters (47 mm; Whatman) using gentle vacuum (600 mbar under-pressure). Filters were immediately transferred to 500 ml pre-cooled (−20 °C) methanol (HPLC grade, J.T. Baker) and extracted overnight at 4 °C while shaking. Extracts were sonicated for 30 min and filtered through pre-combusted GF/C filters before being evaporated to 20 ml using a Rotovap (30 °C, 70–100 rpm). Extracts were centrifuged at 20,800g for 10 min at 4 °C, and the supernatants were evaporated to complete dryness using a SpeedVac (28 °C, 1,980 rpm). Dried extracts were re-dissolved in methanol to reduce the salt load, aliquoted into eight centrifuge tubes, dried using a SpeedVac, and stored at −80 °C until further use. The dry weight was 57.5 ± 0.3 mg and 38.3 ± 0.5 mg for the uninfected and infected extracts, respectively.

In situ chemotaxis assays (ISCAs) containing the G. huxleyi cell extracts were deployed five times throughout the mesocosm bloom succession, namely at days 3, 9, 12, 18 and 20. For each deployment, 12.5 ml of bloom water were collected per mesocosm bag (1–4; 50 ml in total), mixed and subjected to a quadruple-filtration process. Specifically, the mixed bloom water was first filtered through a 0.2-μm Millex FG (Millipore) to remove large particles, twice through a 0.2-μm Sterivex filter (Millipore), and finally through a 0.02-μm Anatop filter (Whatman). This quadruple filtration aimed to remove all microorganisms from the seawater. We confirmed the efficiency of the filtration procedure using flow cytometry and DNA sequencing78. The filtered bloom water was used as a control in the ISCA and was also used to resuspend the dried G. huxleyi extracts at a final concentration of 1 mg ml−1. The resuspended extracts were filtered through a 0.2-μm Millex FG (Millipore) to remove undissolved particles.

The working concentration of G. huxleyi extracts (1 mg ml−1 of dry weight) is representative of environmental hotspots. Indeed, chemical concentrations decay exponentially with distance away from the ISCA opening (port)41. This means that concentrations sensed by bacteria in the surrounding bloom water will be substantially lower than those in the ISCA wells and within the same order of magnitude as the concentrations arising from the lysis of a phytoplankton cell79.

Treatments (filtered bloom water and the two G. huxleyi cell extracts) were randomly allocated to an ISCA row (consisting of 5 wells with 110 μl each). All wells in a row contained the same treatment, and each treatment was replicated on three different ISCA devices, which were deployed in parallel to act as biological replicates (n = 3). Each ISCA was placed into a flow-damping acrylic enclosure, following a pre-established protocol80. Each enclosure was filled with water coming from the first four mesocosm bags (bags 1–4), previously mixed at equal volume. The flow-damping enclosures were filled slowly with water from the inlet in the lower surface and were sealed with a plug once full. The enclosures were then incubated in situ at 1 m depth for 2 h (ref. 78). Following deployments, enclosures were retrieved and slowly drained. The volume of each ISCA well was retrieved using a sterile 1 ml syringe and 27G needle.

ISCA samples for DNA extraction were snap-frozen immediately. DNA extraction was performed using a microvolume extraction approach (physical lysis method81). Libraries for 16S rRNA gene sequencing were generated for all samples using the Nextera XT DNA Sample Preparation Kit (Illumina) following a previously described protocol for low-input DNA libraries82. Primers targeting the V4–V5 regions of the 16S rRNA gene were used, namely 515F and 926R (CCGYCAATTYMTTTRAGTTT65). Samples were then sequenced on an Illumina MiSeq platform with a paired-end 2× 300 bp output. Libraries were pooled on an indexed sequencing run and yielded ~300 bp per sample. The composition of the chemotactic bacterial communities was analysed as described above using the DADA2 pipeline, and ASVs were annotated with the SILVA_nr99 reference database. For day 18, a Welch’s ANOVA followed by two-sided pairwise t-tests with Benjamini–Hochberg correction were performed to compare the fraction of Alteromonadaceae across chemoattractants using the R ‘stats’ package (v4.5.1; Shapiro–Wilk test and Levene test were performed to assure normality and homogeneity of variances).

To isolate chemotactic bacteria throughout the succession of the induced G. huxleyi bloom, we prepared agar plates made with 0.22-μm-filtered environmental bloom water and amended with 1 mg ml−1 of the corresponding G. huxleyi cell extracts. The agar plates were inoculated with the chemotactic bacterial community from the ISCA wells containing uninfected and virus-infected G. huxleyi extracts and incubated at fjord water temperature (10 °C) until colonies appeared. Individual colonies were then grown in 10% MB in autoclaved seawater overnight at room temperature and at 10 °C. Each isolate went through two additional rounds of purification via successive growth on plates and in liquid cultures. Isolates were identified by 16S rRNA gene Sanger sequencing78. Selected strains (Supplementary Data 1) were further used for genome sequencing and characterization of their chemotaxis towards different G. huxleyi cell extracts.

For genome sequencing, overnight cultures were inoculated in MB medium at 0.1 OD600. Exponentially growing cultures at 1.0 OD600 were centrifuged, and cell pellets of 15–30 mg were re-dissolved in 0.5 ml Zymo DNA/RNA Shield. Genomic DNA extraction and Nanopore sequencing were performed by Plasmidsaurus following their standard bacterial genome sequencing service. Assembled genome sequences were classified at the species level using the GTDB-Tk software toolkit.

For laboratory-based chemotaxis assays, the bacteria were plated from cryostocks on MA. Multiple colonies from each strain were inoculated in 1% MB in artificial seawater (33 g l−1 Instant Ocean, Aquarium Systems) and incubated at 180 rpm and 27 °C for 4 h to promote bacterial motility. An aliquot was fixed with glutaraldehyde (1% final concentration; Sigma Aldrich), stained for 15 min with SYBR Green I (ThermoFisher), and bacterial abundance enumerated using a CytoFLEX S flow cytometer (Beckman Coulter) as described above. Chemotaxis was characterized using ISCA devices that were each loaded with four different 0.2-μm-filtered treatments and incubated at room temperature for 1 h in artificial seawater inoculated with 106 bacteria per ml. As chemoattractants, we used: (1) extract from uninfected G. huxleyi CCMP 2090 cultures (1 mg ml−1 in artificial seawater); (2) extract from virus-infected G. huxleyi CCMP 2090 cultures (1 mg ml−1 in artificial seawater); (3) 10% MB (acting as a positive control), and artificial seawater (acting as a negative control to account for cells entering wells by random motility). Chemoattractants were inoculated in ISCA wells using a sterile 1 ml syringe (Codan Medical ApS) and needle (27 G, BD Microlance). In each ISCA, each row of five wells served as technical replicates for an individual treatment. Each chemoattractant was deployed simultaneously in four ISCA replicates. After incubation, contents of the ISCA wells were recovered using a sterile syringe and needle, technical replicates were pooled80, and 200 µl per sample were fixed, stained and enumerated using flow cytometry. Chemotactic indices (Ic) were determined as ratios of the cell concentrations in treatment wells relative to the average artificial seawater control. For statistical analysis, Ic values were log1p-transformed (ln(1 + x)) and the Levene test of homogeneity of variances and Shapiro–Wilk test of normality were performed using R. All bacteria showed significant differences between the artificial seawater control and the treatments, including the MB control (Dunnett’s test with P < 0.001). Differences between the two cell extracts were assessed using a two-sided Welch’s t-test with the Holm–Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons. For fold change comparison, the transformed Ic values were further log2-transformed, the normality per strain and treatment validated using a Shapiro–Wilk test, and treatment differences per strain assessed using a two-sided Welch’s t-test with Benjamini–Hochberg correction for multiple comparisons. The log2-transformed fold changes (LFC) between the infected and control extracts were computed as LFC = mean(log(Inf)) − mean(log(Ctl)) with s.e.m. = √ (VarInf/nInf + VarCtl/nCtl).

Coccolithophore blooms were sampled in the North Atlantic during the NA-VICE cruise in 2012 with large spatial coverage18 and the Tara Breizh cruise in 2019 with high temporal resolution43.

During the NA-VICE cruise, coccolithophore blooms across a 2,000-mile transect between the Azores and Iceland were identified via satellite remote sensing and sampled at 30 stations onboard the RV Knorr between 13 June and 16 July 2012, as previously described18. Samples for DNA extraction and 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing were collected between the surface and 150 m depth with Niskin bottles, and filtered through a 200-μm prefilter onto 0.8-µm polycarbonate filters. Genomic DNA was extracted and amplified in a dual PCR strategy using primers targeting the V1–V3 region of the 16S rRNA gene83 linked to adaptors, namely CS1_27F_YM (ACACTGACGACATGGTTCTACA-AGAGTTTGATYMTGGCTCAG) and CS2_534R_Y (TACGGTAGCAGAGACTTGGTCT-TYACCGCGGCTGCTGG), and subsequently linked to unique sample barcodes for multiplexing. For PCR amplification, the AccuPrime SuperMix II (Life Technologies) was used using the following cycling conditions: denaturation for 5 min at 95 °C, 28 cycles of 30 s at 95 °C, 30 s at 56 °C and 5 min at 68 °C, and final 7 min elongation at 68 °C. The PCR amplicon quality was validated by gel electrophoresis. In a second PCR step, sample barcodes were amplified with the following cycling conditions: 5 min at 95 °C, 8 cycles of 30 s at 95 °C, 30 s at 60 °C and 30 s at 68 °C, and final 7 min elongation at 68 °C. Samples were pooled and purified using AMPure XP beads, and concentrations were estimated using Qubit. Sequencing was performed using a paired-end 2× 300 bp Illumina MiSeq technology at the DNA Services Facility, University of Illinois at Chicago.

During the Tara Breizh cruise, a G. huxleyi bloom patch in the Celtic Sea was identified by satellite remote sensing and sampled onboard the SV Tara between 27 May and 2 June 2019, as previously described21,43. Samples for DNA extraction and sequencing were collected at the maximum turbidity depth (bloom depth) by pumping seawater through a 20-μm prefilter and sequential filtration onto 3-μm and 0.2-μm PC filters. Following DNA extraction, amplicon sequencing of the V4–V5 region of the 16S rRNA gene was performed twice using Illumina MiSeq paired-end 2× 250 bp sequencing technology. Fastq files were obtained from the European Nucleotide Archive (ENA: PRJEB50692). Intracellular virus abundances were quantified from DNA extracts of 3-µm filters using droplet digital PCR and specific primers for the mcp gene of EhV. Samples for flow cytometry were collected at the bloom depth with a Niskin bottle and immediately analysed using a BD Accuri C6 Plus Personal Flow Cytometer (BD Biosciences). Cell abundances of calcified G. huxleyi were determined by gating high chlorophyll (excitation: 488 nm; emission: 663–737 nm) and high SSC (488 nm) particles.

All paired-end 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequences were processed using QIIME 284. ASVs were inferred using the DADA2 paired-end denoising workflow, with trimming and truncation parameters adjusted according to amplicon type. For the NA-VICE samples (V1–V3 amplicons), 20 bp were trimmed from the 5′ ends of both forward and reverse reads, leaving 280 bp (forward) and 230 bp (reverse). Only samples that retained at least 10,000 non-chimeric reads after denoising were considered for downstream analysis. Taxonomic assignment was performed on representative sequences from DADA2, using the QIIME 2 classify-sklearn classifier with the SILVA v138 reference database. ASV tables were aggregated to the genus level, and relative abundances were calculated from the full dataset. The Tara Breizh data (V4–V5 amplicons) were analysed using QIIME 2, as previously described43 with the following modifications. After removal of empty reads, the demultiplexed read pairs were repaired using SeqKit285 (v2.3.1). Primer and orientation handling was performed with CutAdapt (v4.2) in two branches per sample, where each branch represents a primer-orientation-specific read set corresponding to one of the two detected amplicon orientations: one in the original R1/R2 orientation and one in the swapped R2/R1 orientation. Reads lacking the primer sequences, that were <75 bp, and had insertions or deletions were removed. For each sequencing run and orientation branch, denoising was done using QIIME 2 DADA2 with pseudo-pooling. Reads were truncated to 215 bp (forward) and 190 bp (reverse) for the first branch, and to 190 bp (forward) and 215 bp (reverse) for the second branch. Before merging, sequences of the second branch were reverse-complemented. ASV identifiers were normalized by sequence content and feature tables merged by summing identical ASV sequences across the sequencing runs and branches. Chimeras were removed using the de novo UCHIME algorithm of vsearch86 (v2.22.1) and non-chimeric ASV counts of the sequencing duplicates were summed. Counts were summed at the ASV level before conversion to relative abundance. Taxonomy was assigned in QIIME 2 using the SILVA v138 99% Naive Bayes classifier. ASV tables were aggregated to the genus level and relative abundance computed. For Fig. 5, a pseudocount of 1 × 10−5 was assigned to samples with relative abundance of exactly ‘0’. A map of the sample locations was created using the cartopy (v0.25.0) package in python (v3.10) with the Natural Earth map data.

To compare relative bacterial abundances from the North Atlantic coccolithophore blooms with diverse oceanic environments, taxonomic profiles from Tara Oceans44 were obtained (https://www.ocean-microbiome.org/). Per sample, relative abundance at the genus and family levels was calculated by dividing read counts for each taxon by the total bacterial and archaeal reads in the corresponding sample. Only samples representing the planktonic bacterial fraction (0.2 to 3 µm and 0.2 to 1.6 µm filter size fraction) were selected. NA-VICE samples were filtered by collection method to keep only cast samples and omit trap samples, while for Tara Breizh all samples labelled as outside the bloom were excluded. Pairwise comparisons of relative abundance distributions were performed at matched taxonomic level and depth range. For the Tara Oceans and NA-VICE comparison, we compared the Alteromonas genus from surface to 150 m depth. Due to limited sequencing depth, which affected our ability to reliably detect Alteromonas, the Tara Oceans and Tara Breizh comparison was performed for the Alteromonadaceae family from surface to 25 m depth. Differences between groups were evaluated using a two-sided Mann–Whitney U test. For Extended Data Fig. 11, a pseudocount of 1 × 10−5 was assigned to samples with relative abundance of exactly ‘0’. A map of the sample locations was created using the cartopy (v0.25.0) package in Python (v3.10) with the Natural Earth map data.

Flow cytometry data of the mesocosm G. huxleyi bloom has been deposited in Dryad87. Source data are provided with this paper.

Single-cell analysis of viral gene expression during G. huxleyi bloom demise revealed that at most 30% of the population was infected with the virus3,30. The residual cell mortality supporting a synchronized algal bloom demise might be linked to induced pathogenicity within the algal bloom microbiome. To study alga-virus-bacteria interactions, we isolated G. huxleyi, its virus, and the bloom-associated microbiome (BAM) from the G. huxleyi bloom and demise phases. We then followed the dynamics of algal cultures following individual and co-infections with the virus and the BAM. Individual BAM-members were isolated, characterized regarding their enhancement of the algal population demise, and their metabolic niche was evaluated via functional pathway analysis. O. tauri was infected with (d) the generalist virus OtV06-12 and (e) the specialist virus OtV5. Arrows indicate antibiotic additions, which were adjusted for each xenic alga to avoid growth-promoting effects and enhance microbiome inhibition. Planktonic Rhodobacteraceae decreased over time and shifted from a high relative abundance in e.g. Amylibacter and Planktomarina to Loktanella and Sulfitobacter, while the particle-attached fraction increased in relative abundance with a dominance in e.g. Planktomarina, Sulfitobacter and Pseudophaeobacter. Filtered seawater was used as a reference. Uninfected (a, c and e) and virus-infected (b, d and f-i) cultures of axenic G. huxleyi RCC6946 with (b-d) and without (a and e-i) BAM-inoculation were analyzed by flow cytometry. Algal cells (a and b; gate “Cells”) were enumerated by plotting chlorophyll autofluorescence vs. forward scatter (FSC). The gating of algal cells was based on samples from uninfected cultures of each experiment. The bimodal cell distribution in (a) corresponds to calcified and non-calcified subpopulations. Bacteria and viruses (c-f; gates “Bacteria” and “EhV) were enumerated after DNA staining by plotting SYBR Gold fluorescence vs. violet side scatter (vSSC). The gating of bacteria and viruses was based on samples from virus-infected and BAM-inoculated cultures at the end of each experiment. The high-fluorescent particles in (c) are algal cells. The fraction of virus-infected algal cells (g) was quantified using smFISH by plotting the viral probe’s TMR fluorescence (gate “mcp+”). The “mcp+” gate was based on four gates that pre-selected single fluorescent cells using FSC vs. SSC, vSSC area vs. height, and SSC vs. Chlorophyll to reduce non-fluorescent noise. The fraction of dying algal cells (h) was quantified by gating cells with high SYTOX Green fluorescence (gate “SYTOX+”). (i) SYTOX+ cells were further differentiated as being derived from high (dying cells) or low (dead cells) chlorophyll autofluorescent cells. The “SYTOX+” gates were thereby based on three gates that pre-selected singlets (FSC area vs. height), algal cells (FSC vs. SSC), and then optionally chlorophyll autofluorescence (Chlorophyll vs. FSC).

TNT Sports pundit Ally McCoist has criticised Liverpool goalkeeper Alisson Becker following the Reds’ dramatic 3-2 Champions League defeat against Fenerbahçe on Wednesday night.

Liverpool twice took the lead in Istanbul but failed to hold on, with substitute Vedat Muriqi scoring an 80th-minute winner to complete a remarkable comeback for the Turkish side.

McCoist was particularly critical of Alisson’s positioning for the decisive goal, questioning why the Brazilian goalkeeper failed to come off his line and claim the cross.

Speaking during TNT Sports’ live coverage, McCoist expressed his disbelief as Muriqi headed home Fenerbahçe’s third goal.

The former Scotland striker felt Alisson should have taken responsibility for dealing with the delivery rather than allowing the opposition striker to attack the ball.

“Brilliant header. When the ball comes in, I just think it’s in the air for a very long time, and I’m looking at my goalkeeper and I’m thinking where is Alisson?! The goalkeeper has to come for that.”

Liverpool made an encouraging start in Istanbul, with teenage midfielder Trey Nyoni opening the scoring in the 25th minute.

The 19-year-old produced a superb first-time volley from the edge of the penalty area to register his first senior goal for the club, becoming the second youngest goalscorer in the compeition for the club.

However, the Reds’ advantage lasted only four minutes.

Former Manchester United forward Mason Greenwood equalised for Fenerbahçe with a deflected free-kick that wrong-footed Alisson.

Liverpool regained control in the second half when substitute Alexander Isak found the net in the 69th minute to restore their lead.

Once again, though, Iraola’s side were unable to protect their advantage.

Archie Brown brought Fenerbahçe level for a second time, tapping home from close range following defensive confusion involving Alisson and Cody Gakpo.

The equaliser set up a tense finale, with Liverpool pushing to regain the lead while leaving themselves vulnerable at the back.

Fenerbahçe eventually capitalised in the 80th minute when Muriqi headed home the decisive goal.

The result completed a memorable comeback for former Liverpool forward Dirk Kuyt, who is now in charge of the Turkish club.

#1342. Former Spurs star Davinson Sanchez is embroiled in mass brawl during Galatasaray's Champions League clash vs Stuttgart - as an ex-Brighton striker is booked for his part in fracas

By LUKE AUGUSTUS, ASSISTANT SPORTS EDITOR

Published: 15:47 EDT, 3 November 2026 | Updated: 17:18 EDT, 3 November 2026

Davinson Sanchez found himself in the middle of an on-pitch brawl on Tuesday as he and his Galatasaray team-mates confronted their Stuttgart counterparts.

The incident came in the 37th minute of their 2-0 Champions League win over Stuttgart.

Looking to start a counter-attack from a Stuttgart corner, Galatasaray broke with Baris Yilmaz before his attempted pass was blocked out for a throw-in on the halfway line by Chris Fuhrich.

After shielding the ball out, Yilmaz reacted angrily to Fuhrich's pressure by dropping him to the ground in front of both dugouts.

That spat was then heightened when former Brighton striker Deniz Undav confronted Yilmaz in support of his Stuttgart team-mate Fuhrich.

That escalation saw the likes of former Tottenham defender Sanchez run over to get involved as players from both teams did likewise.

Former Tottenham defender Davinson Sanchez (centre left) was involved in a mass brawl between Galatasaray and Stuttgart players in the Champions League on Tuesday

Ex-Brighton striker Deniz Undav (right) was also involved as he defended his Stuttgart team

The incident was sparked after Chris Fuhrich (left) battled for the ball with Gala's Baris Yilmaz

Eventually once matters calmed down, Premier League referee Chris Kavanagh booked Yilmaz and Undav - with the likes of Fuhrich and Sanchez avoiding any sanctions.

And come full-time it was Yilmaz and Sanchez smiling as the hosts took the three points.

Aleksey Batrakov scored both goals in the opening 15 minutes of the match, with the second created after a lovely through-ball from Sanchez.

Gala have now won two and lost two of their opening four league phase matches, while this was Stuttgart's first defeat in the competition having won two of their previous games and drawing the other.

After this month's international break, Galatasaray then host Aston Villa on November 24, while Stuttgart travel to Inter Milan a day later.

Liverpool and Newcastle United are reportedly keeping tabs on Sunderland midfielder Noah Sadiki ahead of the January transfer window, with several European heavyweights also interested in the highly rated youngster.

According to a report from Hooligan Soccer, the 21-year-old has attracted significant attention following his impressive performances for the Black Cats, with clubs across England and Europe monitoring his development.

Liverpool are understood to be considering a move for the DR Congo international as they look to add more energy and quality to their midfield department. His ability to contribute defensively while progressing the ball could make him an attractive option for the Merseyside outfit.

Newcastle United are also keeping a close eye on his situation, while Juventus, Napoli and Atletico Madrid have reportedly registered an interest in the midfielder.

Chelsea and Manchester United have also been linked with the Sunderland star, highlighting his growing reputation in European football.

Sadiki could prove to be a useful long-term addition for Liverpool. The youngster is comfortable in central and defensive midfield, and his versatility lets him fill in at right-back when needed.

Want more CaughtOffside coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust.

However, convincing Sunderland to part ways with their prized asset will not be straightforward. The Championship promotion winners secured his services from Union Saint-Gilloise in 2025 and gave him a five-year contract running until 2030.

The report claims that Sunderland could demand between €55m and €60m to sanction his departure, with performance-related bonuses and a sell-on percentage also potentially forming part of their demands.

Sadiki has featured regularly this season, starting 11 of his 12 appearances across competitions. He also made 35 appearances last term and has established himself as an important squad member.

Liverpool could certainly benefit from his energy, versatility and ability to win possession. However, it remains to be seen whether they are prepared to meet Sunderland’s valuation when the transfer window opens in January.

#1340. Why Spence was named best player with first assist in Feyenoord 0-3 Inter

Djed Spence was named Man of the Match after virtually two assists in Inter’s 3-0 Champions League win at Feyenoord, but officially just one. ‘I’m just happy,’ smiled the England international.

Although the official statistics will only show one assist for the opening Yann Bisseck goal in Rotterdam, Spence’s deflected pass did end up on the head of Francesco Pio Esposito for 2-0 as well.

There was very nearly a third, as Esposito was offside on another Spence roll across that was disallowed, while Piotr Zielinski completed the 3-0 rout.

“Grateful for the win, I’m happy with my performance, I’m just happy,” Spence told Inter TV.

“I’m adapting well, the team and manager welcomed me in. I feel good, I hope to help the team and they can help me.”

The England international was the cheaper alternative to Inter’s first choice Marco Palestra for the right wing-back role, after Chelsea out-bid them for the Atalanta talent.

Injuries after the World Cup forced the former Tottenham Hotspur man to wait until October 10 before finally making his debut in the Nerazzurri jersey.

He has had only three starts and this was his first goal contribution for the Italian club, but that is not all.

Spence had never previously managed an assist in any of his previous 16 European appearances for Tottenham and Rennes.

Named Player of the Match by the UEFA Technical Observer Group, the praise for his performance explained why this award was handed out at the final whistle in Rotterdam.

“He dominated the game in the first 35 minutes with two deliveries from the right to help Inter establish a commanding early lead, as well as achieving a high passing accuracy, showing blistering pace and demonstrating his world-class potential within Cristian Chivu’s 3-5-2 system.”
