#1264. Ronaldo stays on under cloud as Messi exits internationals

Just hours before Lionel Messi played his last match for Argentina, Cristiano Ronaldo posted his latest salvo in a row with Portugal. Ronaldo wants to play on despite the troubles, while Messi bathed in adulation.

They are the two players who have defined the last two decades. As football became ever more popular, commercial and dominant in the cultural and sporting landscape, Cristiano Ronaldo and Lionel Messi remained its twin peaks.

Along with that has come endless social media posts, stories and discussions about who is better. Does Messi's World Cup and two Copa America titles with Argentina trump Ronaldo's Euro 2016 win and two Nations League titles? Or does the Portuguese's greater number of goals mean more? How about their club honors?

It is, essentially, a subjective argument and not one that can ever be resolved. It remains to be seen whether that's also true of the public spat between Ronaldo and his Portugal coach Jorge Jesus.

On Tuesday, Messi scored a 126th goal in his 208th game for Argentina. Shortly before he did, Ronaldo posted a 2,000-word statement in which he stopped short of quitting the national team but said there was an "absolute breakdown of trust" between him and the coach.

Ronaldo's comments refer to Portugal's recent match against Norway in which he said he was initially to be rested before being asked to warm up as a substitute without ever being brought on. The striker, 41, walked away from the team's camp for the remainder of the international break, but said the story is not over.

"I can promise all my fans, and naturally especially all Portuguese people, that we will have one or more farewell matches. There will be time for that," said Ronaldo, who plays for Al-Nassr in Saudi Arabia.

"Despite the absolute breach of trust in the coach's word, as anyone who witnessed these conversations can attest, I should not have done it," Ronaldo said. "The responsibility is entirely mine. I apologize to the Portuguese people once again, but the breaking of one's word has, for me, a defining impact.

"I felt that, from that point on, my staying would only harm the group, and I did what I have always said I would do if I didn't feel useful: I picked up my bags and left," he continued before suggesting he accepted there may be a need for the coach or federation to punish him.

It was a long way from the emotional scenes in Rosario, Argentina. Instead of anger and recrimination, the overriding emotions there were gratitude, nostalgia and sadness.

"Not coming anymore is going to be deeply painful. I swear I'd like to play for the rest of my life, because playing for the Argentina national team is the most beautiful thing that can happen to you," Messi, who now plays his club football for Inter Miami in the US, told the 80,000 fans who had packed in to see him score a penalty in a 3-0 win over Benin.

For some, the contrasting evenings offered a neat synopsis of the pair. Ronaldo, less naturally gifted than his counterpart, has made the most of his talents with a singular focus which many believe often makes him prioritize himself over the team. He has had similar fallouts with managers and head coaches before, including Jose Mourinho at Real Madrid, Erik ten Hag at Manchester United and Portugal's 2022 World Cup coach, Fernando Santos.

Ronaldo's much-discussed aim to reach 1,000 career goals is held up by some as further evidence of where his motivations lie.

"You know what my goal is. I want to win trophies, and I want to reach that number (1,000 goals) that you all know. I will reach the number for sure, if no injuries," he said last December. He is currently on 979.

For others, that is simply what is required to be the best. While Messi's quiet character and general refusal to play out his life in public suggest a more humble character focused on helping the team, his genius has undoubtedly changed the teams around him. In the 2026 World Cup, he barely broke into a run but still led an otherwise fairly limited Argentina to the final with eight goals.

There will be no more Messi goals for Argentina and, despite his promises, no absolute assurances that the world will see Ronaldo in a Portugal shirt again. For now, both will head back to their club sides to play out their twilight years away from the intensity of Europe's top leagues. But wherever they go from here, the spotlight will keep following.

#1263. Saliba has fight on his hands to usurp ‘unbelievable’ Konsa

From the moment Ezri Konsa pulled on an Arsenal shirt, he has moved with all the composure of a man who knows exactly where to be and when. The centre-back has required no adaptation period in north London, where he has filled the considerable shoes of William Saliba with such class that Arsenal have hardly missed the Frenchman at all.

The loss of Saliba to a long-term back injury was supposed to be a major problem for Arsenal. Instead, the situation has now reached a point where some fans are wondering how Saliba will get back into the side. That may prove a little extreme, but the fact there is even a discussion is proof of Konsa’s superb impact at the Emirates Stadium.

“Unbelievable,” Mikel Arteta, the Arsenal manager, said of his £55m signing. “He’s come to a huge club and to position yourself in that manner, and to perform at the level he is, it is very difficult to do. We are really lucky to have him.”

In Arsenal’s latest victory, their seventh from eight matches in the Premier League this season, Konsa offered all of his usual defensive security and calmness in possession. Even more excitingly, he also scored his first goal for the club, smashed in from close range after a corner had caused chaos in Everton’s penalty area. It was Arsenal’s first set-piece goal of the season.

“I have been waiting to score my first goal for a while,” Konsa said. “I spoke to the set-piece coach before the game and he told me he’s been waiting for my goal as well. We felt as players that it was coming, and today was the day.”

Some eyebrows were raised when Arsenal paid such a large fee to sign Konsa from Aston Villa. The Villa fans, though, were not among those who questioned the price or the player’s ability. They have known for years at Villa Park that Konsa is a player of the highest quality, and they will not be surprised by his exceptional start to his Arsenal career.

The same is true of the Arsenal players. Arteta asked the England internationals in his squad about Konsa before buying him, and the feedback was overwhelmingly positive. Konsa was already close friends with Declan Rice, Bukayo Saka and Eberechi Eze before completing his transfer from Villa.

Konsa’s start to life at Arsenal is all the more impressive because he did not even have a pre-season. He effectively came straight from the World Cup into the club, and has been starting games since early September. His first start was against Chelsea, when he endeared himself to the home fans with a crunching tackle on former team-mate Morgan Rogers.

Konsa, 29, has quickly built a strong relationship with Gabriel Magalhães, his defensive partner who scored Arsenal’s other goal here against Everton, from Ben White’s cross. For both centre-backs to find the net felt like a throwback to last year, when Arsenal were so dangerous from crosses, and underlined how Arteta’s team are capable of hurting their opponents in many different ways.

The nature of the goals might give a misleading impression of Arsenal’s performance, though. This was not a gritty win. Arteta’s side produced some excellent passing moves and circulated the ball with menace throughout the game. They were also a little open at times, especially in the first half when Everton created a handful of decent chances.

Thierno Barry missed the best of those opportunities, with the score at 1-0. It was the closest the visitors came to hurting the champions, aside from some of James Tarkowski’s full-blooded tackles. “I felt we didn’t really get to a level that was good enough to get near them,” admitted David Moyes, the Everton manager.

The victory, combined with Manchester City’s defeat earlier in the day, put Arsenal level on points at the top of the table. Aside from the extraordinary thrashing at Brighton, Arteta’s side have looked just as solid, if not more so, than last season. That speaks volumes of the quality in the team, of course, but also says plenty about the way Konsa has adjusted to his new surroundings. Thanks to him, Saliba’s absence has not hurt at all.

“Great feeling, it always is. A clean sheet, a goal – my first goal for the club – so a fantastic day overall.

“I’ve been waiting to score my first goal for a while. I spoke to the set piece coach before the game and he told me he’s been waiting for my goal as well, so it was only right that I got the goal today.

“I’ve come to this stadium for many seasons, I know how tough it is to play against us. It’s not surprising to me.

“We are champions and to be champions you’ve got to win games consistently. This is our home and we want to win as many games here as possible.”

All over at the Emirates and the champions go level on points with Manchester City at the top of the table.

They kept another clean sheet and scored from a set-piece again. All is right in Arsenal’s world!

Oscar Bobb’s first Premier League goal for Fulham earned a 1-0 win over Coventry that lifted the Cottagers clear of the relegation zone.

Bobb produced a fine bit of individual skill to strike in the 80th minute as he twisted his way into the box and bent a shot into the far corner, only his second goal for the club in any competition since his £27million move from Manchester City back in January.

That was enough to give Fulham their first away win in nine attempts, a run that dated back to February, only a week after they ended their winless start to the league campaign by edging out Hull 1-0 as the pressure continues to ease on Alvaro Arbeloa.

Josh King had earlier hit the post for the visitors, who edged Coventry in just about every department to leave Frank Lampard’s side second-bottom of the table.

The hosts had only brief spells of sustained possession in Fulham’s half, but did little to trouble Bernd Leno on a frustrating afternoon which bought the CBS Arena back down to earth after their 4-1 win over Newcastle in their last home outing.

Odegaard drives a shot high over the ball as Arsenal close in on another clean sheet.

Probably sums up Zubimendi’s season so far that he finally gets some meaningful minutes in the Premier League and ends up getting smashed in the face and covered in his own blood. This is after he got injured in a cool-down a few weeks ago. When your luck’s out...

Brilliant play from Oscar Bobb as he cuts inside on his left foot and bends a shot into the far bottom corner for the away side.

Treatment is needed for Zubimendi after he is caught on the nose by Barry.

Big chance for Everton. Garner whips a teasing cross into the box, Dewsbury-Hall meets it with his head on the run but the ball flies just wide of the post.

EvertonOFF Johnson, Mykolenko ON Dibling, Hackney

Tarkowski is the latest yellow card for Everton after a foul on Havertz.

Eze with a poor cross into the box. He fails to run back quickly and Arteta sprints to the edge of the touchline and goes berserk at the midfielder.

How have Arsenal reacted to their top scorer Saka being injured? Both of their centre backs have scored for the first time this season.

On his 200 Premier League appearance for Arsenal, Gabriel marks it with his first goal of the season.

It is a lovely move with slick one-touch passing. The ball is fed to White making a run down the outside and he clips the ball to the far post for Gabriel to head home.

OFF Merino, Lewis-Skelly, GyokeresON Calafiori, Guimaraes, Havertz

Garner is booked for Everton now after barging into Merino off the ball.

Arteta is shown a yellow card for something. Not sure what for yet. But the Arsenal manager is looking to make some changes off the bench.

Arsenal have been guilty of overplaying today. Opting for the extra pass rather than taking a shot. The game is open at the moment and that makes things dangerous for the home side.

Yellow card for Lewis-Skelly after bringing down Johnson. Gabriel is back on the pitch and seems happy enough to continue.

Arsenal have defensive options in Timber, Hincapie, Calafiori and Mosquera if Arteta wants to avoid taking any risks.

A worry for Arsenal as Gabriel jars his knee into the ground as he tries to clear the ball. The Brazilian is receiving treatment and hobbles off the pitch.

Gabriel immediately raised his hand for medical attention after making that clearance. He really extended his leg to get the ball away. Looks to be in a lot of pain.

Latest corner from Arsenal after Eze’s shot is blocked by Rohl. Rice’s delivery into the near post is headed clear to Odegaard, who shoots ambitiously from distance and Pickford collects the ball comfortably.

Arsenal get the match restarted. The longer the match goes on without extending the lead, Everton will think they have a chance.

Before today, Arsenal had averaged five corners per match in the Premier League this season. In the first 45 minutes here, they had 10 corners.

Yellow card for Mykolenko after he catches White wide on the right. Rice whips the ball in and Merino meets it with a flick goalwards but the ball goes over the bar.

That is the final touch of the half and the players are running off to get dry!

Big chance for Everton. White thinks he has time when he heads the ball back to Raya but he does not connect well and Barry is there to pick it up and he flicks a shot at goal but Raya reacts quickly to parry the ball.

Raya is penalised for taking too long with the ball and Everton have a cheap corner. Danger is cleared by Arsenal as they force Everton back into their half.

The conditions are terrible at the moment. Heavy wind and rain causing havoc.

A lot of set-pieces for Arsenal today as they continue to put Everton under the cosh. Can they take advantage of their dominance again before the break?

Arsenal have found their groove again, with Madueke twice going close to extending their lead. Rice, Lewis-Skelly, Odegaard and Merino are forming a box in midfield and Everton don’t seem to know how to shut them down.

Another effort at goal for Madueke. This one is a snapshot from the edge of the box that goes into the side netting.

Madueke should do better. Rice finds him and the winger drives into the box. He takes a shot but drags a right-footed effort wide.

Chance for Arsenal. Rice finds space behind the Everton midfield and drives forward. He plays a pass to Lewis-Skelly, who lays it off to Eze. The England midfielder sidefoots a cross into the box but no one in an Arsenal shirt is there to meet it.

Courtesy of Opta: Arsenal scored their first set-piece goal in all competitions (not including penalties) since May of last season against Crystal Palace, ending a run of 13 games without one.

George is looking lively for Everton. He tries to come inside and whip an effort to the far corner but the ball deflects wide.

From the corner, Gabriel clears off the line after Raya loses track of the ball.

Everton have responded impressively to the Konsa goal and have been the better team since falling behind. Midfielders Garner and Armstrong are growing into the game quite nicely.

Everton have responded well to going behind here. The early goal against them will have ripped up any plans to sit deep and play on the counter.

Set-pieces are back on the menu for Arsenal. Ezri Konsa’s first goal for the club is their first goal from a corner this season, which will come as a relief to set-piece coach Nicolas Jover. “Set piece again, ole ole,” sing the Arsenal fans. Arteta’s side had started the game on the front foot.

Arsenal had not scored from a corner this season... until now. Konsa breaks the deadlock after a melee in the box and his pokes the ball into the net.

A couple of early set pieces from Declan Rice. Everton do well to clear the danger. But have another one now...

Horrible conditions at the Emirates today. The rain has been lashing down. The Emirates drainage system is usually able to cope with this sort of thing. If the wind picks up, that’s likely to be a bigger problem for the two teams.

After a minute’s applause in honour of Ken Friar, the match makes a prompt start at the Emirates.

“Yeah, we’ve had a good start. Obviously, we had a bit of a blip last week against Chelsea. I don’t think we, as a team, won first and second balls enough and that’s something the manager wants us to get back to today. You’ve got to win your battles.”

On what makes Arsenal difficult to play...

“They’re reigning Premier League champions, a top side that has been knocking on the door to win the title for a few years before as well. They’re a team at a high level but this is what Premier League football is all about and it’s up to us to get a result.”

“Well, we play every two-and-a-half days so we didn’t have much time to recover, so we need full energy. There are certain specific players as well that they fit really well for the game that we expect today and that’s how we start.”

“A very competitive team, a really well organised team. I think that it’s very clear what they want to do, where they want to take the game. The threats, when they have a space to run, any time that they are able to put the ball in their box, you know the presence and aggression that they have. So, yeah, we have to really be at it and be very aggressive from the beginning.”

One of the clearest signs a football club is in a good place is when the debate switches from whether the team are winning to how they are winning.

This is currently Arsenal and Mikel Arteta’s world. For years, Arsenal coaches and players were asked how and when they would start collecting major trophies again. With no concern about their capacity to challenge for top honours over the coming years, the style has become the main focus.

It’s a welcome “problem” – or some might argue a non-existent one – for Arteta while his side is so strong. Building a fortress is the expensive, time-consuming and difficult part. Once it’s constructed and established, how you decorate it is a matter of taste.

Whether neutrals will hold the current champions in the same regard as the great Arsène Wenger sides will be a trivial concern if Arteta does what no Arsenal manager has since 1935 – defend the league title – and then add a few more, which is a serious possibility based on the balance of power in England and the likely punishment heading Manchester City’s way.

Today there will be tributes to Ken Friar, who passed away at the age of 92 earlier this year. Advertising boards outside the Emirates Stadium have been taken over by images of Friar, who had a remarkable 70-year association with the club.

In today’s programme, captain Martin Odegaard has written the following: “It’s exceptional people like Ken Friar who have built the club into what it is today, and we as the current team are the ones privileged to continue his legacy.”

This is a first Premier League start of the season for Viktor Gyokeres, who has been behind Kai Havertz in the pecking order over the past few months. Gyokeres has yet to score in nine appearances in all competitions this season, although he would (understandably) make the point that it’s harder to do so when you are coming off the bench late in games.

For Arsenal, Arteta shuffles his team after the draw against Bayern: White, Lewis-Skelly, Merino, Eze and Gyokeres start.

Max Dowman, who scored a memorable goal in this fixture last season, is on the bench.

For Everton, Jack Grealish misses today’s game due to sickness, while Jarrad Branthwaite is absent because of concussion protocols despite finishing last week’s match with Chelsea after a head collision with Emi Martinez.

Arsenal: Raya, White, Gabriel, Konsa, Lewis-Skelly, Rice, Merino, Odegaard, Madueke, Eze, Gyokeres.Subs: Arrizabalaga, Timber, Hincapie, Calafiori, Mosquera, Zubimendi, Guimaraes, Dowman, Havertz

Hello and welcome to coverage from the Emirates as Premier League champions Arsenal host Everton.

Mikel Arteta’s men produced a good performance in midweek to draw with Bayern Munich in the Champions League while David Moyes’s squad have had the week off following their 2-0 defeat by Chelsea last weekend.

Arteta said: “We’re having three games in six days so we know what’s happening, especially when the games are so demanding and the necessity is to win. We know that, so we prepare the players for those scenarios and do the best we possibly can.

“I know David so well and how he sets the team, the quality they have in their organisation and individually. It’s no coincidence they didn’t lose before their last game. They have a really good team, which we know because in recent clashes, it’s always been a really difficult game for us.”

Both teams enter this game having been beaten just once this season but eight points separate them with Arsenal in second and Everton in eighth.

Moyes said: “It’s not an easy game and never has been over many years. We look forward to it; they had a game in midweek, and we have to try and capitalise on that. I thought we did really well last year against them; we played really well down at Arsenal, and I hope we can do the same.

“When I look back at the team we had out, we were pretty threadbare at that time, but we did a good job, and I hope we can do it again. Obviously Arsenal have some many different tools in their bag and people they can use in different positions, so we’re fully aware of the team we’re up against and the level.”

Former Arsenal players Ainsley Maitland-Niles and Christian Norgaard could feature for Everton this afternoon.

#1262. Suspected pneumonic plague in Siberia: What we know about the disease

After a worker at a Russian plague research institute in Siberia died October 2, 2026, nearly 200 of her contacts were under medical observation. But authorities there denied pneumonic plague had caused the death.

UPDATE: Following initial reports raising concerns that a lab worker had died accidentally of pneumonic plague, the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) said it was now also "closely monitoring the situation."

However, in a statement published October 6, 2026, the ECDC said that "based on the limited information currently available, there are no reports of secondary cases and no evidence of sustained human-to-human transmission that would cause further spread of the disease."

Following the death of a Russian laboratory worker, there is speculation about an outbreak of pneumonic plague, a highly contagious bacterial infection of the lungs. Russia denies there is a broader risk to the community.

Russian officials have said the laboratory worker's death was not caused by a plague pathogen. The 28-year-old died of "pneumonia of unknown origin," according to Russia's Interfax news agency, citing Rospotrebnadzor, Russia's disease-control agency. According to that agency, samples taken from the woman showed no microorganisms "related to her professional activities." This contradicts earlier information.

Local media had previously reported that the woman, who worked at an institute dedicated to fighting plague, had dropped a test tube.

She reportedly died on Friday, October 2, 2026, at the district hospital in Shelekhov, a town near Irkutsk in Siberia.

According to official Russian figures, authorities placed two hospitals and a children's clinic under quarantine. Local reports said staff at the institute were being quarantined at their workplace. The US news site Axios has reported that around 200 people who had been in contact with the woman had been placed under observation. There were no further reported infections.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Even so, distrust of how Russia handles information persists. On one of DW's Russian-language social media channels, a user wrote: "It wouldn't surprise me if this turns into a disaster now, both in terms of the spread and the quarantine measures."

All that is known for certain, at the time of writing and first publication (October 5, 2026), is that pneumonic plague is highly contagious.

Pneumonic plague is a form of plague that infects the lungs. Like every form of the disease, it is caused by Yersinia pestis, a bacterium usually found in small mammals, such as rodents and in the fleas that feed on them.

The World Health Organization describes the pneumonic form as the most virulent type of plague.

Its incubation period can be as short as 24 hours, and it is the only form that passes easily from person to person through respiratory particles released when a sick patient coughs. This is why, according to the WHO, it can trigger severe epidemics.

Symptoms appear quickly: high fever, headache and weakness, followed by a rapidly worsening pneumonia with shortness of breath, chest pain and a cough that often brings up blood.

A person can catch pneumonic plague by breathing in the bacteria directly, or by developing it when bubonic and/or septicemic plague go untreated and spread to the lungs.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Pneumonic plague is not a separate disease. It is one of three forms of plague: bubonic, septicemic and pneumonic.

What sets them apart is where the infection settles in the body, and that shapes how the disease spreads and how deadly it is.

Bubonic plague is the most common form and the one most people think of when they hear the word "plague." It usually follows a flea bite. The bacteria travel to the nearest lymph node, which swells into a painful lump known as a bubo. According to the WHO, it rarely spreads between people.

If bubonic plague goes untreated, the bacteria can move further through the body. If they spread into the bloodstream, the disease can become septicemic plague, which causes bleeding under the skin, tissue death in the fingers and toes, and organ failure. If the bacteria reach the lungs, the illness becomes pneumonic plague, the form that can pass from person to person through the air. Both septicemic and pneumonic plague can also develop directly, without a bubo appearing first.

Left untreated, bubonic plague kills between 30-60% of patients. The septicemic and pneumonic forms are always fatal without treatment.

Pneumonic plague is curable, but only if treatment starts quickly. The WHO warns that without treatment it can kill within 18 to 24 hours of the first symptoms.

Common antibiotics can cure the infection, and recovery rates are high when patients are treated within about a day of falling ill.

Speed is what decides the outcome. Doctors are advised not to wait for laboratory confirmation and to start antibiotics as soon as plague is suspected, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

The drugs themselves are not rare or specialized. They are standard, widely used antibiotics, and patients usually need a course of up to two weeks. To stop the infection spreading, patients are kept in isolation, and wearing masks helps protect those around them, the WHO says.

People close to a patient are treated as well, even if they have no symptoms. Both the WHO and the CDC recommend a seven-day course of preventive antibiotics for close contacts of anyone with pneumonic plague.

The WHO does not recommend a plague vaccine for the public. It reserves vaccination for high-risk groups, such as laboratory staff who work with the bacterium and health workers.

#1261. Nobel Prize in chemistry goes to Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai

Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai won the Nobel Prize in chemistry for their groundbreaking discoveries related to the origin of chirality and life's building blocks.

The Nobel Prize in chemistry on Wednesday was awarded to Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai "for the discovery of non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis."

Kagan, who is 95 years old and was born in France, is affiliated with France’s Université Paris-Sud, and Soai, who is 76 years old and was born in Japan, is based at the Tokyo University of Science.

The scientists share the Nobel Prize for answering longstanding questions in chemistry about life's origins.

Specifically, the duo solved an age-old mystery that has long puzzled chemists: some molecules, like amino acids, exist as two variants that are mirror images of one another, but just one of the variants out of the two is found in living organisms.

The two answered questions about why life chooses one variant over another.

The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced the winner in Stockholm.

In chemistry, life's building blocks are what scientists call homochiral, after the Greek words for "same" and "hand."

The Nobel Committee said the chemistry prize recognizes discoveries that have enabled chemists to drive chemical reactions that lead to homochirality.

"Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai have provided a solution to a chemical mystery that is over a century old: how homochirality can emerge spontaneously," Heiner Linke, chair of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry, said in a news release. "The chemical reactions they have developed are spectacular."

The duo's discoveries, the news release said, "have been decisive for chemists who design reactions for the manufacture of pharmaceuticals."

#1260. '90s art scene in the UK: An international, edgy trendsetter

The 1990s are remembered for Brit-pop and provocative fashion, but beyond the nostalgia, it was a decade of cultural experimentation and social change. Tate Britain's new exhibition looks past the familiar icons.

The 1990s in Britain are often remembered through a haze of nostalgia consisting of rave culture, Britpop and provocative art and fashion by the likes of Tracey Emin and Alexander McQueen.

Undeniably, the decade was a time of major change in British society — the long reign of Margaret Thatcher had come to an end and the West entered a period of relative post-Cold War stability.

Meanwhile, British cultural icons like Oasis, the Spice Girls and Vivienne Westwood garnered international fame.

But Tate Britain's new exhibition "The 90s: Art and Fashion," which opens on October 8 and runs through February 14, 2027, urges viewers to look beyond the familiar names and images.

Even though now prominent artists such as Damien Hirst and Juergen Teller are among the show's 70 contributors, the exhibition also aims to highlight the creative input of those in communities which were left out of the mainstream discourse.

After all, says chief curator Edward Enninful in the exhibition's program, "the energy of the 90s was not concentrated in a single movement, but distributed across communities, disciplines and geographies that have not always been equally represented."

For Enninful, the exhibition is personal: The Ghanaian-born British fashion editor, stylist and creative director became the youngest-ever fashion director of i-D Magazine in the 90s at age 18, helping shape the diverse and experimental London fashion scene of the 1990s. He later became editor-in-chief of British Vogue in 2017. Enninful writes that he and his co-curators aimed to present a body of work which "reflects a broader landscape of practices and voices that shaped the period, many of which operated beyond the structures of visibility at the time." The exhibition pays special attention to artists of color and women whose work was not necessarily showcased as prominently at the time.

Black masculinity became "a site of cultural negotiation" in Britain in the 90s, writes co-curator Helen Little in the program text: "Figures such as Chris Ofili, Steve McQueen, Keith Piper, Koto Bolofo and Ozwald Boateng reimagined the Black masculine, challenging the racist specter of Black men, who had been defined as part of a masculinity crisis linked to post-industrial decline and excluded from the narrative of 'Cool Britannia.'"

Just like "Swinging London" in the 1960s, "Cool Britannia" became a widespread phrase to refer to the 1990s as an era during which British youth culture, pop music, art and political optimism boomed.

The 90s also offered artists plenty of chances to create without waiting for support from traditional gatekeepers. Britain entered the decade in recession, but that economic uncertainty also left artists free to do what they wished.

Empty buildings and industrial spaces were turned into informal venues. A 23-year-old Damien Hirst orchestrated "Freeze," a self-organized student exhibition in 1988 in a disused London warehouse. It became a landmark early art exhibition for the generation of artists known as the "Young British Artists" or YBA.

Artists Sarah Lucas and Tracey Emin opened The Shop, a temporary art gallery and social space in 1992, as a place where exhibitions could develop outside established galleries. Lucas and Emin also paved the way for women artists thanks to their deeply personal works and their edgy expressions of female liberation. While the Spice Girls helped make feminism accessible to a younger generation of Brits in the 90s by popularizing the "girl power" slogan and shaping "identity through agency power and resistance," as Tate curator Helen Little argues, Emin and Lucas meanwhile "presented a new visual language of clothing as art to tackle societal taboos around female sexuality, vulnerability and desire" — from t-shirts with provocative slogans to a grunge look of scuffed Dr. Martens boots with razor blades. Their work "held a mirror up to gender, behavior and identity," Little writes.

At the same time, the British fashion industry came into the international spotlight.

In a feminine sensuality counter to the gender stereotypes dismissed by Emin and Lucas, waif-like Kate Moss came to represent the feminine ideal of the 1990s. Dubbed "heroin-chic," the style was an antithesis to the glamorous, athletic physiques of the supermodels who preceded her. Corinne Day's photographs of the model led to the raw aesthetic to be labelled "grunge" after the anguished style of rock music hailing from Seattle and led by Nirvana.

The trend has undergone significant cultural reexamination since then: "Along with the look also came criticism that the strung-out look of drug or alcohol addiction was glamorized while encouraging serious eating disorders in a generation of young women," points out Alex Farquharson, director of the Tate Gallery in his foreword to the exhibition.

The 1990s were also an exciting era for Britain in haute couture, as legendary designers John Galliano led Dior, while Alexander McQueen started directing Givenchy at the age of 27.

McQueen's runway presentations were more akin to performance art than commercial fashion shows — and they often included historical critiques. Among them was the famous finale of his Fall/Winter 1998 collection at a London warehouse, during which the model stood in a circle of flames. Titled "Joan," the show was a reference to the killing of Joan of Arc. McQueen designed several other runway shows that reflected on British history, with topics of conquest and punishment repeatedly coming to the forefront. His 1995 presentation "Highland Rape" referenced the history of Scotland's subjugation, with the designer describing it as "England's rape of Scotland."

As co-curator Jessica Vaughan points out in her exhibition text: "Art, fashion and photography were not simply transgressive reactions … but reflected a genuine public unease with Britain's global identity and its past." In a world that can now feel increasingly mediated by screens, algorithms and established platforms, the artwork of the 90s offers a reminder of the value of physical spaces and fresh DIY creativity of the last smartphone-free decade.

#1259. Unai Emery has closed gap between Aston Villa and Europe's elite - but rampant Barcelona proved there is still a way to go as Lamine Yamal dazzles, writes OLIVER HOLT

Published: 17:17 EDT, 3 November 2026 | Updated: 11:27 EDT, 4 November 2026

John McGinn heard the question. His eyes darted around Barcelona's packed media auditorium for a second or two on Monday night. What was it like to be about to play in the Nou Camp, the Aston Villa skipper had been asked, as if this were to be some sort of spin off from Bill and Ted's Excellent Adventure.

McGinn was careful with his answer. He did not seek to downplay the nature of the occasion or the thrill that comes with lining up in such a majestic arena. But he was determined not to play the wide-eyed ingenu. 'What our club is trying to do now,' McGinn said, 'is make this normal, make this a yearly experience.'

So when he and his team-mates walked up the flight of steps from the dressing rooms into the vast bowl of the stadium on Tuesday evening, they were here to show that they were not arrivistes. Villa is a historic club. They won this competition in 1982, ten years before Barcelona ever did. They were not here for a treat or to get patted on the back just for turning up.

It is nearly 20 years since Liverpool became the last English club to win here and nobody gave Villa too much chance of ending that drought. They are being told constantly that the odds are stacked against them and that their much-admired manager, Unai Emery, may be tempted by the entreaties of struggling 'giants' elsewhere.

That was the reason why this game early in the league phase had attained so much importance. For Villa, it was a symbol of something they aspire to. They want to get used to belonging in this company, to walking up those steps, to emerging into the stadium in the pouring rain, and staring at players of the calibre of Lamine Yamal, Rodri and Pau Cubarsi staring back at them.

It still feels as if they stand on the cusp of something bigger but they blew their shot at proving that on Tuesday night. They needed to be at their best to have a chance of beating Hansi Flick's side, which sits atop LaLiga, and they were far too naïve in defence to get close to causing a shock. They are rising but this was a step too far at this stage of their evolution.

Lamine Yamal (centre) and Barcelona had plenty to smile about after beating Aston Villa 3-0

Yamal opened the scoring for Barcelona after just seven minutes with this left-footed finish

Raphinha (right) doubled Barca's lead after half-time with this strike at the Spotify Nou Camp

The Nou Camp, which is still in the midst of an extensive renovation and was only about two-thirds full, was ringed by towering yellow cranes, peering down at the floodlit patch of green. From their lofty vantage point, they saw Villa get off to the worst possible start.

Only seven minutes had gone when Emery's team gift-wrapped a present for the home side. Zion Suzuki played the ball out short to Joao Gomes but Gomes panicked under pressure from the Barcelona press and the close attention of Pedri. He played the ball square without looking, straight to Yamal.

Of all the players he could have found, Gomes had to find Yamal. The Spain superstar squared up Pau Torres and then curled the ball around him with a gentle caress of his left boot. Suzuki was helpless. The ball nestled in the corner of the net. Barcelona had scored 56 goals in 14 games before this match. Extending the hand of generosity to them must have felt particularly galling for Emery.

Villa almost hit back immediately. A stinging volley from Matty Cash was deflected wide and Barcelona looked jittery at the back. Nicolas Jackson played a square ball to Johan Manzambi, who should have equalised but scuffed his first-time effort wide of Joan Garcia. Barcelona were thankful for Garcia's intervention when he raced out of his goal to dispossess Jackson as he charged on to a through ball.

Yamal was rampant. His battle with Ian Maatsen was a mismatch and Maatsen was booked after 11 minutes for hacking him down. Villa were still intent on playing themselves into trouble. Suzuki repeated his mistake when he tried to play the ball out to Joao Gomes. This time, Pedri beat him to it and the loose ball fell to Gordon. Gordon hit his shot towards the corner but Suzuki redeemed himself by diving to push it away.

Barcelona had the better of the play. They looked like scoring every time they went forward. Time and again, either Raphinha or Yamal found space to run at the Villa defence, which was barely coping. Even in that context, though, it was an open game. Villa had chances, too. Manzambi forced a fine save out of Garcia. A Jackson breakaway was thwarted by a last-ditch block.

But seven minutes after the break, Barcelona doubled their lead. Fermin Lopez played a clever ball to Raphinha, who had found a yard of space in the box. Raphinha, LaLiga's leading scorer this season, drilled a left-foot shot goalwards and it deflected off the heel of Torres, wrong-footed Suzuki and rolled over the line.

Barcelona put the game out of reach midway through the half when Joao Cancelo forced his way past McGinn on the left flank and hit a sumptuous cross into the box with the outside of his right foot. Raphinha gambled on the path of the ball, darted behind his marker and tucked the ball away.

Raphinha completed the scoreline with this cute finish as Barcelona completed their victory

For Aston Villa, this will be a learning curve as they look to go far in the Champions League

Villa manager Unai Emery will have plenty to think about after another Nou Camp defeat

Substitute Leon Goretzka hit the face of a post for Villa late on but the game was already gone. There was no shame in losing to a team who are one of the favourites to win the competition this season but there was frustration in the way Villa had handed their opponents the advantage.

Emery looked bedraggled as he stood on the touchline in the rain, arms folded, shaking his head. This was his 15th defeat in 16 visits to the Nou Camp. As Villa's coach fights to edge his team closer to the elite of the game, this game will become just one more bad memory.

#1258. Comprehensive mapping of essential-gene interactions in M. tuberculosis

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Mycobacterium tuberculosis, the causative agent of tuberculosis, remains the world’s deadliest pathogen1. Despite intensive study, many of its genes remain uncharacterized, which limits the insight that can be gained into tuberculosis biology and constrains drug development. Genetic interaction (GI) mapping is a powerful strategy to define functional relationships between genes by quantifying how the phenotypic effects of combined perturbations deviate from expectations based on single-gene perturbations2,3. Here we develop a dual-sgRNA CRISPR-interference platform that enables high-throughput GI mapping in mycobacteria. We address key technical challenges in library construction and data interpretation by incorporating unique barcodes for each sgRNA pair and implementing a robust statistical pipeline for GI detection. Focusing on essential genes, we generate comprehensive GI maps in the model mycobacterium Mycobacterium smegmatis and the pathogen M. tuberculosis. These maps recapitulate known biology, uncover thousands of previously unrecognized interactions and identify functional connections between essential genes and drug targets. By generating AlphaFold3-based protein–protein interaction predictions4 for all gene pairs in our GI maps, we show that a subset of GIs is likely to reflect underlying physical associations. Validation of selected GIs confirms both novel biological relationships and opportunities for synergistic targeting. Overall, this work establishes a generalizable framework for dual-gene perturbation and defines the architecture of essential-gene networks in mycobacteria, advancing both our understanding of tuberculosis biology and the rational design of combination therapies.

Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), the world’s leading infectious cause of death1, is among the bacteria that have been most extensively sequenced, but the functions and interactions of many of its genes remain poorly understood. This knowledge gap limits our understanding of the genetic foundations of tuberculosis (TB) and hinders the development of effective therapies.

Genetic interaction (GI) mapping is a powerful approach for deciphering the functional relationships between genes2,3. It involves systematically assessing how perturbing one gene modifies the phenotype associated with perturbing a second gene. A GI is defined as a combined phenotype that deviates from the expectation based on single-gene perturbations. Positive interactions occur when dual perturbation produces a milder phenotype than expected, whereas negative interactions—including synthetic lethal effects—result in a more severe phenotype. Applied at scale, GI mapping yields quantitative interaction profiles that serve as high-resolution phenotypes3. These profiles can generate functional hypotheses for uncharacterized genes, reveal surprising roles for genes of known function and identify connections between distinct biological pathways3. Moreover, they can highlight potential synergistic and antagonistic drug–target relationships, informing combination therapies5.

GI mapping in Mtb has historically been constrained by biological and technical challenges, including slow growth, biosafety requirements and limited early genetic tools. The development of high-density transposon mutagenesis libraries combined with hybridization- or sequencing-based readouts (TnSeq)6,7 constituted a major advance, permitting genome-wide identification of conditionally essential genes8 and GI mapping in deletion mutants9. However, such approaches are typically restricted to non-essential genes, excluding most antibiotic targets. CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) has since emerged as a complementary technique10,11,12,13, enabling conditional and tunable knockdown of both essential and non-essential genes. In bacterial systems, dual-gene knockdowns have been used to identify GIs among small gene sets14, and larger-scale efforts have paired individual deletion or knockdown strains with genome-wide libraries15,16. Dual-CRISPRi and dual-TnSeq approaches for comprehensive GI mapping have been implemented in Bacillus subtilis and Streptococcus pneumoniae17,18,19. However, technical limitations have thus far precluded the development of a comparable system in Mtb.

To enable high-throughput GI mapping in Mtb, we developed a dual-single-guide RNA (sgRNA) CRISPRi platform for mycobacteria. Addressing key challenges in library construction and data analysis, we devised a robust experimental and statistical pipeline for high-confidence detection of GIs. Using this platform, we mapped GIs among nearly all essential genes in Mycobacterium smegmatis (Msm) and Mtb, prioritizing this technically demanding class of genes because of their centrality to cellular processes and importance as antibiotic targets. These maps recapitulate known biological relationships, validating the platform, and also uncover thousands of novel GIs. We further performed AlphaFold3 co-folding for all gene pairs (approximately 600,000) represented in the GI maps, identifying GIs that are likely to reflect physical associations and offering a basis for mechanistic hypotheses. Finally, we validated selected predictions from the maps, including drug–drug interactions and roles in the electron transport chain (ETC) for several genes of unknown function. Together, these maps constitute a powerful resource for elucidating Mtb biology and guiding the rational design of combination therapies.

To enable dual-sgRNA CRISPRi-based GI mapping in Mtb, we adapted the Combinatorial Genetics En Masse (CombiGEM) framework20 to the Mtb CRISPRi platform10, assigning each sgRNA a barcode, and using a cloning workflow that preserves sgRNA–barcode linkage and positions paired barcodes in close proximity (Extended Data Fig. 1a). This design permits accurate quantification of dual-sgRNA strain abundance by barcode sequencing, facilitating high-throughput GI mapping.

GI detection for essential genes requires sgRNAs that impose a precise fitness cost: sufficient to reveal interactions, yet not so severe as to mask additive or synergistic effects. Compounding this challenge, the combinatorial scale of dual-sgRNA libraries necessitates selecting only a small number of sgRNAs per gene. To define the optimal fitness cost for GI detection, we performed a pilot screen in Msm using a panel of 16 genes that are predicted to interact. We selected up to 24 sgRNAs per gene (Supplementary Methods and Supplementary Table 1) spanning a broad range of fitness costs, cloned a dual-sgRNA library containing all pairwise permutations and performed a GI screen using the workflow planned for larger-scale studies (Extended Data Fig. 1b). The resulting data allowed us to identify the sgRNA strength window that best supports GI detection under these conditions: an approximately 8% reduction in fitness per generation (Extended Data Fig. 1c–h and Supplementary Discussion).

To establish feasibility, we built a comprehensive essential-gene GI library in Msm. Guided by the pilot screen, we selected up to two sgRNAs per gene with reproducible, intermediate fitness costs (Fig. 1a and Supplementary Table 1). The library contains 1,524 sgRNAs targeting 787 genes, plus 10 non-targeting (NT) controls, yielding about 2.3 million sgRNA permutations. Target genes included those that are essential for Msm fitness and those that are non-essential in Msm but essential in Mtb; the latter were targeted by the predicted strongest sgRNAs10. The library was cloned in Escherichia coli, validated by deep sequencing (Extended Data Fig. 2a) and transformed into an Msm strain containing a chromosomally encoded Streptococcus thermophilus (Sth1) dCas9 expression cassette. This yielded a pooled library in which each bacterium carries a single integrated guide plasmid expressing two sgRNAs. We subjected this library to competitive growth, tracking dual-sgRNA strain abundance over time by barcode sequencing. Strain depletion was modelled using a piecewise linear regression10, providing a quantitative readout of fitness.

a, Schematic of the screen. (1) Up to two sgRNAs per gene (log2-transformed fold change (L2FC) –1 to –5) were selected. (2) sgRNAs were assigned barcodes (BCs), and all pairwise permutations were generated. (3) The library was passaged with or without anhydrotetracycline (ATc), and L2FC trajectories were computed from barcode counts. (4) GI scores were calculated for each gene pair (see e,f), and genes were clustered by GI profile correlation. (5) Applications of GI data. b, Distribution of observed L2FC at generation 20 for dual non-targeting (NT), single-targeting (A + NT) and dual-targeting (A + B) constructs. c, Correlation of observed L2FC at generation 20 for single-targeting constructs differing only in sgRNA position (Pos1, position 1; Pos2, position 2). d, Multiplicative model of GIs for sgRNAs targeting genes A and B. Fitness outcomes greater or less than expected indicate positive or negative GIs, respectively. e, Example of GI quantification. Left: L2FC trajectories for a representative dnaJ1 + dnaJ2 dual-sgRNA construct. Right: ΔL2FC (observed − expected) trajectories for all eight dnaJ1 + dnaJ2 constructs. f, Expected versus observed L2FC at generation 25 for all dual-targeting constructs. Black line, x = y; red line, generalized additive model (GAM) fit. GI scores were computed as the median GAM residual per gene pair. g, Distribution of GI scores across all gene pairs. Shaded regions denote statistically significant (p > 0.5) interactions. h, Heat map of GI scores for all gene pairs, hierarchically clustered by Pearson correlation of GI profiles. Values beyond ±5 are clipped. i, Number of positive and negative GIs (p > 0.5) per gene. j, Distribution of pairwise GI profile correlations among all sgRNAs, and among sgRNAs targeting the same gene. k, GI scores for all genes paired with murA (left) or with cwlM (right). l, Left, dendrogram of all genes, clustered by GI profile correlation. Branches are coloured by nodes enriched (false discovery rate (FDR) < 0.005) for Gene Ontology (GO) terms by Fisher’s exact test. Right, representative clusters.

Growth phenotypes were highly reproducible across biological replicates (Extended Data Fig. 2b,c). As expected, strains with two NT sgRNAs showed minimal depletion, single-targeting strains exhibited moderate depletion and dual-targeting strains showed the greatest depletion (Fig. 1b). sgRNA position within the plasmid had little effect on fitness, indicating consistent activity from both expression cassettes (Fig. 1c).

To identify GIs, we compared the observed fitness of each dual-targeting strain to the expected outcome under a null model of no interaction (Fig. 1d,e). Deviations from this expectation were quantified and corrected for floor effects (Fig. 1f and Extended Data Fig. 2d,e), and then aggregated at the gene-pair level to generate a GI score. Gene pairs with greater-than-expected depletion were assigned negative GI scores, and those with less-than-expected depletion yielded positive GI scores (Fig. 1d). To assess confidence, GI scores were modelled as a mixture of typical deviations (normal distribution) and deviations outside the norm (uniform distribution). Gene pairs with interaction probabilities of 0.5 < p ≤ 0.95 were designated likely interactions, and those with p > 0.95 confident interactions.

The Msm GI map revealed nearly 8,500 interactions (p > 0.5), with negative GIs outnumbering positive ones (Fig. 1g–i and Supplementary Table 2). This 2.7% hit rate across gene pairs aligns with previous GI studies3. Most genes interacted with fewer than 15 partners, but a subset exhibited high connectivity, consistent with hub-like behaviour that has been observed in other organisms, such as yeast3 (Fig. 1i). Out of 787 targeted genes, 64 (8.1%) showed no interactions under these conditions. Notably, GI strength did not correlate with gene vulnerability10, confirming that our fitness-based sgRNA selection accounts for gene vulnerability (Extended Data Fig. 2f). sgRNAs targeting the same gene exhibited highly correlated interaction profiles (Fig. 1j), underscoring the reproducibility of measured GIs.

Illustrative examples confirm that the map captures known or mechanistically plausible functional relationships. We observed a strong negative GI between the Hsp40 chaperones dnaJ1 and dnaJ2 (Fig. 1e), consistent with their known synthetic lethal relationship21. Another strong negative GI, between cwlM and murA (Fig. 1k), is consistent with the proposed role of CwlM in binding to MurA, stimulating its activity, and promoting peptidoglycan precursor synthesis22.

With individual GIs providing initial confidence in the dataset, we next sought a global assessment of the functional signal encoded in the map. To this end, we analysed correlations among GI profiles, because profile similarity often reflects similar gene function3.

Pairwise correlation and clustering revealed that genes with related biological functions tended to group together (Fig. 1l). We systematically annotated the tree, identifying 63 functionally coherent clusters containing 2 to 48 genes each. Representative clusters spanned functions including cell-wall synthesis, protein degradation, cell division, cofactor and nucleotide synthesis, the ETC, and protein folding and ribosome rescue (Fig. 1l, top to bottom, left to right). Several observations highlight the biological relevance of these clusters. First, cwlM and murA share not only a strong negative GI (Fig. 1k), but also highly correlated GI profiles22 (Fig. 1l). Second, the two genes most closely associated with the mycolic acid transporter mmpL3—pgfA and ttfA—were previously shown to interact physically with MmpL3 and support mycolic acid transport23,24. Third, the transcription factors whiA and whiB2, which are involved in cell division and act in a co-dependent manner in Streptomyces, clustered with each other and with ftsZ, consistent with their established roles25 as transcriptional activators of ftsZ. Many clusters also contained previously uncharacterized genes, as well as functionally annotated genes with unexpected correlations, suggesting unrecognized biological connections. Barring technical limitations (for example, polar effects), these clusters offer functional predictions by placing genes in the context of their network relationships.

Encouraged by the validity of the Msm map, we next extended our approach to Mtb. Following the same experimental blueprint, we constructed a dual-sgRNA library containing up to two sgRNAs per gene with reproducible, intermediate fitness costs (Supplementary Table 1). The library includes 1,483 sgRNAs targeting 762 genes, most of them essential for in vitro Mtb growth, plus 10 NT controls, yielding about 2.2 million sgRNA permutations. The library was cloned in E. coli, validated by deep sequencing (Extended Data Fig. 2a) and transformed into an H37Rv Mtb strain containing a chromosomally integrated Sth1 dCas9 cassette. Competitive growth and barcode sequencing were performed as in Msm.

As in Msm, growth phenotypes were highly reproducible across biological replicates (Extended Data Fig. 2g,h). Dual-NT, single-targeting and dual-targeting strains depleted on average in the expected order, from least to most (Fig. 2a). sgRNA position within the plasmid had a greater effect than it did in Msm (Fig. 2b), but the effect was modest and deemed acceptable, because our GI model accounts for sgRNA position. GIs were quantified, corrected for floor effects (Fig. 2c and Extended Data Fig. 2i,j) and aggregated at the gene-pair level to generate a GI score and confidence estimate, as in Msm.

a, Distribution of observed L2FC at generation 22 for dual-NT, single-targeting and dual-targeting constructs, as in Fig. 1b. b, Correlation of observed L2FC at generation 22 for single-targeting constructs differing only in sgRNA position. c, Expected versus observed L2FC at generation 25 for all dual-targeting constructs. Black line, x = y; red line, GAM fit. GI scores were computed as the median GAM residual per gene pair. d, Distribution of GI scores across all gene pairs. Shaded regions denote statistically significant (p > 0.5) interactions. e, Heat map of GI scores for all gene pairs, hierarchically clustered by Pearson correlation of GI profiles. Values beyond ±5 are clipped. f, Number of positive and negative GIs (p > 0.5) per gene. g, Distribution of pairwise GI profile correlations among all sgRNAs, and among sgRNAs targeting the same gene. h, GI scores for all genes paired with dnaJ1 (left) or with dnaJ2 (right). i, GI scores for all genes paired with murA (left) or with cwlM (right). j, GI scores for all genes paired with secA1 (left) or with secF (right). k, Left, dendrogram of all genes, clustered by GI profile correlation. Branches are coloured by nodes enriched (FDR < 0.005) for GO terms by Fisher’s exact test. Right, representative clusters (from top to bottom: fatty acid biosynthesis, arginine biosynthesis, nucleotide biosynthesis, folate metabolism, thiamine metabolism, menaquinone biosynthesis and protein degradation).

The Mtb GI map revealed nearly 6,500 interactions (p > 0.5), with negative GIs outnumbering positive ones (Fig. 2d–f and Supplementary Table 3). This 2.2% hit rate across all gene pairs parallels the Msm map. Most genes interacted with fewer than 12 partners, but a subset exhibited high connectivity (Fig. 2f), and 3.4% (26/762) of targeted genes showed no interactions under these conditions. As in Msm, sgRNAs targeting the same gene exhibited highly correlated interaction profiles (Fig. 2g), and GI strength did not correlate with gene vulnerability (Extended Data Fig. 2k). We observed strong negative GIs between dnaJ1 and dnaJ2 (ref. 21) and between cwlM and murA (ref. 22) (Fig. 2h,i). Further strong negative GIs recapitulated known or mechanistically plausible functional relationships, including (1) transcription factors and their targets (Extended Data Fig. 3a–c); (2) partially redundant enzymes (Extended Data Fig. 3d,e); and (3) functionally related genes within shared biological processes (Fig. 2j and Extended Data Fig. 3f). Reflecting the biological coherence of the data, clustering by GI profile similarity grouped genes with related functions (Fig. 2k).

To test platform reproducibility, we repeated the Mtb GI screen using a slightly higher concentration of anhydrotetracycline (ATc) to ensure saturating induction of dCas9 and sgRNA (Supplementary Table 3). We refer to the original and replicate screens as experiment 1 and experiment 2, respectively. The second screen showed slightly greater positional variability but also more pronounced depletion of single- and dual-targeting constructs (Extended Data Fig. 4a,b), resulting in a wider distribution of GI scores (Extended Data Fig. 4c–e) and a higher signal-to-noise ratio. Key benchmarks were again met, including concordance among replicates (Extended Data Fig. 2l–o), high GI profile similarity among sgRNAs targeting the same gene (Extended Data Fig. 4f) and a lack of correlation between GI score and gene vulnerability (Extended Data Fig. 2p). Most importantly, the replicate map recapitulated the functional information in the original. Summary metrics, including the overall hit rate (2.3%) and per-gene interaction number (Extended Data Fig. 4g), were comparable; specific GIs were reproduced across the two screens (Extended Data Figs. 3g–l and 4h,i); and functionally related genes clustered together (Extended Data Fig. 4j).

GI scores were strongly correlated between the Mtb experiments (R = 0.82; Extended Data Fig. 4k). However, concordance between interaction probabilities was lower (Supplementary Table 3), particularly near the boundary between the null and interaction distributions, where experiment-specific fits diverged. To reconcile these differences, we extended our statistical framework to jointly model GI scores from both experiments (Extended Data Fig. 4k). The model assigns each gene pair a joint probability and, when sufficiently confident, classifies the interaction as negative, positive or discordant. Joint modelling identified confident GIs for approximately 2.5% of Mtb gene pairs (p > 0.95) and likely GIs for 4.4% (p > 0.5).

Given the substantial but incomplete overlap between the two maps, we retained data from both screens. Unless otherwise specified, the individual Mtb GI scores and downstream analyses presented in the following sections are based on experiment 2, and the joint model provides an integrated assessment of interaction confidence across both experiments.

Having established platform robustness in both Mtb and Msm, we analysed GIs involving homologous genes targeted in both libraries. Consistent with comparative GI work in budding and fission yeast26, homologues showed a modestly higher GI profile correlation than did non-homologues (Fig. 3a,b), reflecting a mixture of conserved (for example, Figs. 1e,k and 2h,i) and non-conserved (for example, Extended Data Fig. 5a–c) interactions. A global comparison of GI scores for homologous gene pairs revealed limited correlation across species (R = 0.26; Extended Data Fig. 5d), which increased substantially when the analysis was restricted to gene pairs sharing the same biological process annotation (R = 0.57; Extended Data Fig. 5e and Supplementary Table 4). Likewise, within-process GIs were conserved at a higher rate than the overall set of interactions (Extended Data Fig. 5f). Together, these findings indicate that mycobacteria recapitulate the pattern of GI conservation observed in budding and fission yeast, in which interactions that link genes in the same biological process are preferentially conserved relative to interactions that link distinct processes26.

a,b, GI profile correlations between Msm and Mtb homologues in experiment 2 (a) and between identical genes across Mtb experiments (Mtb experiment 1 versus Mtb experiment 2; b). Each of the 100 black lines in each panel shows the density obtained using a random sample of non-homologous (a) or non-identical (b) gene pairs. c, Heat map of log2 odds ratio (OR), testing for enrichment or depletion of significant negative GIs (p > 0.5) within pathway pairs in Mtb. Gene pairs were categorized by GI presence or absence and pathway-pair membership, and association was assessed by Fisher’s exact test. Positive and negative log2(OR) values indicate more and fewer GIs than expected, respectively. Only results with |log2(OR)| > 2 and q < 0.0001 are shown. Hollow circles indicate pathway pairs that fail these thresholds after removing possible polar effects (gene pairs ≤ 5 genes apart). See Extended Data Fig. 5g for all significant (q < 0.05) pathway pairs. d,e, Distribution of s.c. ipTMs for co-folded Mtb protein pairs with mean s.c. ipTM ≥ 0.2 (d) and for all protein pairs (e). Black dots and grey lines represent the mean and s.d. of s.c. ipTMs across all pools. f, Distribution of PPI confidence across bins of GI score and GI profile correlation in Mtb. Gene pairs were binned by GI score (left) or by GI correlation (right), and the fraction of corresponding protein pairs falling into each mean s.c. ipTM category is shown. Per-bin gene-pair counts are indicated. PPI confidence: none (mean s.c. ipTM < 0.05), low (0.05 ≤ mean s.c. ipTM < 0.2), medium (0.2 ≤ mean s.c. ipTM < 0.4) and high (mean s.c. ipTM ≥ 0.4). g–n, AlphaFold-Multimer models and GI and PPI metrics for selected Mtb pairs: MurA and CwlM (g), DnaN and DnaE1 (h), DesA2 and DesA1 (i), EtfD and EtfB (j), Rv3212 and Rv1002c (k), AftD and TmaT (l), WecA and Rv3355c (m) and AftB and Rv3035 (n).

We next examined the functional organization of Mtb GIs by testing for enrichment of interactions within and between biological processes (Supplementary Table 4). We focused on negative GIs, because they are more abundant in our dataset and more likely to reflect functional relationships, following the precedent in yeast3. Gene pairs comprising genes in the same biological process were enriched for negative GIs (on-diagonal; Fig. 3c and Extended Data Fig. 5g), consistent with limited tolerance for simultaneous knockdown within essential pathways. Negative GIs were also enriched among gene pairs spanning distinct biological processes—for example, genes involved in synthesizing different components of the cell envelope (such as arabinogalactan and lipoarabinomannan), and genes involved in DNA replication and DNA repair (off-diagonal; Fig. 3c and Extended Data Fig. 5g). Beyond these process-level patterns, gene pairs with highly correlated GI profiles were themselves enriched for negative GIs (Extended Data Fig. 4l), consistent with the expectation that genes acting in the same pathway are more likely to share interaction partners and interact with each other3.

To investigate the molecular basis of GIs, we asked how frequently they reflect physical associations. Because no large-scale experimental protein–protein interaction (PPI) map exists for Mtb, we generated PPI predictions using pooled AlphaFold3 co-folding4,27 across the approximately 600,000 gene pairs screened in the Mtb and Msm GI libraries. We identified 15,240 candidate PPIs using a size-corrected interface predicted template modelling score (s.c. ipTM) cut-off ≥ 0.05 (Fig. 3d,e, Extended Data Fig. 6a–h and Supplementary Tables 2 and 3). Because size correction systematically reduces ipTM scores, this threshold is necessarily permissive, yet the overall hit rate (2.6%) remains low. Many of these candidates achieve higher ipTM scores when evaluated pairwise with AlphaFold-Multimer28. Consistent with observations in yeast3, gene pairs with negative GIs or highly correlated GI profiles were enriched for predicted physical interactions (Fig. 3f). Nevertheless, many lacked a predicted PPI, because GIs can arise from pathway-, process- or network-level relationships without direct binding. Overall, this resource identifies gene pairs that are both genetically and physically linked, providing a framework for predicting their molecular mechanisms. We present several representative examples spanning both known22,29,30,31 (Fig. 3g–j) and previously unrecognized (Fig. 3k–n) biological connections.

Previous studies have shown that GIs can predict drug–drug interactions5. To test whether this principle holds in our dataset, we analysed GIs among established drug targets.

One of the strongest negative GIs in both Mtb and Msm involved aspC (alanine aminotransferase16,32) and ddl (d-alanine-d-alanine ligase; Fig. 4a). Although previously unknown, this interaction is mechanistically plausible: AspC is crucial for biosynthesis of l-Ala, which is required by Alr (alanine racemase) to produce d-Ala, the substrate for Ddl (Fig. 4b). aspC also showed a negative GI with alr. Alr and Ddl are the targets of d-cycloserine33, a second-line agent for multidrug-resistant TB. Consistent with the GI data, CRISPRi-based chemical–genetic interaction (CGI) profiling of d-cycloserine identified aspC as one of the top sensitizing hits (Fig. 4c,d and Supplementary Table 5). Moreover, a paper published while we revised this one reported synergy between an AspC inhibitor and d-cycloserine34.

Another set of novel, mechanistically plausible interactions involved PptT, a phosphopantetheinyl transferase that activates acyl carrier proteins (ACPs) required for lipid biosynthesis and is an active drug development target35. PptT showed negative GIs with kasA, hadB and hadC (Fig. 4e), which catalyse steps in the FAS-II pathway responsible for mycolic acid biosynthesis (Fig. 4f), and are likewise being pursued as drug targets36,37. Consistent with the GI data, CGI profiling of thiolactomycin, a KasA and KasB inhibitor, identified pptT as a top sensitizing hit (Extended Data Fig. 7a and Supplementary Table 5). Moreover, co-treating Mtb with thiolactomycin and the PptT inhibitor 8918 produced strong synergy in both the H37Rv reference and clinical Mtb strains38 representing diverse lineages (Fig. 4g,h). This synergy was specific: neither thiolactomycin nor 8918 synergized with control drug treatments (Extended Data Fig. 7b–g). Although KasA inhibitors and rifampicin are synergistic39, kasA and rifampicin’s target rpoB did not show a negative GI (Supplementary Table 3). In this case, KasA inhibition is likely to potentiate rifampicin by increasing envelope permeability and intracellular rifampicin exposure, rather than through a target-based mechanism39. Supporting this interpretation, knockdown of rpoB did not sensitize to thiolactomycin in our CGI screen (Extended Data Fig. 7a). These examples show how KasA inhibition can drive synergy through both target-specific and chemotype-specific mechanisms, and how GI mapping can disentangle these modes of action. Combined inhibition of PptT and the HadAB and HadBC dehydratases likewise produced strong synergy (Fig. 4i,j), providing further evidence that negative GIs can predict drug–drug interactions.

To assess whether positive GIs likewise have predictive value, we focused on the pks13–efpA pair. Pks13 and EfpA are essential proteins involved in mycolic acid biosynthesis and lipid translocation, respectively, and both are active targets for TB drug development40,41. The pair showed a strong positive GI (Fig. 4k), predicting drug–drug antagonism, which was confirmed by checkerboard assays of preclinical Pks13 and EfpA inhibitors (Fig. 4l and Extended Data Fig. 7h,i).

As a final proof-of-concept, we examined PknA and PknB, essential eukaryotic-like serine/threonine kinases that regulate Mtb growth and division and are promising drug targets42. pknA and pknB exhibited strong negative GIs with embA and embB (Fig. 4m), which encode arabinogalactan biosynthetic enzymes targeted by the first-line TB drug ethambutol43. Co-treatment with ethambutol and the PknA and PknB inhibitor V49 resulted in borderline synergy in checkerboard assays (Extended Data Fig. 7j), but clear synergy in bacterial killing assays (Fig. 4n). This bactericidal interaction seemed to be specific: pknA and pknB did not exhibit negative GIs with ATP synthase genes (Fig. 4m), and V49 did not enhance killing by the ATP synthase inhibitor bedaquiline44 (Fig. 4n). Although V49 and bedaquiline showed borderline synergy in checkerboard assays (Extended Data Fig. 7k), this might reflect the same uptake-mediated effect proposed for KasA inhibition and rifampicin, rather than a target-based interaction39. Together, these results illustrate how GI mapping can reveal combination effects that are missed by conventional growth-inhibition assays.

Beyond the specific interactions discussed above, the Mtb GI map offers broader opportunities for drug discovery. Strong GIs between currently pursued TB drug targets are rare, consistent with the general scarcity of target-based synergy and antagonism45. Nonetheless, the map reveals thousands of previously unexplored interactions among established and potential drug targets across diverse pathways. We cover several of these interactions in the Supplementary Discussion and Extended Data Figs. 8 and 9. The map also identifies a set of ‘pleiotropic sensitizers’—including ppk, macE, dnaA, rnc, treS, sodA and pknG—that showed strong negative GIs across numerous targets, consistent with findings from our previous CGI studies39. Inhibitors of these pleiotropic sensitizers could potentiate multiple drug classes by globally altering bacterial metabolism, stress responses or regulatory networks, making these genes promising candidates for combination therapy aimed at amplifying the activity of diverse antibacterial agents.

Oxidative phosphorylation—the combined activities of the ETC and ATP synthase—has emerged as an important antibiotic target in Mtb and related pathogens. Clinically validated examples include the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved ATP synthase inhibitor bedaquiline44 and telacebec (Q203)46, a clinical drug candidate that targets complex III. In mycobacteria, complex III2IV2 (Fig. 5a) is the primary terminal oxidase that establishes the proton gradient driving ATP synthesis47. This supercomplex (larger than 700 kDa) consists of 24 protein subunits47 that position 18 redox cofactors to enable electron transfer coupled with proton translocation. In eukaryotes, numerous proteins chaperoning the maturation of complex III and IV have been identified, and defects in these assembly factors cause severe hereditary diseases48. In mycobacteria, the mechanisms of complex III2IV2 assembly and cofactor incorporation remain mostly unknown49.

We identified a cluster of genes of unknown function that strongly correlated with genes encoding subunits of complex III2IV2 and with genes involved in cofactor biogenesis, in both Msm and Mtb (Figs. 1l and 5b,c and Extended Data Fig. 10a). Many of these uncharacterized genes also showed negative GIs with the alternative, partially redundant terminal oxidase, cytochrome bd oxidase (cyt. bd), encoded by cydA and cydB (Fig. 5d,e). Synthetic lethality with cyt. bd is a hallmark of defects in complex III2IV2 in mycobacteria50. We thus hypothesized that these genes contribute to the assembly or function of complex III2IV2. Several lines of evidence support this hypothesis: (1) independent single-strain knockdowns using sgRNAs not included in the screen validated the GI results in both Msm and Mtb (Fig. 5f–i); (2) complementation experiments in Msm ruled out off-target effects and established the functional equivalence of Mtb homologues (Extended Data Fig. 10b); (3) these genes showed negative GIs with each other in Mtb (Extended Data Fig. 10c); (4) AlphaFold3 predictions suggest physical interactions among several of these genes and with CtaD, a complex IV subunit (Fig. 5j,k and Extended Data Fig. 10d); and (5) knockdown of these genes in strains lacking cyt. bd reduced oxygen consumption, an indicator of complex III2IV2 activity (Fig. 5l and Extended Data Fig. 10e–g), and increased sensitivity to Q203 to varying extents (Fig. 5m and Extended Data Fig. 10h).

To extend these findings biochemically, we focused on ms2764, selected for its AlphaFold3-predicted interactions and the tractability of generating a functional 3×Flag-tagged construct with correct membrane topology. To our knowledge, there are no previous studies of ms2764 or its Mtb homologue rv2698, which encode membrane proteins containing a DUF3093 domain that seems to be restricted to Actinobacteria. Affinity purification of Ms2764–3×Flag followed by mass spectrometry (AP–MS) showed co-purification of complex III2IV2 subunits and several other uncharacterized genes in the cluster (Fig. 5n). Motivated by this evidence of physical interaction, we generated an ms2764 knockout and assayed respiratory activity in inverted membrane vesicles (IMVs). As shown previously51, NADH-driven IMV acidification can occur even when complex III2IV2 is inhibited or absent, whereas succinate-driven IMV acidification requires functional complex III2IV2. Similar to IMVs from a ∆qcrB strain, ∆ms2764 IMVs were capable of NADH-driven acidification but not succinate-driven acidification, indicating loss of complex III2IV2 activity (Fig. 5o) and providing biochemical evidence that Ms2764 contributes to complex function.

Closer inspection of these uncharacterized genes revealed that one (rv2235 or ms4311; here renamed surf1) contains a well-conserved SURF1 domain, known in other species to facilitate the incorporation of haem a3 into CtaD (ref. 49). A second gene (rv0102 or ms4702; here renamed ctiP) probably encodes a distant CtiP homologue (25% sequence identity) that, in Corynebacterium, seems to mediate CuB insertion into CtaD (ref. 49). Consistent with this proposed role, ctiP is encoded adjacent to chalkophore biosynthesis genes in Mtb, which supply copper to complex IV under copper-limiting conditions and during infection52. This genomic context suggests that CtiP collaborates with chalkophores to metallate complex IV. rv1342c (ms4900) and lprD are induced under iron starvation53, consistent with the iron dependence of complex III2IV2 activity, whereas rv1457c (ms3118) and rv1458c (ms3119) are located immediately upstream of ctaA, which catalyses the final step of haem A biosynthesis. For the remaining genes, no precedent links them to the ETC. They encode predicted integral membrane proteins (rv2698 (ms2764) and rv1083 (ms5260)) and lipoproteins (lppL, rv2980 (ms2396)). These uncharacterized genes might therefore participate in cofactor trafficking or installation or represent previously unrecognized subunits of complex III2IV2. Although further studies are required to define their molecular roles, these findings show how our GI platform enables hypothesis generation for previously uncharacterized genes.

A large portion of the Mtb genome remains poorly understood.
