a, Construction of dual-sgRNA libraries. Single-sgRNA constructs were cloned individually. To assemble the dual-sgRNA library, all single-sgRNA plasmids were pooled and subjected to two parallel digestions: (1) MfeI + XhoI to generate a backbone library, and (2) EcoRI + SalI to excise the sgRNA–barcode fragment and generate an insert library. Ligation of these two products places two sgRNA cassettes in tandem, followed by their corresponding unique barcodes. To quantify sgRNA abundance, the barcode region is amplified using flanking NGS primers. b, Overview of the pilot GI library design. Up to 24 sgRNAs were selected for each of 16 target genes. The resulting dual-sgRNA library was transformed into Msm and serially passaged +/–ATc, with samples collected every 2.5 to 5 generations. The relative abundance of each sgRNA pair was quantified by sequencing the barcode region. c, Density plot of ΔL2FC versus expected L2FC projected at generation 25 for all dual-targeting constructs in the pilot library. Vertical lines mark the expected L2FC window between –10 and –2. d, Heat map of GI scores for all dual-targeting constructs in the pilot library. Each row and column corresponds to a single sgRNA, and each cell represents a dual-targeting construct. sgRNAs are grouped by target gene and, within each gene, are ordered by sgRNA strength, as defined by the L2FC of the sgRNA when paired with a non-targeting sgRNA at 25 generations (weaker sgRNAs at the top/left; stronger sgRNAs at the bottom/right). Gene pairs highlighted in e–h are marked with dashed boxes. e–h, Scatter plots of ΔL2FC versus expected L2FC projected at generation 25 for all dual-sgRNA constructs targeting glgB and glgE (e), ponA1 and ponA2 (f), folA and folP1 (g) and rpoB and macE (h). Vertical lines mark the expected L2FC window between –10 and –2.

a, Library metrics. Metrics are shown for the plasmid library after cloning in E. coli and for the corresponding mycobacterial library after transformation into either Msm or Mtb. Mycobacterial libraries were sequenced from the initial (Generation 0, G0) sample of the uninduced (–ATc) condition. Mtb experiment 1 and experiment 2 were derived from the same plasmid library. b,c,g,h,l,m, Heat maps of the Pearson correlation between sgRNA counts across all time points and replicates for the (b,c) Msm, (g,h) Mtb experiment 1 and (l,m) Mtb experiment 2 libraries. For each experiment, the (b,g,l) –ATc samples and (c,h,m) +ATc samples are shown on separate heat maps. d,i,n, Density plots of uncorrected ΔL2FC versus expected L2FC at 25 generations for all dual-targeting constructs in the (d) Msm, (i) Mtb experiment 1 and (n) Mtb experiment 2 libraries. e,j,o, Density plots of corrected ΔL2FC versus expected L2FC at 25 generations for all dual-targeting constructs in the (e) Msm, (j) Mtb experiment 1 and (o) Mtb experiment 2 libraries. Corrected ΔL2FC values are calculated as the residual (observed – GAM-predicted L2FC) for each dual-targeting construct. For more information, see Methods: ‘Quantification of GIs’ and Figs. 1f and 2c and Extended Data Fig. 4c. f,k,p, Density plots of GI score versus combined gene vulnerability for all gene pairs in the (f) Msm, (k) Mtb experiment 1 and (p) Mtb experiment 2 libraries. Combined gene vulnerability is defined as the sum of the vulnerabilities of the two genes in each pair.

a–l, GI scores in Mtb experiment 1 (a–f) and Mtb experiment 2 (g–l) for all genes paired with whiB7 (a,g), with ftsR (b,h), with mtrA (c,i), with ndh (d,j), with ponA1 (e,k) or with dnaE1 (f,l). Arrows mark specific interactions.

a, Distribution of observed L2FC at generation 20 for dual-NT, single-targeting, and dual-targeting constructs, as in Fig. 1b. b, Correlation of observed L2FC at generation 20 for single-targeting constructs differing only in sgRNA position. c, Expected versus observed L2FC at generation 25 for all dual-targeting constructs. Black line, x = y; red line, GAM fit. GI scores were computed as the median GAM residual per gene pair. d, Distribution of GI scores across all gene pairs. Shaded regions denote statistically significant (p > 0.5) interactions. e, Heat map of GI scores for all gene pairs, hierarchically clustered by Pearson correlation of GI profiles. Values beyond ±5 are clipped. f, Distribution of pairwise GI profile correlations among all sgRNAs, and among sgRNAs targeting the same gene. g, Number of positive and negative GIs (p > 0.5) per gene. h, GI scores for all genes paired with secA1 (left) or with secF (right). i, GI scores for all genes paired with murA (left) or with cwlM (right). j, Dendrogram of all genes (left), clustered by GI profile correlation. Branches are coloured by nodes enriched (FDR < 0.005) for GO terms by Fisher’s exact test. Representative clusters (right, from top to bottom: fatty acid biosynthesis, arginine biosynthesis, DNA replication, folate metabolism, thiamine metabolism, menaquinone biosynthesis, and protein degradation). k, Scatter plot comparing GI scores in Mtb experiment 1 and Mtb experiment 2, coloured by joint model hit class. See Methods for additional details. l, Distribution of GI scores for gene pairs grouped into 10 equal-width bins by GI profile correlation. Gene pairs separated by five or fewer genes were excluded to minimize potential polar effects. Boxes indicate the interquartile range (IQR), centre lines indicate the median, and whiskers extend to 1.5 × IQR; outliers are not shown.

a–c, GI scores in the Msm GI screen (left) and the Mtb GI screen (right) for all genes paired with crp (a), with fumC (b) or with whiA (c). d,e, Density plots of GI scores in Msm versus Mtb for (d) all homologous gene pairs and (e) homologous gene pairs sharing the same biological process annotation (“category” in Supplementary Table 4, excluding “Unknown”). The total number of gene pairs included in each analysis (n) is indicated in the plot titles. f, Percent of Mtb GIs conserved in Msm. The two gene pair sets defined in d,e were first filtered to retain only Mtb GIs (p > 0.5 in experiment 2). An Mtb GI was considered conserved if the corresponding gene pair in Msm was also called as a significant interaction (p > 0.5) with the same sign (positive or negative). For each set, percent conservation was calculated as the number of conserved GIs divided by the number of Mtb GIs. The analysis was performed twice: once without additional filters (corresponding to the full bar height) and once excluding potential polar effects (gene pairs ≤ 5 genes apart; corresponding to the filled portion). g, Heat map of log2 odds ratio (OR), testing for enrichment or depletion of significant negative GIs (p > 0.5) within pathway pairs in Mtb, as in Fig. 3c. Only results with q < 0.05 are shown. Hollow circles indicate pathway pairs that fail this threshold after removing possible polar effects (gene pairs ≤ 5 genes apart).

a, Co-folding pool sizes (number of monomers) generated by size-aware bin packing for all gene pairs screened in Msm. All pools have exactly one copy of each monomer (that is, the co-folding screen captures only heterodimers). Six additional pools with >25 monomers not shown. b, Co-folding pool sizes (total residues) generated by size-aware bin packing for all gene pairs screened in Msm. 40 additional pools with fewer than 4,450 residues not shown. c, Co-folding pool sizes (number of monomers) for all gene pairs screened in Mtb, as in a. Five pools with >25 monomers not shown. d, Co-folding pool sizes (total residues) for all gene pairs screened in Mtb, as in b. 36 pools with fewer than 4,450 residues not shown. e, Uncorrected mean ipTM scores for all gene pairs screened in Mtb. Red line is the correction factor, calculated as (0.0044 × \(\sqrt{{l}_{1}\,+\,{l}_{2}}\,\)) − 0.036, where (l1, l2) are the lengths of each protein in the pair. f, Size-corrected (s.c.) mean ipTM scores for all gene pairs screened in Mtb. g,h, Distribution of s.c. ipTMs for co-folded Msm protein pairs with mean s.c. ipTM ≥ 0.2 (g) and all protein pairs (h). Black dots and grey lines represent the mean and s.d. of s.c. ipTMs across all pools.

a, Volcano plot showing results from an Mtb CRISPRi-based CGI screen with the KasA and KasB inhibitor thiolactomycin. Knockdown of kasA and pptT sensitizes Mtb to thiolactomycin, whereas knockdown of rpoB does not. #1257. Footy Fix: Who will win Ballon d'Or as Harry Kane, Kylian Mbappe, Lamine Yamal, Lionel Messi vie for prize

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The attention of the soccer world will be fixed on London to start the week, where a months-old question will finally be answered: Who's going to win the Ballon d'Or? I'm Pardeep Cattry with a lookahead to Monday's ceremony, plus a preview of what's to come as action resumes in the EFL Cup.

Monday, Oct. 26🇫🇷 Ligue 1: Paris Saint-Germain vs. Lyon, 3:30 p.m. ➡️ beIN Sports🏆 Ballon d'Or ceremony, 4 p.m. ➡️ DAZN

Tuesday, Oct. 27🇮🇹 Serie A: Roma vs. Cagliari, 3:45 p.m. ➡️ Paramount+🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿 EFL Cup: Fleetwood Town vs. Arsenal, 4 p.m. ➡️ Paramount+

Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo may no longer be the frontrunners for the Ballon d'Or, but their decades-long command over soccer's most prestigious individual accolade still colors the way we all look at the award. The air of mystery that should be a fixture in the run-up to an awards show still feels foreign, the ability to gauge the eventual winner a fresh challenge for many. That's especially true this year, particularly on the men's side, where none of the usual indicators apply.

A handful of deserving players make up the list of nominees once again, but none fit the prototype of an eventual Ballon d'Or winner, rightly or wrongly. The award often goes to the best player on a team that won the biggest prize on offer in the last year, a path that would lead you straight to Spain's golden ball winner, Rodri. The midfielder hardly feels like a slam-dunk pick after spending much of last season building his form following an ACL injury, which might lead you to a member of Paris Saint-Germain's UEFA Champions League-winning team. Vitinha, the Portuguese midfielder, might actually have a shot but there are buzzier names in the mix that are equally worthy. The favorite might actually be someone else entirely – Harry Kane, the England captain and Bayern Munich talisman who has steadily established himself as his generation's greatest goalscorer over the years. Here's James Benge on Kane's case in the final batch of Ballon d'Or power rankings.

There is no obvious candidate on the women's side, either, though Alexia Putellas might just be the favorite if the usual patterns apply. The voting body will be inclined to select someone from Barcelona's UEFA Women's Champions League-winning side and with three-time Ballon d'Or winner Aitana Bonmati out of the running after dealing with a broken leg last season, Putellas playing a central role with eight goals and six assists in Europe before leaving for London City Lionesses in the summer. She is one of eight members of that squad among the list of nominees, the list of 30 an eclectic selection of some of the world's best players. The NWSL's nominees include Temwa Chawinga, the league's back-to-back MVP with the Kansas City Current and the headliner for a Malawi side that made a run to the Women's Africa Cup of Nations, and U.S. women's national team standout Rose Lavelle, who scored the game-winner for Gotham FC in last year's NWSL Championship.

#1256. Nobel Prize in literature goes to Canada's Anne Carson

Carson won for her "bold and inventive oeuvre." The decorated poet and essayist is known for her reverence for Latin and Greek classics.

The Swedish Academy awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in literature to Anne Carson on Thursday, praising her "bold and inventive oeuvre."

Her work has "in playful dialogue with the classical tradition...created new forms for contemporary literature," said Ingrid Carlberg, permanent secretary of the academy.

The 76-year-old writer is a longtime professor of classics, creative writing, and comparative literature at prestigious institutions like McGill and Princeton universities. She is only the 19th woman of 123 laureates to win the award.

Born in Toronto in 1950, Carson moved with her family among several small towns in Canada during her youth. She has credited a beloved Latin teacher for sparking her interest in language and classics.

Her first book of criticism, 1986’s Eros the Bittersweet, was published to great acclaim and has had significant influence on other classicists, poets, and even film and television. Carson has also published her own poetry such as the 2001 collection The Beauty of the Husband as well as highly regarded translation of ancient Greek poets such as Sappho and Sophocles.

Carson is also heavily influenced by the King James Bible and more modern writers including Emily Dickinson and Virginia Woolf. She has received numerous awards such as the T.S. Eliot Prize for Poetry, a MacArthur fellowship, and the PEN/Nabokov Award.

Deeply private, Carson often declines to speak about her personal life in interviews and discourages autobiographical interpretations of her work. However, she did reveal in 2024 that she has Parkinson's disease.

The winner of the Nobel Prize in literature receives prize money of 12 million Swedish kronor, equivalent to about $1.2 million. The winner also receives a medal and a diploma at an official ceremony in December, and is expected to deliver a speech known as a Nobel lecture.

On Friday, the winner of the Nobel Peace Prize will be announced, followed by the Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel on Monday.

Henry Pollock was at the centre of an East Midlands derby flare-up that sparked a second-half Leicester onslaught as Northampton were overpowered at a sodden Mattioli Woods Welford Road.

The England back row, never knowingly far from controversy, escalated a brawl at the end of the first half that Leicester prop Joe Heyes revealed “added fuel to the fire” of a Tigers side who roared impressively when they returned after the break.

The incident fired up a sell-out crowd and Leicester brought what had up to that point been a drab game to life with a storming second-half performance.

Three tries in a pulverising 13-minute spell overturned a half-time deficit and put the hosts on course for a bonus-point win over their arch-rivals that took them to second place in the Prem table.

Pollock, withdrawn after 52 minutes, may wish to reflect on the wisdom of riling the Tigers in their own lair.

“That was a proper Tigers second half and a really pleasing performance,” Geoff Parling, their director of rugby, said.

“We got on the front foot and showed our power. The way the guys problem-solved was brilliant and I’m just really pleased with the emotional energy they threw into that game.

“The way we were physically for each other – I’m really pleased.

“The challenge for us, if we want to be a title-winning team, is to play like that when it isn’t Northampton Saints. We have to play with that heart – the fire we showed in our chests – but also the calmness we showed too.

“I think if we play our game to the best of our ability we can knock over anyone.”

Parling has made five changes from the side that endured a 41-17 defeat to Pau.

Solomone Kata returns from injury to start at inside centre, with Gabriel Hamer-Webb and Jack van Poortvliet also coming into the backline to replace Ollie Hassell-Collins and Tom Whiteley respectively.

In the pack, Joe Heyes joins Archie van der Flier and Jamie Blamire who retain their places in the front row, while the second row make up of Cameron Henderson and Ollie Chessum remains unchanged.

Aaron Wainwright comes back into the starting lineup in the back row, with Finn Carnduff moving to openside flanker, with Olly Cracknell going at No 8.

Leicester: F Steward; A Radwan, W Wand, S Kata; G Hamer-Webb; B Searle, J van Poortvliet; A van der Flier, J Blamire, J Heyes, C Henderson, O Chessum, A Wainwright, F Carnduff, O Cracknell.

Replacements:  R Asiata, T Haffar, W Hurd, J Thompson, J Moro, T Whiteley, O Bailey, G Pearson.

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of Leicester Tigers v Northampton Saints.

The Prem’s derby weekend continues today at Mattioli Woods Welford Road, where Geoff Parling’s side go head-to-head in with their East Midlands rivals.

Both Leicester and Northampton have two wins from the opening three rounds of the season and with both sides involved in a number of high-scoring encounters already in the new campaign, we could be in for a real treat.

Tigers started the season with a 38-40 loss at home to Saracens, but bounced back quickly with wins over Gloucester and Newcastle Red Bulls. They will be itching to right a few wrongs after suffering a chastening Champions Cup defeat in Pau last week.

Northampton, meanwhile, have notched up wins over Newcastle Red Bulls and Bath either side of loss to Bristol Bears.

A win today for Saints would be their first on the road since defeating Exeter Chiefs at Sandy Park in April.

“It (the East Midlands derby) means a lot to everyone, we know it will be a great atmosphere at Mattioli Woods Welford Road,” said Parling.

“I don’t think with this sort of game either team has to build it up too much emotionally because that just comes, so I think it’s actually about being really really calm in the moment.”

“Hopefully we can put the best of ourselves out there and I’m sure Saints will be able to do exactly the same.”

Saints are without a victory in Leicester since January 2023, when a single point decided the 18-19 result.

Since then, the last five meetings between the sides have been won by the hosts on the day – with Saints last taking home the bragging rights when a Tom Litchfield hat-trick helped Northampton to a 45-31 win on home soil in last season’s league play-off.

Kick-off gets underway at 3.05pm. Stay with us here for all the latest updates.

#1254. Premier League Power Rankings: Manchester United falling fast; Tottenham Hotspur, Bournemouth rise

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Eight games into a campaign, patterns are supposed to emerge as teams begin to lock into midseason form. This season of the Premier League is no exception, except the pattern is a new one – expect chaos until further notice.

Several teams are experiencing a regression to the mean after rocky starts to the season, evidenced by the weekend's most notable games. Aston Villa are surging up the table after a 2-1 win over Manchester City, Bournemouth defeated Manchester United in style with a 3-0 triumph at Old Trafford and Tottenham Hotspur have gone from zero wins to two in a week, a 2-0 win at Chelsea their most impressive performance in months. Others are also putting their early season results behind them, but it feels like they are crashing back down to earth – Brentford were held to a 1-1 draw at Hull City, while Ipswich Town were unimpressive in a 1-1 draw against Nottingham Forest.

A fascinating theme is beginning to emerge along the way. It feels like there are more midtable teams than usual, even if some sit as high as seventh (someone has to, after all). Then there are those that seem like relegation contenders but are several spots above the drop zone because, somehow, there are that many teams worse than them. There's a frenetic feeling to the Premier League table and, by extension, the latest edition of power rankings but the show must go on.

Here's how each Premier League team is looking after the latest round of games.

Arsenal's 2-0 win over Everton was not glamorous but the Gunners won't care. They're level on points with Manchester City and well-positioned to compete for the title, much as they have been all season.

Manchester City's short-lived grip on first place is gone after their defeat to Aston Villa, one that raises questions about their ability to go the distance in Enzo Maresca's first season in charge.

Liverpool are slowly but steadily figuring things out with Andoni Iraola at the helm, a 2-0 win over Brighton and Hove Albion their most impressive result yet. A top-four spot feels like a realistic aim for this season, even if they are not the finished product just yet.

Fabian Hurzeler's side played a fairly even game with Liverpool, so their stock should not drop too much but the Reds did map out a plan to neutralize their attack-minded tendencies, which might be something opponents borrow from in the coming weeks and months.

This is where the extreme midtable energy of the Premier League comes in – Chelsea were deeply unimpressive against Spurs, unconvincing at almost every turn. Most teams in England's top flight, though, are worse off so the Blues hang onto fifth for now but they will be worth keeping an eye on.

Between a 3-0 win over AC Milan in the UEFA Europa League and their triumph at Old Trafford, it has been a fun week to be a Bournemouth fan. Those wins are a sign that things are finally clicking – they might be 13th in the league but they rank third on expected goal differential, a signal that things were always trending in the right direction.

Aston Villa's slow start is officially a thing of the past, Unai Emery's side smartly outmaneuvering City to prove just that. They are officially a team on the rise.

Leeds United's unstylish but effective consistency means they continue to hang out in the top half of the table but playing even against an unimpressive Sunderland side is not the kind of thing a team earns plaudits for.

There's no reason Brentford should not target a top-half finish but much like Leeds above them, an even game against relegation contenders Hull City is not indicative of the team's overall qualities.

Manchester United really have their hearts set on scaling down the table as fast as they can, don't they? The Red Devils should be better than this but their mistake-prone nature continues to be costly.

A win over Coventry City is one thing but a victory at Chelsea is another. More specifically, it's the kind of thing that ensured Spurs would dig themselves out of their early season hole and perhaps sets them up for some more normal results in the short-term.

There is no shame in losing to the reigning champions but Everton did not make much of a dent in the match, the Toffees seemingly resigned to being permanent residents of the middle of the Premier League's table for the foreseeable future.

For all their faults, Fulham have done well enough to pick up the points expected of them, the latest coming in a win over Coventry City. Barely cracking 0.5 expected goals along the way, though, is not something to write home about.

Conventional wisdom suggests that the other shoe will drop for Hull City but it hasn't yet, especially after picking up a well-earned point against Brentford.

Add Nottingham Forest to the list of anomalies this season, sitting firmly in the relegation zone despite ranking fifth in the league on expected goal differential. Case in point – they tallied 2.29 expected goals to Ipswich's 0.46 but tied 1-1 anyway. Until they solve that problem, they are doomed to less-than-ideal spots on the table.

Ipswich were lucky to pick up a point against Forest but the early season success is a thing of the past for them, too.

Eighth-place Newcastle United seem to be riding their luck – they rank 19th in the league on expected goal differential – but creating a five-point cushion above the drop zone by way of a win over Crystal Palace counts for something.

Sunderland will value the point they picked up against Leeds but they are in the midst of an unexciting season, which is hardly a position of strength for a team in desperate need of points.

Palace will take some solace from the fact that they outplayed Newcastle but in their case, the results actually reflect their form.

Coventry were neck-and-neck with Fulham on expected goals in defeat but considering the Cottagers put up a paltry number, there's not much the newly promoted side can brag about.

#1253. Newcastle Confidential: REVEALED - Players 'confused' by Matthias Jaissle's instructions, why formation tweak is a possibility, Joelinton injury worry and new transfer guru's methods explained

Published: 12:00 EDT, 4 November 2026 | Updated: 12:01 EDT, 4 November 2026

Newcastle’s players are ‘confused’ by what Matthias Jaissle wants from them, a source close to the dressing room has told me.

I've been told the squad remains supportive of Jaissle and there is a determination to get things right for the head coach – senior players accept there is a responsibility on them – but there is also a desire for clarity over what it is they are being asked to do on the field.

Jaissle said in the wake of Monday's 1-0 home defeat by Everton that he could not understand why the team had not followed his instructions and executed the tactics they had worked on in training. He said the plan was not to play ‘long balls’.

Sources also say Jaissle spoke to his players afterwards about their press not being what he wanted and their passing being too slow in the opposition half.

However, I have been told some players are unsure as to the playing style and strategy, and that has led to those in deep positions getting the ball forward as quickly as possible, invariably with a long pass. There are also some within the dressing room wondering why the team continues to play with a No 10 when they do not have a specialist in that position.

Another source close to a senior player says the logical solution is a return to the 4-3-3 of recent seasons. There was word from inside the training ground that Jaissle was considering such a change ahead of the trip to Crystal Palace last month, so it is not off the table.

The demand from supporters to find a place for teenager Sean Steur in the midfield could yet see a tweak to the system, especially as Jaissle believes he and Nico Gonzalez are not suited to playing together as a two.

Newcastle's players are understood to be 'confused' by what it is head coach Matthias Jaissle wants from them

The demand from supporters to find a place for teenager Sean Steur (left) in the midfield could yet see a tweak to the Newcastle system

Joelinton is a fresh injury concern and medical staff will know in the next 24 hours if he is set to miss Saturday’s trip to Fulham, I can reveal. The Brazilian was feeling some muscle discomfort post-match on Monday and there is hope that the issue is related to a severe case of cramp.

However, I understand that is yet to be confirmed and, given Joelinton’s history of muscle strains, including his hamstring, no chances will be taken. The 30-year-old only returned from a thigh injury three weeks ago having been sidelined since the summer.

In better news, Matias Fernandez-Pardo and Lewis Miley are set to return for the game at Craven Cottage.

I understand Fernandez-Pardo wanted to be included in the squad for the visit of Everton but was told by staff he needed more training. The Belgian had missed the previous two matches with what is being described as a ‘tricky virus’ and only returned to training over the weekend.

Fernandez-Pardo arrived on Tyneside insisting he wanted to be used as a central striker following his £51million move from Lille. However, Jaissle currently prefers William Osula in that position and Fernandez-Pardo will likely be competing for a place out wide at Craven Cottage.

Miley, meanwhile, was also pushing for involvement on Monday after recovering from a glute issue. The 20-year-old’s return is timely given the midfield struggles of late, as well as the fresh worry over Joelinton and Jacob Ramsey’s suspension following his red card against Everton.

Matias Fernandez-Pardo is available again for Newcastle after suffering with a ‘tricky virus’

One player who almost certainly won’t come in for a start is Aladji Bamba, although we are told he will NOT be going out on loan in January.

The 20-year-old has appeared for just 27 minutes since his £30m arrival from Monaco in the summer, and he has not featured at all since September 19.

But despite potential availability issues in midfield, Jaissle does not feel Bamba is ready to start Premier League matches. That has led to a suggestion among some that he could be loaned out in January, especially as he has made only 12 senior starts in his career.

However, I understand the plan is for Bamba to remain on Tyneside and there has been encouragement with his recent performances in training.

Aladji Bamba has impressed in training of late and won't leave on loan in January despite his lack of first-team minutes

It has been interesting speaking to those who know a little more about Newcastle's new head of recruitment Tomas Amaral, who was virtually unknown in the UK before his appointment last month.

The Portuguese, 35, has been described as a 'bookworm and laptop obsessive', a meticulous talent-spotter who works long into the night. Amaral, who spent four years scouting for Benfica and was most recently sporting director at Spartak Moscow, has also spoken previously of the dangers of clubs signing good players who do not fit the manager's system.

He believes recruitment should begin with a clear footballing identity, rather than collecting talented individuals and hoping they somehow fit together. He also argues that scouts should challenge managers over transfer targets, rather than simply indulge their wishes.

Interestingly, his recruitment strategy involves two lists – one identifying players good enough for the club, the other those specifically suited to the manager's demands. For him, character and adaptability are considered just as important as ability.

He was part of the Benfica scouting team who identified Enzo Fernandez when signing him from River Plate in 2022. The midfielder was sold to Chelsea for a near £100m profit the following year.

Amaral’s arrival at least gives clarity to the recruitment structure inside St James’ Park, and he would appear to have a busy 12 months ahead given what feel like obvious areas for improvement across the pitch. I understand there is scope to spend in January should the club feel it necessary.

Beneath first-team level, Newcastle have cast their scouting net a little wider this week with two promising teenagers from Gambia arriving on Tyneside.

We understand Omar Marong and Alieu Saine, both 16, will stay for a two-week trial and train with the academy. They are products of the Today Makes Tomorrow Academy and have been identified under the club’s new global talent drive.

The pair caught the eye during Gambia’s triumph at September’s West African Under-17 Championship. Central midfielder Marong captained the side, while winger Saine finished as joint-top scorer with four goals. Neither player can join permanently until turning 18 because of FIFA regulations, but Newcastle are keen to assess their potential.

Meanwhile, the club are also set to appoint a specialist scout in Africa.

Finally, Newcastle prospect Matheos Ferreira could soon be at the centre of an international tug of war.

The 18-year-old, born in Ashington and raised in Berwick, has been called up by Brazil Under 20s for friendlies against Japan and Singapore this month. He is the only English-based player in the squad.

Newcastle prospect Matheos Ferreira could play for England, Italy or Brazil

But Ferreira, whose father is Brazilian and mother Italian, also qualifies for England and Italy. He has previously represented England at youth level and recently obtained an Italian passport.

I have seen him play a handful of times and there is certainly plenty of talent and potential. Interestingly, he has been operating as a No 10 at times this season, having come through the ranks as a winger.

Maybe there is a No 10 inside the club after all…

#1252. Who's to blame for Manchester United's decline? Ranking the biggest culprits

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

It's happened again. Another season, another Manchester United crisis. No longer does the end of daylight savings time herald the harsh winter ahead. Instead, it is the boos that ring around Old Trafford as the United faithful turn their ire on the same owners, the same executives and the same players, well aware it will be a different coach that pays the price.

Sunday's 3-0 defeat to AFC Bournemouth was remarkable only for the sheer unremarkability of it. In the 74 years after their first meeting in the 1949 FA Cup third round, Bournemouth won three games against Manchester United. In the last two years they have won three games: all at Old Trafford, all 3-0. Freddie Kruger is treading the boards at the Theatre of Dreams.

Although maybe that analogy is not quite apt. After all, the one positive that you could say about a Krugerian nightmare is that it tends to be a one-and-done situation. No such luck if you happen to be a Manchester United supporter. Could any of them now believe that sacking Michael Carrick would fix anything about this club? They've tried the Eddie Howe-esque Premier League mainstay, the relentless winner a la Antonio Conte, the graduate of the Ralf Rangnick pressing academy in the mold of Julian Nagelsmann. Their shortlist only needs an ex-Ajax coach to sweep the quadrants of post-Sir Alex Ferguson ineptitude. Fred Grim to Manchester United? Well, doesn't that sound about right?

This is a club suffering under profound mismanagement, the sort that no one individual can marshal on their own. So there's plenty of blame to spread around. Let's start doing so, in reverse order of course. Gotta keep you on the page as long as we can. Build some suspense. Who might be top, you wonder? Well you probably know. But you know most every AAA movie is going to end with the hero triumphant. The joy is in the journey to the inevitable end point.

Now look, the soon to be former Manchester United manager is not without his faults, as Bruno Fernandes so robustly articulated after the 4-1 defeat in Como. There have been some very weird technical decisions here this season and a head coach with a scintilla of authority probably could have got this team to stop taking so many shots from outside the box. And yet did anyone at Manchester United genuinely think they'd unearthed the next great coach when they threw him the salvage our season post-Ruben Amorim job?

That Carrick did so much more than that, guiding United to Champions League qualification through a third-placed finish, spoke to his ability to keep things simple. He retained what had worked from his predecessor, tidied up some of the complexities of the formation and rode Bruno Fernandes' player of the season form as far as he could go. It is not his fault that United have not kicked on since. What had the 45 year old achieved in three seasons at Middlesbrough that suggested a coach who would do much more than what most coaches do, get a team to perform at or around its talent level?

Maybe when the stars align, when his team has a game a week and a fully fit squad he could achieve something better than the field but it is no more sensible to project out Carrick's future off the spring hot streak than it is to discount his coaching ability because he has struggled to cope with the first confluence of injuries, unfortunate results and player ill-discipline of his tenure.

Old Trafford seemed to have the right sense of it on Sunday. "It's Carrick you know," reverberated around the ground until the minute he was down the tunnel. Then it was both barrels for everyone else.

No one associated with Manchester United should apologize for having exacting standards. A well-run version of this club would make every decision based on improving their title-winning prospects either in the short or medium term. There should be no need to take the long way to the Premier League summit.

Having said all that, goodness it does not take much to send this club into a doom spiral of nostalgia and despair. When Lisandro Martinez served notice on Jason Wilcox and the hierarchy United had performed pretty well in defeat away to Atletico Madrid, a result that few in the Champions League field could credibly bemoan. Their form had wobbled but only a dodgy Erling Haaland goal had taken Manchester City past them and the last two Premier League results had been disappointing but not disastrous draws.

In short things were not going well but the difficulties were explicable. Up to the loss at the Metropolitano at least one of United's major problems was they had scored fewer goals than their expected goals (xG) for and conceded more than the xG value of their opponents shots. Their actual goal difference was minus-one, their expected goal difference was a shade under plus four. There's some heavy lifting being done in there by thrashing Ipswich Town and Sabah but the aggregate of a good team probably does contain a couple of thrashings as well as games where you play even against seemingly inferior teams like Fulham.

In short, just as United weren't as good as last season's rise to third place -- the defense started wobbling quite dramatically into the spring -- they aren't really as bad as 16th in the table, a point clear of the relegation zone might have you believe. A clear-eyed assessment both of the relative talent of United and the rest of the league would say that this is a good team vulnerable to a wobble. Just stay the course, keep calm in the dressing room and block out the noise.

But, of course... this is Manchester United we're talking about.

Sir Jim Ratcliffe certainly talked a good game when he finally got his hands on the sporting infrastructure at Old Trafford in February 2024, his $1.6 billion investment for around a quarter of the club affording him INEOS Group control of football operations at United. No longer would this be a club in hock to the first team head coach, the Ferguson way of thinking to be replaced by a brain trust that included the sporting director, "probably the recruitment guys" and, for reasons, the chief executive and Ratcliffe himself. "In modern football, you need to decide what's your path and stick to your path," the new minority owner insisted.

In the two and a half years since Manchester United's path has led them to: openly canvass the market for a replacement for manager Erik ten Hag, trigger an extension clause in his contract when they couldn't find anyone better, spend over $400 million outfitting the Dutchman with new players, sack him within four months, hire a coach in Ruben Amorim who had talked himself out of better jobs thanks to his insistence on playing a 3-4-3, finish 15th, sack Amorim just as their analytical profile was on an upswing because he had fallen out with his employers, bring in Carrick temporarily and then permanently, spend almost all their budget on midfielders, get dragged in public by Martinez.

That's just the condensed lowlights. It's fair to say that you don't hear much any more about Project 150, the ambitious vision to mark a century and a half of the club with a 21st top flight title. Perhaps by 2028 sporting director Wilcox will have got round to fixing the defense having blown so much of the 2025 summer budget on attack before then spending nearly $200 million on a midfield that needed upgrades but got Youri Tielemans, Andrey Santos and Carlos Baleba while the left back spot was left untouched.

It would say everything about the cataclysmic mismanagement at a senior level if Wilcox -- like so many at the club a man with little top level experience of the role he has been thrust into -- gets the man said to be his preferred choice to succeed Carrick, Eddie Howe.

The same Eddie Howe who spent a hugely successful two years with Dan Ashworth at Newcastle United. The same Dan Ashworth who Manchester United spent £4.1 million on the poaching of and, five months later, firing of. The same Manchester United who in INEOS' period running the show rank ninth in the Premier League for points, 10th for expected goal difference. Still, at least they sacked staff and cut costs. Who ever could have imagined that as a fix for a business' problems?

Speaking after Sunday's 3-0 loss to Bournemouth, Harry Maguire pulled no punches. "At the moment it's nowhere near good enough and something needs to change," he said. He's not wrong. And yet the only constants at this club sit second and first in our rankings. Cast your mind back to the 4-0 thrashing at the hands of Brentford in August 2022, Erik ten Hag's second game in charge and oh, what, half a dozen crises ago. The starting back four for Manchester United on that Saturday evening in west London? Diego Dalot, Harry Maguire, Lisandro Martinez, Luke Shaw. The starting back four in draws against Fulham and Everton more than four years later? Dalot, Maguire, Martinez, Shaw.

There are players at this club who have seen off half a dozen permanent managers. Some might not have lasted that long but in their time they have been frozen out or put up for sale. Few have paid the price for inconsistency. Why would you respect the authority of the head coach if you have spent three or four years in the Old Trafford dressing room and seen so many cycle through without any apparent accountability for the playing staff. It seems notable that Cristiano Ronaldo's bombing out by Ten Hag was followed by one of the most impressive runs of results in the last half decade. Players discovered their actions had consequences and started playing like that.

Now, they talk like they are bulletproof. Imagine Martin Odegaard used a post-match interview to mouth off about Mikel Arteta's tactics. Would he ever play for Arsenal again? That's a question Mesut Ozil and Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang can answer. When a player did not perform for Pep Guardiola's Manchester City, he was swiftly sold. Meanwhile United's squad is preserved in aspic. Their defense moves like it is.

These are not players who lack for talent. United's first choice attack rivals any bar Manchester City and Liverpool. Their midfield needs careful construction to mitigate for its lack of pace but it has quality. When the mood takes them Maguire, Martinez and Shaw are perfectly solid defenders. As the graphic above suggests, this is a team that can have moments of extreme competence. That is how United got to third a few months ago. Were they helped by the coach's tactics or the hierarchy's recruitment? Not really but that does not make these expensive, well-remunerated players innocent bystanders, unable to arrest the decline.

More than two decades after Malcolm Glazer loaded debt onto Manchester United to fund his purchase of the club, what has been accomplished beyond a steady degradation of this behemoth of English culture. Being owned by the Glazers, who have not put any money into the club since the takeover, is estimated to have cost the club at least $1.5 billion, much of it spent on servicing debt from the initial takeover. It should be noted that 15 major trophies have been won in the time the Glazers have owned the club but 10 of them came in the period where Ferguson's sheer magnetism held the club together.

There is an argument to be made that United's commercial income skyrocketed under current ownership and certainly this was a club that was among the first to realize that every region could have its own bespoke set of sponsors, that there was always another billboard or patch on the jersey to splash with a logo. Those brands were not, however, flocking to United because of anything the Glazers had done. United were the dominant force in English football at just the right moment to benefit from the Premier League moving from national to global obsession.

Far from custodians, the Glazers are the most deleterious of landlords. An extractive force, they provide minimal service and value while taking their management fees, dividends, repayments and then the riches Ratcliffe paid for a slice of the pie. All of their money could have gone into retaining United's preeminence in the English game or at least staving off the impact of their indifference. As if to make the metaphor particularly on the nose, on their watch Old Trafford has decayed such that the cost of renovation, an estimated $1.6 billion, might just make a case for the planned new stadium that no supporter seems to want.

A club that even in fallow years ranks among the top 10 revenue generators in football has found itself on a cost-cutting drive for which Ratcliffe is the face both because the Glazers' debt acts as a competitive drag and because ownership showed no interest nor aptitude in improving the on-field product. If the players represent a culture that is accountability-lite then it is ownership that enables it. When we start this piece by warning that nothing will change post-Carrick it is because we have seen enough to know that nothing changes until those who tolerate this degradation of Manchester United are no longer in a position of power.

#1251. How a multibillion-dollar oilfield has ignited the UK-Argentina feud over the Falklands

Argentina and the UK once fought a war over the Falkland Islands. Now, the multibillion-dollar Sea Lion oil project has reignited old tensions, with Buenos Aires seeking to put a stop to the plans.

Home to fewer than 4,000 people and located in an isolated corner of the South Atlantic Ocean, the Falkland Islands don't often feature in global business headlines.

However, a UK-Israeli oil exploration project in the North Falkland Basin is stoking long-running tensions between Argentina and the people of the archipelago.

Argentina has laid claim to the islands, which it calls Las Malvinas, for two centuries. In 1982, the dispute over the islands' sovereignty led to a war between the UK and Argentina, though British control was quickly restored after Argentine forces invaded the islands.

A 2013 sovereignty referendum on the islands returned a 99.8% vote in favor of remaining tied to the UK as a self-governing British Overseas Territory.

The Sea Lion oilfield project has brought the issue back to the surface. Last month, Argentine President Javier Milei threatened to launch an international legal challenge against the UK unless the project was stopped within two weeks.

The oil project is being run by Israeli company Navitas Petroleum and the UK's Rockhopper Exploration and has the full support of the Falkand Islands Legislative Assembly, which has pursued the project since 2010. The companies plan to begin extracting oil from the Sea Lion oilfield by early 2028.

Milei says the project is "the illegal plundering of our resources" and that he will take the matter to the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea, an independent judicial body responsible for the application of the United Nations' Convention on the Law of the Sea.

Stacy Bragger, a member of the Falklands Islands' 12-member assembly, told DW that the dispute was "nothing new" and that Argentina is using the oil project as "a vehicle to pursue their sovereignty claim."

He thinks Milei may be stepping up rhetoric ahead of the 2027 elections in Argentina.

"When there's elections coming up, the Falklands is a very convenient tool to use in order to rally people together and distract them from domestic problems," he said.

Henry Ziemer, an analyst with the Americas program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington, says the Falklands is "a perennial sore spot in Argentine politics" and that since the 1980s, various governments have raised the issue in an attempt to rally support and to "stoke the fires of nationalism."

Howerver, he thinks Milei's intervention is noteworthy given that he had previously been open to better relations with the UK on the issue. He agrees that it may be a strategy to "boost approval ratings at a time when the government is under a lot of strong domestic pressure."

Even if Milei sees political gain in the issue, the possibility of the Sea Lion project being successful would significantly raise the economic stakes for all concerned.

The project has a budget of $1.8 billion (€1.6 billion) and could generate revenues of more than double that for the Falkland Islands. The companies hope that at its peak, the field will produce up to 50,000 barrels per day and could last for up to 35 years.

That would substantially increase the Falklands' current annual GDP, which is almost entirely dependent on the volatile fishing sector and tourism. The administration is even looking into the possibility of creating a sovereign wealth fund if the oil project is successful.

"It's a very significant project for us with a lot of potential for our future," said Bragger. "It's been a big effort to get to this point and assuming all goes to plan, we want to retain as much value as possible."

However, beyond playing to domestic politics, Milei may also spy an opportunity for Argentina to position itself as an energy player amid the war in Iran and the troubles in the Strait of Hormuz.

Argentina's own domestic oil sector is growing, with production surging at Patagonia's Vaca Muerta, one of the world's largest shale developments. Were Milei's legal efforts to prove successful, there may be further gains.

"When natural resources overlay existing territorial disputes and bad blood, that tends to galvanize a lot of conflict," said Ziemer.

However, Bragger counters that Milei and Argentina have no legitimate claim to either the Falklands or whatever oil wealth may be extracted over the coming years.

"They don't respect our right to self-determination," he added. "They don't respect our right to develop our own resources. They just want to colonize us."

Milei plans to put pressure on the Falklands by stepping up existing economic sanctions. Andrea Clausen, chief executive of the Falklands since 2025, recently described this campaign as "economic warfare."

Many international suppliers and shipping companies already refuse to supply the Falklands for fear of angering Argentina. Now, Milei's government has initiated sanctions against 60 people involved in the Sea Lion project.

In a televised address last month, the Argentine president also vowed to sanction the companies involved in the project. Such a move could cast doubt on the project, which previously collapsed in 2014 and 2020, due to financing troubles, oil-price weakness and delays caused by sanctions.

Navitas this week confirmed that two contractors had pulled out of the project due to sanctions concerns, and that it was replacing them. There are also concerns that Milei could try to garner international support in favor of his position, with US President Donald Trump recently suggesting that US support for the status quo on the islands was "under review."

Bragger played this down, pointing to recent comments from US Secretary of State Marco Rubio confirming support for the Falklands. Ziemer said it would be "very shocking" if the US came down on the side of Argentina.

While uncertainty reigns over whether the oil project ultimately gets going or not, there is little expectation that the dispute could lead to a return of armed conflict like in 1982.

"That's a step too far, and the situation would have to dramatically deteriorate before we would see the potential for military conflict," said Ziemer.

When it comes to the NWSL Shield, Gotham FC is taking the long road. If they manage to lift it, it'll be because they have a great goalkeeper to keep away any spoilers. Ann-Katrin Berger is back on the team of the week honors for keeping a newly eliminated and motivated Orlando Pride from deterring Gotham's quest for the title. She faced 19 shots, eight attempts on target, and made seven saves in a narrow but crucial victory.

Angel City's Evelyn Shores has become a bona fide two-way player this season and stands out on a backline that has Sarah Gorden and Savy King. She's back on the team of the week for another stellar performance, where she was instrumental in building up play and keeping the backline in shape. She led defenders on the team in duels (seven) and co-led in clearances (two) and interceptions (two).

Not that Tierna Davidson needed any more bullet points on her long resume for NWSL defender of the year, but scoring headers in the box was already on there. She did it again for Gotham FC and scored a decisive game-winner to keep the club ahead in the NWSL Shield race

Captain fantastic for @GothamFC second goal! 🎯Tierna Davidson doesn't miss in the box 💪Catch all the action on @CBSSportsNet 📺 pic.twitter.com/IJjecaVBDs

#1249. Barcelona headline Women's Champions League Matchday 3 as league phase hits midway point

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The 2026-27 UEFA Women's Champions League will reach the midway point of the league phase as Matchday 3 action kicks off Wednesday. The league phase table hardly looks like a final verdict, with only one team on maximum points, while some clubs are comfortable with split results and others are desperate to keep their campaigns alive. Matchday 3 offers an opportunity to either shake up the table or for clubs to separate themselves, with just four rounds of play left before February's knockout playoffs. Fans can watch all the action across CBS Sports platforms. Paramount+ will livestream matches all season, while select fixtures will also air on CBS Sports Golazo Network and CBS Sports Network. With Matchday 3 split across Wednesday and Thursday, here are four things we're keeping an eye on:

The reigning title holders return to the Champions League with even more hardware than before. The club and several players racked up plenty of honors at the Ballon d'Or ceremony on Monday. The club took home best club, manager Pere Romeu nabbed women's coach of the year, Vicky Lopez won best young talent and Cata Coll was named best goalkeeper.

Alexia Putellas, now with London City Lionesses, was awarded the women's Ballon d'Or, largely for her accomplishments during her final season with FC Barcelona, since the voting period ran from August 2025 to July 2026.

After defeating Paris FC 5-2 on Matchday 1, Barcelona followed up with a 6-0 blowout of Roma on Matchday 2. They're cruising during the league phase, especially with an attack powered by several standouts, including Lopez, Claudia Pina, Kerolin and Ewa Pajor.

Pajor, the Polish international, is now the all-time leading scorer in the Champions League's group and league phases, with 18 goals.

A new UWCL record for Ewa Pajor 👏Her 18th goal makes her the highest scorer in UWCL group/league phase history 👑Stream every UEFA Women’s Champions League game on @paramountplus 📺 pic.twitter.com/2LaFr3y5cj

They'll visit HB Koge on Thursday, and the Danish side is steadily growing into the competition after picking up its first win by beating Servette 5-1. The league phase leaders will be favorites to win, but Koge might not make it comfortable, as they play with nothing-to-lose energy.

OL Lyonnes made one of the biggest statements of the league phase so far with an opening-day 8-0 demolition of Servette, in which Melchie Dumornay scored a brace and Marie-Antoinette Katoto scored a hat trick. They're a Champions League mainstay and perennial contenders, but they were shut out by Chelsea on Matchday 2, with Blues goalkeeper Hannah Hampton putting her stamp on the tournament.

HANNAH HAMPTON STANDING ON HER HEAD 🤯Stream every UEFA Women’s Champions League game on @paramountplus 📺 pic.twitter.com/gd2mxcGJIF

OL Lyonnes will now face another club unbeaten in the league phase, Inter, on Wednesday. Inter have a win and a draw and have shown they are a plucky side to deal with, but if OL want to be lethal contenders, they have to make a statement against the tournament debutants. Dumornay's creativity and Katoto's clinical finishing, with U.S. women's national team defensive midfielder Lily Yohannes anchoring the midfield and a stacked roster around them, will be a tough challenge for any team, especially those newer to the league phase. Chelsea, meanwhile, have to contend with Roma, an Italian squad that's well on its way to another Champions League crashout, showing little improvement in year two of the new league phase format with just one draw over two games. If the Blues could keep OL off the scoreboard, they should be confident they can do the same against Roma, and if they don't, it'll bring more questions about the club's ability to manage Champions League expectations. German side Bayern Munich welcome Real Madrid in a showdown that could tip the league phase table. Bayern had a chance to make an opening-day statement but instead gave up a two-goal lead and settled for a draw against Manchester City, before picking up a crucial win away against Benfica in Portugal. Matches in this competition have often been won or lost late, and veteran Pernille Harder had her say for Bayern at Benfica, scoring her 50th UWCL goal in the 3-0 victory.

50 UWCL GOALS FOR PERNILLE HARDER 🌟She becomes just the fourth player in competition history to reach the milestone 👏Stream every UEFA Women’s Champions League game on @paramountplus 📺 pic.twitter.com/wG9RWk22sl

Real Madrid's two consecutive draws in the competition leave everyone wanting more. Colombia international Linda Caicedo is elite and has consistently shown her quality over the two matches, and if she and Felicia Schroder continue to build chemistry in attack, they'll be a dangerous combo to deal with.

The meeting between the German and Spanish clubs on Wednesday will be a key fixture to watch, as a win for either could put it in a more favorable position in the league phase table at the halfway point.

There were plenty of doubts around Paris Saint-Germain heading into the tournament, given their steep fall from Champions League grace. After a miserable campaign last season, the Parisians got off to another worrisome start with a 1-1 draw against Real Madrid, in which they trailed for over 70 minutes before equalizing from the penalty spot. They quickly followed that up with a five-goal win over OH Leuven on Matchday 2, and now find themselves in a far better position than they were last year. Next up is Manchester City, a side that is still on the hunt for its first win of the tournament. Two sides carefully rebuilding their UWCL pedigree could produce either a cagey matchup or a momentum-shifting performance. Arsenal continue to baffle on the pitch. After a smash-and-grab for all three points on opening day against underdogs HB Koge, the Gunners were challenged by Paris FC in a 2-2 draw the following matchday. Winning ugly doesn't hide the fact that this is a team that has struggled to break opponents down, despite a talented roster, and it raises fair questions about manager Renee Slegers and her tactical approach. Goals from Alessia Russo and Georgia Stanway help, but there is more that's expected from the group that won the UWCL title in 2025, even with Mariona Caldentey managing an injury at the moment. If they struggle against Benfica on Wednesday, it'll cast more doubt on the club's direction this season.

The bottom of the league phase table is already somewhat crowded, even with some unexpected clubs at the moment, but that's what makes the midway point of the tournament so exciting. Manchester City and Real Madrid might steal eyeballs, as neither team can keep drawing for much longer, but former dark horse BK Hacken and last year's dancing debutants OH Leuven have struggled to find the net. Hacken join Servette with zero points through two matchdays and will face Paris FC on Thursday. Paris FC are eager to take the next step in the UWCL, from unpredictable underdogs to bona fide contenders. Whoever drops points in the head-to-head could be out of the race for the top 12 in the league phase.

#1248. Decoding the regulatory programs governing glioblastoma plasticity

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Glioblastoma is incurable and resistant to therapy despite genomic stability under treatment1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8, suggesting that non-genetic cellular plasticity is a central driver of progression. Whether such plasticity reflects stochastic state switching or is governed by predictable gene regulation has remained unclear9,10,11,12,13. Here we introduce scDORI (single-cell deep multi-omic regulatory inference)—a deep-learning framework that infers enhancer-driven gene-regulatory networks at single-cell resolution—and apply it to single-nucleus multiome profiles of more than one million cells from primary glioblastomas. Integrating computational inference with systematic perturbation screens across patient-derived models, we show that a structured regulatory program with an asymmetric interplay of activators and repressors governs cellular plasticity in glioblastoma. The resulting transition landscape is hierarchical and predictable, but permits cross-lineage trajectories that are absent from normal neurodevelopment. Within this landscape, low-plasticity states such as the neuronal-like state are not stable differentiation end points but actively maintained configurations, stabilized by a network of safeguard repressors that silence alternative fates. We identify MYT1L as the dominant member of this network, and show that it binds to and represses master regulators of every alternative state to consolidate neuronal-like identity. MYT1L restricted plasticity even under standard-of-care therapy and suppressed tumour growth and invasion in vivo. Conversely, loss of MYT1L reactivated plasticity and accelerated malignant features, indicating that low-plasticity identity requires continuous repression. These findings reframe malignant cell state stability as a balance between activation and continuous repression, and nominate safeguard repressors as candidate therapeutic targets that are distinct from differentiation-inducing activators, with potential relevance across cancers in which phenotypic switching drives therapy resistance.

The capacity of cancer cells to switch phenotypic states, also called cellular plasticity, is a hallmark of cancer and is involved in tumour initiation and progression, including therapeutic resistance1. Glioblastoma (GB), the most common primary brain tumour in adults, is characterized by profound cellular heterogeneity and a dismal prognosis2,3. Although the genomic landscape of GB has been catalogued extensively, actionable genetic drivers remain scarce, and clinical responses to targeted therapies have been minimal4,5,6. Longitudinal studies have underscored the limited contribution of therapy-induced genetic evolution in GB and revealed remarkable clonal stability despite treatment7,8, suggesting that non-genetic mechanisms, such as epigenetic plasticity and transcriptional reprogramming, are central to adaptation and treatment resistance in GB. Seminal single-cell transcriptomic studies have shown that malignant GB cells occupy a continuum of cellular states resembling developmental progenitors (for example, oligodendrocyte precursor cell (OPC)-like and neural progenitor cell (NPC)-like), as well as astrocytic and mesenchymal-like phenotypes9,10. Patient-derived xenograft models have demonstrated that individual GB cells can give rise to multiple states, implying substantial plasticity10,11. However, whether these state transitions follow stereotyped routes or variable trajectories12,13, and how gene-regulatory mechanisms promote or constrain them, remain poorly understood.

Here, and in a companion study14, we address these questions by integrating single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) and chromatin accessibility (single-nucleus assay for transposase-accessible chromatin using sequencing; snATAC-seq) profiles from more than one million cells from isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH)-wild-type primary GBs. Using a computational approach (single-cell deep multi-omic regulatory inference; scDORI) and systematic transcription factor (TF) perturbations, we decode enhancer-driven gene-regulatory networks (eGRNs) at single-cell resolution and map the regulatory landscape that underlies the identity and plasticity of GB cells. Specifically, we model the gene-regulatory processes that govern GB cell states, identify key transcriptional regulators for each state, elucidate their roles in driving cell-state conversions and reconstruct a hierarchical roadmap of GB transitions. Our analyses reveal a structured landscape of GB state transitions shaped by epigenetic ‘highways’ and ‘barriers’. Neuronal-like cells emerge as a constrained, low-plasticity state stabilized by a network of transcriptional repressors that actively silences alternative malignant fates. We identify MYT1L as the key repressor in this network: gain-of-function of MYT1L restricts plasticity and induces a neuronal-like identity in patient-derived GB cells, and reduces tumour growth after transplantation in mice; by contrast, removal of MYT1L enhances plasticity and malignant features. These findings suggest that enforcing repressive barriers could lock GB cells into less adaptive states, and identify plasticity restriction as a potential therapeutic strategy.

Together with our companion study mapping spatio-temporal trajectories in GB tumours14, our findings reveal a conserved, epigenetically controlled hierarchy of cell states and transition routes in GB. Our work establishes transcriptional repressors as key suppressors of plasticity and underscores the potential of targeting the epigenetic foundations of state switching in brain cancer.

To characterize the regulatory landscape of GB, we generated a multiome snRNA–snATAC-seq atlas (see the companion study14), spanning parallel gene-expression and chromatin-accessibility profiles of more than one million cells collected across multiple sites (4–15) from 12 IDH-wild-type primary GB tumours, including peritumoral regions. In line with previous studies10, malignant GB cells exhibited vastly heterogeneous transcriptional profiles, ranging from developmental-like (OPC-NPC-like, OPC-like, OPC-neuronal-like, NPC-neuronal-like and astrocyte (AC)-progenitor-like) to glial injury response and hypoxia-associated (AC-gliosis-like, gliosis-like and hypoxia) phenotypes, as well as cycling signatures (proliferative) (Fig. 1a and Extended Data Fig. 1a).

a, Experimental set-up, uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) plot and annotation of the RNA modality of 368,054 TME and 657,275 GB cells from 12 patients with IDH-wild-type GB profiled by snRNA–snATAC-seq. Colours and labels denote states of the indicated malignant GB and TME cells. b, Schematic of computation of the epigenetic plasticity score. A linear classifier trained on gene expression to predict transcriptional states is applied to gene accessibility profiles, with ambiguity of predictions indicating epigenetic plasticity. c, Epigenetic plasticity score determined using the approach in b, visualized for all cells on the UMAP plot in a. High scores denote high epigenetic plasticity. d, Confusion matrix for the accessibility-based predictions from the classifier in b: state prediction probability on the basis of gene accessibility profiles (rows), averaged across cells from each transcriptionally defined state (columns). Off-diagonal mass reflects accessibility compatible with several transcriptional states, the ambiguity that drives the epigenetic plasticity score in b. Malignant states (yellow box) show the lowest accuracy, indicating increased epigenetic plasticity. e, Average epigenetic plasticity score for the indicated cell states across n = 12 patients. Malignant states differ in plasticity, with NPC-neuronal-like and OPC-neuronal-like states showing the lowest levels (P = 5.0 × 10−6, two-sided t-test). Box plots show the median and interquartile range (IQR); whiskers are 1.5× IQR. f, Variance component analysis of epigenetic plasticity, assessing the contribution of patient, cell type and other sources of variation (residuals). Illustrations in a,b created in BioRender; Mall, M. https://biorender.com/51tfsoq (2026).

First, we investigated the epigenetic plasticity of GB cells, assuming that accessible gene regions without active transcription indicate epigenetic plasticity. Inspired by a previous study15, we quantified how well accessibility profiles of cell-state markers predict transcriptionally defined cell states (Fig. 1b, Extended Data Fig. 1b,c, Supplementary Table 1 and Methods). Cells whose chromatin profiles yield uncertain predictions are scored as more epigenetically plastic. Our analysis revealed that malignant cells exhibit greater epigenetic plasticity than non-malignant tumour microenvironment (TME) cells and analogous neurodevelopmental cell types (Fig. 1c and Extended Data Fig. 1d–f), with chromatin accessibility in malignant cells often being compatible with multiple cell states (Fig. 1d). However, the extent of this plasticity varied significantly across GB cell states (Fig. 1e), and NPC-neuronal-like and OPC-neuronal-like cells stood out as the least plastic states. The variations in epigenetic plasticity could not be explained by differences in global coupling between gene expression and accessibility, were robust to differences in cell numbers per state and were consistently observed across patients (Fig. 1f and Extended Data Fig. 1g–j). These data suggest that specific regulatory mechanisms underlie GB plasticity and govern cell-state heterogeneity.

To determine the specific gene-regulatory processes that underlie the observed differences in epigenetic plasticity, we aimed to identify relevant TFs, cis-regulatory elements (CREs) and their interplay across GB states using eGRNs. Established eGRN inference methods are not designed for the heterogeneity of a single-cell tumour atlas like ours16,17,18,19,20,21,22. Specifically, existing methods assume discrete, predefined cell-types and therefore cannot capture the continuous, cell-state-specific variation in eGRNs that defines malignant heterogeneity. Many also scale poorly to datasets of this size23. Moreover, previous methods focus mainly on signatures of transcriptional activation, despite the growing recognition of gene repression as a key regulator of cell identity and plasticity in cancer24,25.

To address these limitations, we developed scDORI, a computational approach for inferring continuous eGRNs and their relationships across cell populations using single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) and scATAC-seq multiome data (Fig. 2a and Methods). Building on autoencoders26, scDORI performs joint dimensionality reduction of gene expression and chromatin accessibility profiles, decomposing both into gene-regulatory modules16,27,28,29,30,31,32 that are hereafter referred to as ‘Topics’. Each scDORI Topic encodes an eGRN in which TFs bind to CREs to control target gene expression, so the factors carry regulatory meaning rather than describing co-variation alone (Fig. 2a). Coupled decoders enforce this structure through established eGRN signatures: peak co-accessibility, TF chromatin binding, CRE–gene linkages and TF–target expression correlations that distinguish activation from repression16,17,18,19,20,21,22 (Extended Data Fig. 2a). By modelling each cell as a mixture of Topics, scDORI can capture continuous variations in eGRNs across cell states, without relying on predefined annotations. Conversely, a single Topic can be active across multiple cell states, enabling the identification of shared aspects of gene regulation. scDORI scales to datasets comprising millions of cells, and performs favourably, compared with existing eGRN inference methods, on benchmarks such as the prediction of enhancer–gene links33 (Extended Data Fig. 2b,c).

Auxiliary decoders impose mechanistic constraints from peak co-accessibility, TF binding, CRE–gene linkages and TF–target expression correlations that separate activation from repression. b, Activity of selected Topics in malignant cells, visualized on the UMAP representation from Fig. 1a. c, Heat map with hierarchical clustering of selected Topic activation patterns across GB states, revealing an activation continuum. Applied to our GB atlas, scDORI identified 31 active Topics with distinct patterns of activity across cells and patients (Fig. 2b,c, Extended Data Fig. 3 and Supplementary Table 2), each capturing co-accessible chromatin regions that were cis-linked to co-expressed genes (Fig. 2d and Extended Data Fig. 4a). Notably, the mechanistic constraints came at no cost to descriptive power: scDORI Topics explained transcriptional variation in tumour cells as well as or better than conventional dimensionality reduction methods did18,29 (Extended Data Fig. 4b,c). Clustering transcriptional GB states according to Topic activity patterns revealed four major regulatory states alongside a distinct proliferative (cycling) population, including developmental states (neuronal-like and OPC-NPC-like) and AC–gliosis–hypoxia states (AC-like and gliosis–hypoxia) (Fig. 2c). Topics specific to individual states reflected gene programs that are characteristic of their developmental counterparts, such as neurotransmitter release in neuronal-like cells (Topic 37), PDGF signalling in OPC-NPC-like cells (Topic 34) and calcium ion homeostasis in AC-like cells (Topic 20)34,35,36 (Fig. 2e, Extended Data Fig. 3a and Supplementary Table 2). These programs were also active in corresponding TME cell types, consistent with tumour cells co-opting developmental pathways.

As well as explaining differences between GB states, scDORI resolved functional heterogeneity within individual malignant states. For instance, in gliosis–hypoxia cells, distinct Topics captured hallmark features such as hypoxic stress (Topic 11), cytokine signalling (Topic 19) and vascular wound healing (Topic 12)37,38,39 (Fig. 2e). scDORI also identified ‘inter-state’ Topics (7, 9, 25, 29, 33, 36 and 49) that span several GB states. Most of these were enriched for programs linked to fate commitment and differentiation, indicating a potential role in mediating state transitions (Fig. 2c,e and Extended Data Fig. 3a,b). Finally, scDORI identified Topics that were broadly active across most tumour cells, reflecting tumour-wide programs, such as inflammatory response (Topic 31) and cell adhesion (Topic 18)40 (Extended Data Fig. 3a,b). The inferred Topics were reproducible across model restarts, consistently represented across patients with GB and transferable to independent single-cell GB atlases10 (Extended Data Figs. 3c and 4d–f). Notably, scDORI Topic-specific eGRNs accurately captured differential expression between GB cell states of these independent atlases (Extended Data Fig. 4g,h).

The eGRN encoded by each Topic directly yielded Topic regulators (TRs), defined as the TFs with the strongest predicted activation of the Topic-specific gene program. On average, scDORI identified about nine TRs per Topic (Fig. 2f, Supplementary Table 2 and Methods). These included known GB cell-state markers, such as ASCL1 in OPC-NPC-like cells (Topic 36), SOX11 in neuronal-like cells (Topic 24) and FOSL1 in gliosis–hypoxia cells (Topic 19), as well as TFs associated with the respective Topic programs, such as hypoxia (NFKB1, Topic 19) and stress response (JUND, Topic 11)10,41,42,43,44. State-specific TRs included lineage-specific TFs, such as SOX6 (Topic 34, OPCs) and TRPS1 (Topic 9, ACs), further supporting the idea that GB cells reuse developmental TFs and gene programs45,46,47. Besides positive regulation, scDORI-inferred repressive links and identified Topic safeguards (TSs): TFs that regulate an identity by silencing gene programs of states distinct from their state of activity; that is, alternative states (Fig. 2g, Supplementary Table 2 and Methods). For instance, ST18 and SOX10 emerged as putative repressors of alternative state programs in neuronal-like and OPC-NPC-like programs, respectively. Several TSs also act as TRs of their own Topic, revealing factors that both activate their own identity program and repress those of alternative states. Collectively, scDORI redefines GB heterogeneity from a gene-regulation standpoint and reveals state-specific activators and repressors, many of which have not yet been described in GB.

The extent to which GB state transitions follow defined regulatory rules, and which TFs drive them, remain central questions in GB biology9,10. We reasoned that if scDORI faithfully captures these processes, then activating the predicted regulators should induce the associated cell states. To test this, we performed a pooled single-cell lentiviral overexpression (OE) screen of 55 TR and TS candidates across three patient-derived GB cell (PDGC) lines, co-cultured with primary cortical cells to provide a neural microenvironment (Fig. 3a, Extended Data Fig. 5, Supplementary Table 3 and Methods).

Transduced cells were co-cultured with primary cortical cells, induced with Dox, sorted by fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) and profiled by scRNA-seq. b, Effects of TF OE on GB state identity. Shown is the proportion of regulators whose overexpression induced the predicted identity shift, evaluated at the state and Topic level (from b and Extended Data Fig. 5g). d, Agreement of high-confidence state drivers from the screen in b with scDORI predictions. Shown are: Pearson correlation between TF level and state probability (dose–response); NES (P < 0.05) of state marker genes among OE-induced differentially expressed genes (DEGs); scDORI state regulation score; and the predicted regulatory mechanism, shown as a bivariate heat map of activation (red) versus repression (blue) strength on state marker genes.
