a, Correspondence between the GB cell-state annotations used in this study and the GB meta-modules defined by Neftel et al.10. Each malignant cell was scored for every Neftel meta-module by signature scoring on log-normalized RNA (excluding the cell-cycle modules G1/S and G2/M), and assigned to its highest-scoring module. Shown is the proportion of cells in each cell state that map to each Neftel et al. meta-module. b, Cell-state prediction accuracy of the classifier in Fig. 1b, trained on gene expression from a random 80% of 16,423 metacells (9,464 GB, 6,959 TME; 12 patients). Accuracy is shown for the held-out 20% (n = 3,285) using gene expression, and for all metacells using gene accessibility. Cell states are predicted less accurately from accessibility than from expression, most pronounced for malignant states, indicating elevated epigenetic plasticity. c, Uncertainty (entropy) of expression-based cell-state predictions per metacell (n = 16,423 metacells). Low uncertainty across all cell states confirms that expression profiles support confident state assignment. d, Evaluation of cell-state prediction accuracy of the cell-state classifier as in b, however trained on human neurodevelopmental cell types of a multi-ome brain atlas (12 donors; early fetal, late fetal and post-natal stages48), evaluated based on gene expression (held-out 20%; n = 512 metacells) and gene accessibility (n = 2,559 metacells). Cell-state predictions show comparable accuracy across modalities, except in progenitor populations. e, Epigenetic plasticity across neurodevelopmental metacells (n = 2,559), analysed as in Fig. 1c,d. Top: Epigenetic plasticity score (prediction entropy) across the cell types in d. Bottom: Percentage of cells from each expression-defined state (columns) assigned to each state from gene accessibility (rows). Off-diagonal values reflect accessibility compatible with several transcriptional states. As expected, radial glia and NPCs show the highest epigenetic plasticity (P = 7.5 × 10−59, two-sided t-test). f, Schematic of the canonical neurodevelopmental lineage relationships among the cell types analysed in d,e. Radial glia sit at the apex and give rise to three differentiation routes: Towards neurons, astrocytes, and oligodendrocytes, with plasticity decreasing along each route as cells mature. g, Global correlation between gene expression and accessibility in GB metacells (Pearson r across n = 21,369 genes), stratified by cell state. The concordance of correlation levels across GB cell states suggests that state-specific differences in epigenetic plasticity are not driven by differences in the global coupling of gene expression and chromatin accessibility. h, Average epigenetic plasticity per patient (n = 12) for the cell states in b, computed with the linear model of Fig. 1e after downsampling each state to equal cell numbers. Plasticity trends match those in Fig. 1e, indicating that the observed differences are not driven by variation in cell abundance. i, Average epigenetic plasticity score of GB states (n = 9) across patients. Although individual patients exhibit variation in plasticity across states, the average plasticity is comparable across patients (one-way ANOVA, P = 0.53). j, Donor-associated variation in epigenetic plasticity within defined cell neighbourhoods, shown as the ratio of the standard deviation of mean plasticity scores across donors to the standard deviation across all cells. Values were computed using k = 10 or k = 30 neighbours for each metacell (n = 4,813 and n = 11,868 metacells respectively), considering neighbourhoods represented by at least three donors, and stratified by state. Donor-associated variation was lower than overall local variation in plasticity across all malignant states. Box plots in c,e,g–j show median and IQR, 1.5 × IQR (whiskers), and outliers. Illustration in f created in BioRender; Mall, M. https://biorender.com/51tfsoq (2026).

a, Two-phase training scheme. Phase 1: Topic construction by joint training of the core autoencoder modules. scDORI embeds paired scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq profiles in a shared latent Topic space, from which three modules reconstruct the data. Module 1 maps Topic proportions to peak accessibility through a linear decoder with batch-specific adjustments. Module 2 predicts gene expression from the denoised Topic-specific accessibility of Module 1, using a learnable gene–peak linkage matrix restricted to a fixed genomic window around each gene. Module 3 reconstructs TF expression through Topic-TF weights. The three modules are trained jointly, minimizing the sum of their reconstruction losses together with regularization terms. Phase 2: Fine-tuning for eGRN inference. A fourth module infers Topic-specific TF–gene-regulatory links. In silico TF–peak binding scores, signed for activation or repression, are weighted by Topic-specific peak accessibility (Module 1) and propagated to target genes through the gene–peak links (Module 2). Learnable TF–gene-Topic weights adjust these links according to TF–target expression co-variation, and activating and repressive contributions are combined into a net regulatory score that predicts gene expression from Topic-level TF expression (Module 3). The encoder, gene–peak links, and Topic–peak decoder are optionally frozen during fine-tuning, with sparsity constraints on the learned TF–gene weights. b, Training runtime of scDORI as a function of dataset size, shown for Phase 1, Phase 2, and both phases combined, measured on subsampled multi-ome data from the GB atlas. Runtime scales to datasets of millions of cells. Empirical runtimes on a single NVIDIA V100 GPU (32 GB). c, Assessment of peak–gene link predictions in three cell lines (IMR90, K562, GM12878) of the published ENCODE dataset76,77, converted to semi-synthetic single-cell multi-ome data as in18 and scored against curated experimentally supported enhancer–gene links from BENGI33 as ground truth. Benchmarks span nine evidence x cell-line combinations available in BENGI, drawn from seven evidence sources derived from chromatin configuration, perturbation, and genomic interaction assays. AUPRC is shown for recovered peak–gene pairs with scDORI and SCENIC+. scDORI achieved higher AUPRC than SCENIC+ in all nine comparisons (P = 2.0 × 10−3, one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test, n = 9 paired comparisons). Illustration in a created in BioRender; Mall, M. https://biorender.com/51tfsoq (2026).

a, Average Topic activity in malignant and TME states. Extended version of Fig. 2c showing data for 31 Topics (all Topics with max activation > 0.1 across cells). Key biological functions of each Topic based on GSEA are shown. Raw values and complete pathway analysis are reported in Supplementary Table 2. b, Activity of GB-associated Topics in all cells visualized on the UMAP representation of Fig. 1a. State-specific, inter-state, and pan-state Topics are labelled accordingly. c, Activity of GB-associated Topics across patients. Shown is the number of patients with at least 1% of their cells exhibiting activity (>0.05) for each Topic. All GB Topics are active in at least 4 out of 12 patients, confirming that Topics capture universal regulatory programs of GB.

a, UMAP visualization of ATAC peaks in the patient atlas using Topic–peak scores (from scDORI Module 1) as embedding. (Left) Z-scored accessibility of peaks in each GB state. (Right) Topic–peak score for selected Topics. Topics identify distinct groups of co-accessible peaks within each GB state, reflecting different gene-regulatory programs active in those states. b, Genomic distance distributions between peak–gene pairs inferred by scDORI or MOFA29. For each peak in a MOFA factor, we picked the closest gene that was also part of the same factor. Red lines mark the cis-distance (150 kb) constraint applied to scDORI. Black lines indicate the ±1 Mb assessment window, and interchromosomal peak–gene pairs are shown separately on the left. c, Comparison of cell type prediction in our GB dataset using three latent space embeddings: scDORI (50 Topics), MOFA (50 factors), and SCENIC+ (AUCell-based TF activity scores from 195 TFs). Logistic regression models were trained to predict cell type labels from the latent embeddings of each method, using n = 9,464 GB and n = 6,959 TME metacells as input. scDORI achieved higher mean per-cell type accuracy (88.0%) than MOFA (80.3%; 17/17 cell types, P = 8 × 10−6) and SCENIC+ (85.2%; 11/17 cell types, P = 2.7 × 10−3), with the advantage over SCENIC+ concentrated in malignant states. P-values were obtained from a one-sided paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test. d, Stability of scDORI gene programs across random initializations. Shown is the Jaccard similarity between the top 500 genes of the most active Topic in each GB state, comparing the reference run (Run 0) against three additional runs trained with different random seeds. A randomized version of the reference Topic–gene set serves as a negative control. Gene programs are recovered consistently across runs. e, Activity patterns of selected scDORI Topics derived from our patient atlas projected onto a reference single-cell GB atlas from Neftel et al.10. Colour denotes average Topic activity, and bars on the left show the proportion of cells from each state in our atlas among the top 5,000 cells for each scDORI Topic. The mapping of scDORI Topics to GB cell states is highly concordant across datasets. f, Activity of selected scDORI Topics within malignant cells of the Neftel GB atlas in e, visualized on a UMAP embedding. Neftel state annotations and Leiden-clustered subpopulations are indicated. g, Performance of scDORI and SCENIC+ eGRNs in predicting DEGs between the Neftel GB cell states shown in e, following the GRaNPA21 framework. For each state pair a logistic regression model was trained to predict whether each gene is up- or downregulated based on the signed TF–gene links in each eGRN. Genes were split into four cross-validation folds, with test genes held out from training. AUPRC is shown for all state pairs. Centre line, mean; error bars, s.d. Both methods outperform randomized control eGRNs (P = 3.1 × 10−5 for each, one-sided paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test, n = 15 pairs) and perform comparably to each other. h, Performance of scDORI and SCENIC+ in predicting DEGs between the Leiden clusters shown in f, computed as in g. AUPRC is shown for every cluster pair, considering either scDORI or SCENIC+ eGRNs. Centre line, mean; error bars, s.d. Both methods outperform randomized control eGRNs (P = 4.4 × 10−19 and P = 4.3 × 10−19, respectively; one-sided paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test, n = 104 pairs).

a, Quality control of the gain-of-function screen described in Fig. 3. Shown are distributions of UMI counts, detected genes, and mitochondrial read fractions, stratified by seeding density (High: 14,000 cells/cm2; low: 9,000 cells/cm2) and biological replicate, separately for each PDGC line (S24, P3XX, and BG5). b, Cells recovered after quality control and barcode demultiplexing. Left: Relative contribution of each cell line, replicate, and seeding density to the total of 261,566 cells. Right: Fraction of cells recovered per TF perturbation, shown for the pooled dataset and for each patient line. TF representation is balanced across lines. n = 3 (BG5) and n = 6 (S24, P3XX). c, Expression bimodality coefficients (BC) of all screened TFs in OE and control cells from b. Each dot is a TF (n = 55). Violin centre line, median; error bars, extrema. Expression is bimodal (BC > 0.555) for every TF in the OE populations and for 54 of 55 TFs in the controls, reflecting heterogeneous expression of the targeted TFs and motivating exclusion of low- and high TF-expressing cells from respective populations in each OE-versus-control comparison. Inset: ASCL1 expression in control and ASCL1-overexpressing cells. d, Effect of the endogenous-expression filter on control cell heterogeneity in b. Each dot is one TF from the OE screen (n = 55), showing the change in state proportions (left) or in average entropy (right) after removing control cells with high endogenous expression of that TF (above the tenth percentile). Centre line, mean; error bars, s.d. Filtering left state heterogeneity essentially unchanged: change in entropy did not differ from zero (P = 0.14, two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test, n = 220) and mean changes in individual state proportions were at most 0.025. e, Proportion of cells from each GB state in unperturbed control populations across pooled or individual PDGC lines in b. Total cell counts per condition indicated above. All GB states are, to varying degrees, represented in control cells across all lines. f, Validation of state regulator ranking by scDORI and SCENIC+. For each GB state, the average change in state probability (Δ state score, OE versus control) is shown for the top N predicted regulators of that state, with the average change in the remaining TFs (54 − N) plotted below for comparison. Shaded regions indicate s.d. intervals. Regulators nominated by scDORI induced their predicted state more strongly than those nominated by SCENIC+ (P = 8.2 × 10−10, one-sided paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test, n = 40 state × N combinations, scDORI higher in 34 of 40), most notably for the neuronal-like and AC-like states. g, Induction of Topic programs after gain-of-function of scDORI-predicted regulators of each Topic. For each top regulator (scDORI regulator score > 0.25), the change in activity of its predicted Topic is shown (Δ Topic score, OE vs. control). Dot size denotes the number of PDGC lines in which the effect was significant (label-permutation test, Benjamini–Hochberg FDR < 0.05) and colour denotes the scDORI regulator score. Regulators of nearly all Topics induced their predicted Topic program. All Topic-level effects per TF are provided in Supplementary Table 3. h, Concordance of Topic- and state-level effects after OE of scDORI-predicted regulators. Each point corresponds to one TF-Topic prediction, positioned by the change it induced in that Topic (x-axis) and in the corresponding state (y-axis), relative to control cells. TFs predicted to regulate several Topics appear once per Topic. Colour denotes the predicted Topic and dot style the significance category (label-permutation test, Benjamini–Hochberg FDR < 0.05). Most regulators induced Topic and state changes consistent with scDORI predictions (Supplementary Table 3). i, Number of DEGs per TF OE condition versus the number of OE cells, per cell line in b. The dashed line depicts a linear regression fit. DEG count scaled positively with the number of OE cells (Spearman r = 0.87, P = 1.9 × 10−50, n = 162 TF × cell-line conditions), reflecting increased statistical power with greater cell coverage. j, Number of upregulated and downregulated genes in TF-overexpressing cells relative to control cells in each PDGC line in b. Bars show the mean ± s.d. of each direction. n = 3 (BG5) and n = 6 (S24, P3XX). Top 100 DEGs per condition are reported in Supplementary Table 3.

a, Availability of TRs across GB states. Left: Schematic illustrating how a TR can be selectively expressed in its native Topic but epigenetically primed in cells of alternative states. Right: Mean chromatin accessibility (colour intensity) and mean expression (dot size) of indicated TRs across GB Topics. Bars on top indicate availability of TRs in Topics of alternative states, either by expression (scaled expression>0.5; purple) or epigenetic priming (scaled accessibility>0.5, scaled expression<0.3; green). b, Average expression (left) and chromatin accessibility (right) of the top TRs (activity score>0.05) of each target Topic within cells of each source Topic. TR expression is largely confined to Topics of the same GB state, whereas TR accessibility extends broadly to Topics of alternative states, indicating epigenetic priming for future activation. c, TAP between Topic pairs, scaled by the number of expressed TFs in the source Topic and by the weight of self-regulatory links in the target Topic. Asterisks denote significant links, defined as those exceeding the 95th percentile of a null distribution from 1,000 randomized GRNs (one-sided permutation test). OPC-NPC-like (25, 34) and AC-like (9, 44) tTopics show multiple strong links towards alternative state Topics, whereas links from neuronal-like Topics remain largely within their own state. Full list of TAP scores provided in Supplementary Table 4. d, Changes in TAP scores when using TR accessibility or expression in source Topic for computation. Positive values indicate TAP links mainly influenced by epigenetic priming of TRs, which encompass many of the links between different states. e, Number of top TRs from alternative states (activity score>0.5) that are epigenetically primed in each GB state. The epigenetic priming of alternative state TRs reflects transition potential patterns. f, Variance component analysis of TAP scores across Topic pairs. Each bar shows the proportion of variance explained by a single biological feature, fitted separately in an ordinary least squares model and stratified by whether the target Topic belongs to the same/related state (yellow; n = 77 Topic pairs), an alternative state (orange; n = 212), or any state (purple; n = 289). Regulatory links inferred from the eGRNs explain the largest share of TAP variance. For transitions towards alternative states, epigenetic priming of TRs contributes more than their expression level. g, TRS values between pairs of Topics. Neuronal-like Topics (24, 37) exert the highest repressive effects towards alternative state Topics. Asterisks label significant TRS links, estimated as in c. Full list of TRS values provided in Supplementary Table 4. h, Repression exerted by each source Topic towards the top 50 marker genes from each state identified by the linear model in Fig. 1b, instead of TRs. Similar to TR-level repression, neuronal-like Topics (24, 49) exert the strongest repression towards genes of alternative states. i, Cumulative repression exerted by individual source Topics towards genes of alternative Topics or states. Neuronal-like Topic 24 exerts the strongest repression against alternative identities. j,k, Net transition potential between Topics, as determined by the difference between TAP and TRS values between Topic pairs. Three distinct regulatory mechanisms underlie net transition potential interactions with alternative Topics: (i) predominant repression (Topic 24), (ii) predominant activation (Topics 9 and 34), and (iii) limited activation or repression (Topic 19). Raw values are provided in Supplementary Table 4. Illustration in a created in BioRender; Mall, M. https://biorender.com/51tfsoq (2026).

a, Schematic of dorsal telencephalon development, depicting neurogenic and gliogenic differentiation trajectories from radial glia towards differentiated neuronal and glial cell types. The shown differentiation hierarchy was reconstructed from available lineage-tracing studies49,50,51. NPC: Neural progenitor cell, OPC: Oligodendrocyte precursor cell, GPC: Glial progenitor cell. b, Activity of selected Topics inferred by scDORI from a developmental brain atlas (n = 12 donors)48. Colour denotes average Topic activity scaled across cell types of dorsal telencephalic origin, collected during early fetal, late fetal, and post-natal development stages. Topic-regulated programs are labelled on the right, determined based on Topic activity patterns, associated genes, and TF regulators. UL: Upper-layer, DL: Deep-layer. Full list of inferred Topics reported in Supplementary Table 5. c, TRs identified in developmental Topics in b recovered canonical lineage regulators, including PAX6 and GLI3 in radial glia114, SOX11 in fetal neurons115, CUX2 in UL neurons116, FOXP2 in DL neurons117, SOX9 in astrocytes118, OLIG1 in OPCs119, and MYRF in oligodendrocytes120, indicating high-confidence prediction of bona fide fate regulators. d, TAP, TRS and net transition potential (TAP–TRS) between pairs of developmental Topics in b. Shown are the respective values scaled by the number of TFs in the source Topic and self-activation in the target Topic. Asterisks denote significant links, defined as those exceeding the 95th percentile of a null distribution from 1,000 randomized GRNs (one-sided permutation test). Progenitor Topics show broad transition potential toward downstream lineages, whereas terminally differentiated cell type Topics show little or no transition potential towards alternative lineages, often constrained by repression. These results reflect the canonical differentiation hierarchy shown in a, as well as dedifferentiation potentials described for OPCs and astrocytes51,52, demonstrating that our transition model captures biologically coherent relationships. Illustration in a created in BioRender; Mall, M. https://biorender.com/51tfsoq (2026).

a, Schematic of the approach used to compute spatial co-activity of Topics across 97 matched tumour sections profiled by Visium spatial transcriptomics. For every section and Topic pair, the pairwise Euclidean distance between Topic A and Topic B spots is computed. Spatial co-activity is defined as the fraction of sections in which the closest 10% of spot pairs are spatially overlapping. Because spatial distance is symmetric by construction, net transition potentials (TAP–TRS) are symmetrized before row-wise Pearson correlation. b, Number of Visium sections and patients represented per Topic pair in the analysis described in a. All Topic pairs were covered by at least 20 sections derived from at least 7 patients, supporting the generalizability of the reported spatial co-activity patterns. Data are presented as mean ± s.d. c, Average spatial co-activity between Topic pairs computed as described in a (right), compared to their symmetric net transition potentials (left). Topic pairs with high net transition potential tend to be spatially co-active, as evidenced by row-wise correlations (Pearson r, right bar). Asterisks denote correlation P < 0.05. A full list of spatial co-activity values between Topics is provided in Supplementary Table 6. d, Schematic of how temporal co-activity of Topics was computed across pseudotime-aligned clonal trajectories. For each Topic pair, we averaged the cosine similarity of their temporal profiles across the top 10% of trajectories in which the two Topics were most temporally proximal, and compared the resulting matrix to net transition potential using column-wise (r1) and row-wise (r2) Pearson correlations, which capture incoming and outgoing transition relationships, respectively. e, Number of clonal populations per patient considered for the temporal analysis in d. A total of 57 clonal trajectories from all 12 patients were considered. f, Average temporal co-activity of Topics as described in d,e compared to net transition potentials (left). Topic pairs with high net transition potential tended to be temporally co-active for incoming and outgoing transitions, as evidenced by column-wise (top bar) and row-wise (right bar) correlations. Asterisks denote correlation P < 0.05. A full list of temporal co-activity values between Topics is provided in Supplementary Table 7. g, Correlation between Topic spatial co-activity and symmetric net transition potentials associated with each source Topic (n = 17). TAP and TRS values were computed using Topic-specific scDORI eGRNs, a union scDORI eGRN pooling links across Topics, SCENIC+ eGRNs, or random eGRNs. Dot colour represents the source Topic. Topic-specific scDORI eGRNs result in significantly higher correlation with spatial co-activity patterns than those derived using alternative GRNs (P = 0.0057 vs. Union; P = 0.0117 vs SCENIC+; paired two-sided t-test). h, Same as in g, but correlating temporal co-activity patterns in f and net transition potentials. Values denote the average between column-wise (incoming links, r1) and row-wise (outgoing links, r2) correlations for each Topic. Net transition potential values estimated with Topic-specific scDORI eGRNs positively correlated with temporal co-activity, significantly outperforming those derived from alternative methods (P = 0.0052 vs. Union; P = 0.0026 vs SCENIC+; paired two-sided t-test). i, Average epigenetic plasticity of cells in each Topic (as in Fig. 1c, top 5,000 cells per Topic) compared with (i) the cumulative net transition potential towards alternative state Topics (Topic-driven plasticity) and (ii) the total repression exerted by each Topic, both computed from Topic-specific scDORI eGRNs, a union scDORI eGRN pooling links across Topics, or SCENIC+ eGRNs. Topic-specific scDORI eGRNs best recapitulate observed epigenetic plasticity, with modelled plasticity and repression showing significant positive (r = 0.71, P = 0.002) and negative (r = −0.512, P = 0.036) correlations, respectively. Yellow boxes indicate P < 0.05. Box plots in g,h show median and IQR; whiskers are 1.5 × IQR. Illustrations in a,d created in BioRender; Mall, M. https://biorender.com/51tfsoq (2026).

a, Predicted regulatory roles of indicated neuronal-like TFs based on scDORI. Heat map colours indicate differences in the number of activated and repressed marker genes of each Topic (top 250). Dot size and colour denote TF-driven regulation of target TRs (TAP/TRS analysis, Supplementary Table 4). Repressors are predicted to broadly silence non-neuronal-like Topics, while activators selectively induce neuronal-like programs. b, OE levels of neuronal-like TFs in a at day 3 post-transduction in S24 PDGCs, quantified by qPCR, normalized to GFP vector controls (n = 3 independent transductions). Data are presented as mean ± s.d. c, Proportion of scDORI or SCENIC+ predicted target genes showing concordant changes in both ATAC-seq and RNA-seq after OE of neuronal-like TFs as in b. PBX1 and SOX4 were excluded because of insufficient changing gene sets (<500). Despite differences in regulon size across methods, the proportion of targets responding to perturbation was comparable. d, Percentage of target gene-regulatory directions accurately (green) or incorrectly (brown) predicted by scDORI or SCENIC+ based on gain-of-function perturbations in b. scDORI more accurately predicted regulatory directionality than SCENIC+, particularly for repressed targets. e, Percentage of Topic peaks (Topic-association score>0.95) opened after OE of neuronal-like TFs as in b, determined by ATAC-seq. Significance determined by one-sided hypergeometric test (BH-corrected FDR < 0.05). Only the pioneer TF ASCL1 induced a strong and significant increase in chromatin accessibility across neuronal-like and OPC-NPC-like Topic regions. f, Expression of top neuronal-like state regulators in GB states (left) and TME neurons (right) in our patient atlas. Dot colour and size indicate average expression and percentage of TF-expressing cells. MYT1L is the only TF exclusively expressed in neuronal-like GB cells at levels comparable to TME neurons. g, Genomic distribution of MYT1L-bound regions (n = 20,620) in S24 PDGCs determined by CUT&RUN after 8 days of MYT1L OE (n = 3) (top). Intensity of CUT&RUN peaks within ± 1 kb from peak summit in OE and control conditions (bottom). h, Differentially accessible regions (DARs) after MYT1L OE compared to control PDGCs in neurospheroid monoculture or co-culture with primary cortical cells (n = 3 each). Shown are the proportion of opening and closing regions, bound or not bound by MYT1L, and their genomic annotation. MYT1L predominantly closes chromatin by binding enhancer and promoter regions. i, Representative genome browser examples of MYT1L-bound TRs closed after MYT1L OE, as in b,g. j, Precision of MYT1L downstream target prediction, assessed at the level of target TFs and all target genes. Predicted MYT1L targets were derived from an average scDORI eGRN across neuronal-like Topics and compared against those of a SCENIC+ eGRN trained on neuronal-like cells. Blue boxes indicate the proportion of predicted targets directly bound by MYT1L (CUT&RUN as in g). Colours denote directional concordance with ATAC-seq and RNA-seq changes after MYT1L OE as in b. scDORI outperformed SCENIC+ in MYT1L regulon prediction, particularly at the TF level. Illustration in b created in BioRender; Mall, M. https://biorender.com/51tfsoq (2026).

a, Chromatin and transcriptional changes induced by primary cortical co-culture on S24 PDGCs compared to neurospheroid monoculture (n = 3 each). Enriched Topic programs in differentially accessible genes (DAGs; nearest gene to differentially accessible peak, FDR < 0.05) and DEGs (fold change>1.5, FDR < 0.05) as determined by GSEA, and the percentage of opening and closing Topic peaks (Topic-association score>0.95) are shown. Dot colour and size denote GSEA normalized enrichment score (NES) and significance, respectively. Asterisks indicate significant changes in Topic peaks (one-sided hypergeometric test, BH-corrected FDR < 0.05). Co-culture broadly opens chromatin across multiple Topic regions, consistent with a plasticity-promoting environment. b, MYT1L levels after Dox-based manipulation in S24 PDGCs co-cultured with primary cortical cells, in therapy-naive and therapy-exposed contexts. (Left) Normalized MYT1L counts from bulk RNA-seq during MYT1L induction (day 6, on) and after withdrawal (day 6 post-dox removal, off), compared to matched controls. (Right) MYT1L levels quantified by qPCR in PDGCs pre-exposed to ionizing radiation or temozolomide (TMZ), with and without MYT1L induction (day 6), compared to untreated controls. n = 3 biological replicates per condition, except for Dox control (n = 2). Data are presented as mean ± s.d. c, Average state association score of differentially closed and opened genes after MYT1L OE in S24 PDGCs with and without prior therapy exposure (ionizing radiation or temozolomide), as in b. Therapy-induced effects are shown below. Colour indicates z-scored state score. MYT1L represses non-neuronal-like gene signatures even under therapeutic pressure. d, Overlap of DAGs induced by MYT1L OE under therapeutic pressure with DAGs from MYT1L OE alone or treatment alone, all identified relative to untreated, unmanipulated controls as in b. Stacked bars show the proportion of closing (left) and opening (right) DAGs attributable to MYT1L OE alone, treatment alone, both, or neither. Most MYT1L-induced chromatin changes are preserved under both treatments, indicating that the plasticity-restricting function of MYT1L is largely retained under therapeutic pressure. e, Chromatin changes in Topic-associated regions and genes after MYT1L OE in therapy-exposed PDGCs in b, computed as in a with respect to untreated, unmanipulated controls. MYT1L-driven effects (Fig. 5f) are conserved under therapeutic pressure, albeit modestly attenuated. f, Representative western blots of MYT1L protein levels in S24 (n = 6 independent experiments, P = 1.8 × 10−6 OE vs control) and P3XX PDGCs (n = 5 independent experiments, P = 0.035 OE vs control), 7 days after MYT1L OE compared to controls, with fold-change quantifications. Uncropped Western blots are shown in Supplementary Fig. 2. (Bottom) MYT1L expression by qPCR 3 weeks after MYT1L knockout (KO) in BG5 PDGCs compared to controls (n = 3 independent experiments, P = 0.072 KO vs control). Centre line, mean; error bars, s.d.; two-sided t-test. g, Enriched Topic signatures in DEGs of MYT1L OE (S24, P3XX) or KO (BG5) compared to controls (n = 3 each), 3 weeks post-transduction, as determined by GSEA. Dot colour and size denote NES and significance, respectively. Neuronal-like identity is enriched after OE and depleted after KO. h, Selected pathways enriched after indicated MYT1L manipulations by GSEA. Dot colour and size denote NES and significance, respectively. All significantly enriched pathways are reported in Supplementary Table 10. MYT1L gain-of-function upregulates neuronal and synapse-related pathways, whereas loss of function upregulates stem cell pathways. i, Morphological changes after MYT1L OE in S24 PDGCs in neural microenvironments. (Left) Representative images of PDGC morphology in co-culture with primary hippocampal neurons (day 7; representative of ROIs quantified at right) and in mouse cortex xenografts (two-photon live imaging, 21 days post-injection; 6 z-stacked regions per mouse, n = 3 MYT1L OE and n = 2 control mice). (Right) Quantification of primary branches and total neurite-like projections from in vitro co-culture experiments (n = 16 control vs n = 17 MYT1L OE ROIs with 7–10 quantified cells per ROI; n = 3 independent experiments). MYT1L OE significantly increases the number and complexity of neurite-like projections. Data shown as mean ± s.d.; P-values for two-sided t-test are shown. Scale bar=100 µm. j, Tumour microtube (TM) interconnectivity in S24 PDGCs monocultures after MYT1L OE (n = 48 control vs. n = 37 MYT1L OE ROIs; n = 3 independent experiments) or knockdown (KD) (n = 47 control vs n = 44 MYT1L KD ROIs; n = 3 independent experiments). MYT1L OE reduced, and KD increased average TM length, yielding fewer and more connected morphologies, respectively. (Right) Total cell counts per ROI confirm comparable cell numbers across conditions. Centre line, mean; error bars, s.d.; P-values for two-sided t-test are shown. Scale bar=200 µm. k, Proliferation time-course of PDGCs after MYT1L OE (S24; n = 5 independent experiments x 10 wells each) or KO (BG5; n = 3 independent experiments x 30 wells each) determined by Alamar Blue assay, normalized to day 0. MYT1L OE and KO significantly reduce and increase proliferation, respectively. Centre line, mean; error bars, s.d.; P-values from two-way ANOVA with Tukey’s test are shown. l, Representative fluorescent microscopy images of tdTomato-labelled S24 PDGC spheroids transduced with Dox-inducible constructs of full-length MYT1L (left), MYT1L DBD fused with a VP64 activator domain (centre), or MYT1L DBD fused with an EnR repressor domain (right). Images of uninduced and dox-induced spheroids were taken on day 7 after embedding and binarized based on intensity. Dashed lines delineate spheroid size at day 0. Total number of spheroids and corresponding growth quantifications are shown in Fig. 5h. Scale bar=1,000 µm. m, Fold change in proliferation of S24 PDGCs after 7 days of OE of the indicated MYT1L constructs in l, normalized to uninduced controls. Full-length MYT1L and DBD–EnR reduced proliferation, while DBD–VP64 enhanced it. n = 8 wells x 3 independent experiments; Centre line, mean; error bars, s.d.; P-values for two-sided t-test against uninduced controls are shown. Illustrations in b,e,i,j created in BioRender; Mall, M. https://biorender.com/51tfsoq (2026).

a, Schematic of MEOX2 manipulation in S24 PDGCs co-cultured with primary cortical cells. MEOX2 OE was induced by Dox addition (MEOX2 on) and subsequently removed after Dox removal (MEOX2 off). b, MEOX2 expression levels after Dox-based manipulation in PDGCs as described in a. Normalized MEOX2 counts in bulk RNA-seq data of PDGCs 6 days after MEOX2 induction and 6 days after MEOX2 removal, compared to controls at equivalent time points (n = 3 each, except Dox+ control n = 2). Centre line, mean; error bars, s.d.; P-values for one-way ANOVA with Tukey’s test are shown. c, Chromatin-accessibility effects of MEOX2 induction and withdrawal in co-cultured S24 PDGCs as in b. Enriched Topic programs in DAGs (nearest gene to differentially accessible peak, FDR < 0.05) as determined by GSEA and the percentage of Topic peaks (>0.95 Topic-association score) opening and closing are shown. Dot colour and size denote GSEA NES and significance, respectively. Asterisks indicate significant changes in Topic-associated peaks (one-sided hypergeometric test; BH-corrected FDR<0.05). MEOX2 induces broad chromatin opening that is retained after withdrawal. d, Pseudotime-ordering of two clonal trajectories depicting transitions from neuronal-like cells toward AC-like or OPC-NPC-like states (n = 3109 and n = 5804 cells each). Trajectories are divided into stages defined by distinct Topic activation patterns: Stage 1, neuronal-like Topics; Stage 2, neuronal-like transition Topics; Stages 3–4, alternative state Topics. White lines demarcate stage boundaries. Average chromatin accessibility and expression of TFs active in cells of each stage are shown along the pseudotime axis. Transitions out of the neuronal-like state are accompanied by progressive chromatin opening of alternative state regulators previously held repressed. e, Predicted TF regulatory interactions along the trajectories in d, inferred from active Topics at indicated stages. Links going in the opposite direction to the trajectory are shaded. Stage 1 is dominated by repressive links targeting alternative state TFs, which are progressively lost as the trajectory advances. f, Repressive effects from TFs in each Topic towards top repressors in neuronal-like Topics. TFs active in non-neuronal-like Topics broadly repress neuronal-like safeguard repressors. Illustration in a created in BioRender; Mall, M. https://biorender.com/51tfsoq (2026).

#1247. Real Madrid striker Kylian Mbappe apologizes after Mao meme comments amid growing backlash in China

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Real Madrid striker Kylian Mbappe issued an apology Tuesday after comments he made about former Chinese leader Mao Zedong led several sponsors to drop him and drew a backlash from Chinese state television. The day after the 2026 Ballon d'Or ceremony, which saw Mbappe leave the London Palladium empty-handed, began with an international drama involving China, Mbappe and LaLiga. It all started when Mbappe told French talk show "The Bridge" that the meme "that makes me laugh the most, it's the one where there's a video of a guy, I think it's a Chinese dictator..." The clip also showed Mbappe's face on an image resembling Mao. To put that into context, a recurring joke, repeated in multiple memes, associates Mbappe with the word "dictator" for his influence in the sport and for how he interacts with teammates and players. During the 2026 World Cup, 2025 Ballon d'Or winner Ousmane Dembele called him "Mbappe Mobut," referring to Mobutu, the dictator who ran the Democratic Republic of Congo for more than 30 years. In September, Mbappe addressed the memes in an interview with France Football, saying that while he understood the jokes, they "sometimes reveal a lack of political and human awareness among people. There's a side that's a bit less funny, because we know the damage people like that have caused throughout history. Being compared to people who murder others, or who have made millions upon millions of people miserable... I don't think I've done that in my life." Two Chinese brands that have deals with the French striker issued statements condemning the player's statements. Mengniu, the country's largest dairy producer, wrote that it, "firmly opposes and has a zero-tolerance policy towards any words or actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people." Later on Tuesday, drinks giant Dongpeng issued a statement as well. "Our company firmly opposes and has a zero-tolerance policy towards any behaviour that offends national sentiments." According to the state-owned Global Times newspaper, Chinese state broadcaster CCTV's apps won't feature news related to the player, and the broadcaster will also stop streaming LaLiga matches.

Mao is obviously one of the most famous figures in modern China's history. He founded the People's Republic of China in 1949 and led the Communist Party until his death in 1976. Much has changed in China since his death, but the Chinese Communist Party still governs the country and sees jokes and memes about Mao as an insult to the party and the nation. Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lin Jian said, "We have noted the relevant reports. Words and deeds that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people will naturally be met with opposition from all sectors of Chinese society."

The French striker issued a statement about the matter: "During a recent interview with me, I commented on an image of myself, but my comment was not appropriate, and I now realise that it hurt the feelings of many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world. I apologise to everyone whom my words upset, as that was never my intention at all. I hold deep respect for the Chinese people and their history, and I express my sincere regret."

LaLiga also issued a statement, defending the agreement they still have in place with Chinese state television. "LALIGA deeply regrets the offence caused to Chinese fans by Kylian Mbappé's recent comments. These comments were made in a personal capacity and do not represent LALIGA. Within the scope of our institutional responsibility, we apologise on behalf of LALIGA and all its clubs. Spanish football stands for respect, coexistence and unity among people from all cultures. We extend our respect to China, its institutions and its people, and deeply value the support of the millions of fans who follow us every week. We reaffirm our commitment to a relationship built over many years. We are working with our partners and institutional counterparts in China to address this situation. Furthermore, in collaboration with clubs and players, we will introduce an awareness and communication protocol aimed at promoting respect for different cultures and helping to prevent similar situations in the future."

LaLiga president Javier Tebas, who recently also had multiple public disagreements with Real Madrid, wrote on X he "cannot allow the actions of an individual to tarnish this relationship or harm the more than 20 clubs competing in our professional leagues and the millions of Chinese fans. We are taking all measures within our power and working directly with our partners and counterparts in China to resolve this situation."

#1246. Early-onset cancer rising worldwide: Causes, risk, prevention

Across Latin America, early-onset cancer rates have risen, especially of bowel, breast and cervical cancers. But it is a worldwide trend.

The numbers are striking. Some cancer rates have doubled in the past 20 years. It's just not yet clear whether we're seeing a rise in actual cases or whether we're seeing more early-stage cases because of better awareness, diagnosis and treatment in hospitals.

Take, for example, colorectal (or bowel) cancer: In 2001, about one in every 26,000 people under 50 in England were diagnosed with it each year. By 2023, the rate of diagnoses was about one in 12,000. Twice what it was at the turn of the century.

That's according to the World Cancer Research Fund (WCRF), an international network of charities, which analyzed registry data from England, the United States and the Netherlands. It found the number of new cancer cases had risen for seven cancers in England alone.

So, rates have doubled, but the numbers overall are still small, said Amy Berrington de Gonzalez, a professor of clinical epidemiology at the Institute of Cancer Research in London.

"Cancer is still very uncommon among young people," Berrington de Gonzalez told DW. "Three times a small number is still a small number."

But she and other scientists still want to know why this is happening, because it is a worldwide trend. Latin America is a case in point.

A 2025 study analyzed registry data from 50 countries and territories up to 2017. It found early-onset colorectal cancer rising in 27 of those regions.

In Latin America, rates rose in Chile, Argentina, Ecuador, Costa Rica and Puerto Rico. Chile's rise — at almost 4% per year — was among the highest.

In Brazil, the evidence comes directly from hospitals. At the A.C. Camargo Cancer Center in Sao Paulo, the number of colorectal cancer patients under 50 grew by 7.6% per year between 2000 and 2023. That's a five-fold increase.

The number of patients over 50 grew even faster — at 8.1% — or about six-fold.

But since these figures came from a single hospital, they do not show whether cases are rising across Brazil. They may only reflect that this one hospital is treating more patients.

"We need better cancer registration systems," said Berrington de Gonzalez, "especially in countries like Brazil and Mexico, where obesity rates have also been increasing."

Marc Gunter, professor of cancer epidemiology at Imperial College London, said he expected Latin America to follow richer countries as diets there become more Westernized and lifestyles more sedentary. "I think it's already happening," he said.

In another study in 2025, involving 42 countries, Berrington de Gonzalez compared data from two age groups — 20 to 49 years and 50 years and older — between 2003 and 2017.

Six cancers — thyroid, breast, colorectal, kidney, uterine and leukemia — had risen among the younger groups in most countries. All but colorectal cancer were seen to rise in older adults, too.

In fact, colorectal cancer stood out. In about a third of the countries, it rose faster in younger adults than in older ones. "It is the one cancer that seems to be increasing in younger people whilst decreasing in older people," said Berrington de Gonzalez.

This has consequences for research. If cancers are rising in all age groups, the causes are likely to be widespread, so studies looking only at young people risk chasing complicated explanations with too little data to test them, she said.

A US study of pancreatic cancer in adults aged 15 to 39 years found the rise was almost entirely made up of early-stage tumors.

The authors said this suggested that instead of the number of cancer cases going up, it was the number of early diagnoses that had gone up. And that can be explained by better awareness in the community, with people getting checked more often.

But the data for colorectal cancer looks different: Some US studies show it rising in advanced stages of the disease as well, which suggests an increase in the number of cases, not just the number of diagnoses.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Obesity is an established cause of at least 13 cancers, according to the WHO's International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC).

According to a 2021 review of existing studies, young adults with obesity were almost twice as likely to develop colorectal cancer before the age of 50.

Obesity has also spread fastest among the young. The WHO reports that obesity rates have doubled among adults since the 1990s and quadrupled among adolescents.

Some also say ultra-processed foods and microplastics cause cancer. But Gunter said the evidence was inconclusive.

"There's a lot of hype," Gunter said, adding that more research was needed. Berrington de Gonzalez agreed: "Diets have changed, but we don't yet know the role they might play."

Gunter said individuals should not be blamed for living in societies built around convenience foods and desk jobs, and that lasting change needed public health policy.

But he also said that young people could lower their cancer risk by maintaining a healthy weight, moving more, eating more fiber and cutting back on processed meat.

"Going for a walk, being more physically active, eating more fruits and vegetables," he said. "Those things are maybe not so trendy, but they are really important."

For a 30-year-old reading this, Berrington de Gonzalez's message was one of reassurance: Cancer at a young age remains relatively rare.

#1245. Are Brighton a Premier League contender? Manchester City EFL Cup match will be biggest test yet

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Is this the year Brighton and Hove Albion make the leap? In their 10th season in the Premier League, the Seagulls have long since moved on from being a side well run enough to keep its distance from the relegation race. Now they might reasonably aspire to another step forward, away from the mass of sides just outside the premium European places and into real contention for Champions League qualification. Indeed, if you are a more exuberant Brighton fan, the question you might be asking yourself is not whether your side has made the leap but whether it has bounded up two tiers over the course of one summer. After all, they sit third in the Premier League table with the division's best attack and its third-best defense; combine those and you have a plus-16 goal difference. Their nearest rival by that metric, Manchester City, is at plus-11. Beat City in the second of this week's doubleheader with Enzo Maresca's side and they will be two points off the league leaders, though Arsenal might well open up a gap. Then again, what do Brighton have to fear from the champions? They've already smashed them 3-0 this season. Even their 2-0 defeat to Liverpool did little to quell Brighton's momentum. Not for the first time in his managerial career, Fabian Hurzeler couldn't resist a snipe at the manager of a big-six opponent in defeat, but he did have a point when he argued that "there was one team who really tried to create and try to win this game." The Seagulls went down swinging at Anfield, drawing seven shot blocks from Andoni Iraola's side. It really was not an exaggeration to say that if Yasin Ayari or Charalampos Kostoulas had scored early on, this might have been another famous win for the boys from the south coast.

Does this all sound too good to be true? Well, then it probably is. Admittedly, Hurzeler's side had looked primed to push on at the end of last season, an impressive run of results in March and April securing an eighth-placed finish and Conference League football. Then, in customary Brighton fashion, their best players left. Danny Welbeck had been their leading scorer, Jan Paul van Hecke the leader in league minutes and a crucial ball progressor, and while Carlos Baleba had endured a down year in which he had battled injuries, he still looked the most likely to ascend to a Moises Caicedo/Alexis Mac Allister level in Brighton's long line of breakout talent in midfield. Brighton could be trusted to replace the players they sold well. Swapping out Van Hecke for Luka Vuskovic already looks like the greatest of swindles on Tottenham, who are happy enough with what they have, even if they might have let the next great center back slip away. It is arguably easier, though, to deal with players you have lost for a fee than with those snared from you by injury. Kaoru Mitoma and Yankuba Minteh were the star wingers in last season's side, the former top 10 in the league for expected possession value added, the latter top 10 for take-ons. These wingers were critical for getting the ball into the box and creating threat when they got there. Injuries mean they have yet to take the field this season. You should not be able to cope with the loss of this much talent for so long. Some of Hurzeler's fixes have been ingenious. Maxim De Cuyper carried plenty of attacking thrust from left back, and after dalliances with a more advanced role last season, he has been converted to it permanently. The careful, steady integration of Kostoulas and Diego Gomez has paid dividends too. Meanwhile, at 35, Pascal Gross is as effective as he has ever been, with four assists and three goals already in this season's Premier League. Gross' pressing has also been critical to Brighton's success. According to data provided to CBS Sports by Gradient, the German international has made eight pressures leading to dangerous situations, placing him in the 99th percentile among Premier League players this season. Kostoulas and De Cuyper are similarly willing runners off the ball, adding up to a team that is even more energetic without the ball this season than it was last. In 2025-26, Brighton led the Premier League in passes per defensive action with 9.3, according to Wyscout. This season they also lead the division in this pressing metric, allowing opponents an average of 7.6 passes per defensive action. It is for that reason that only Wednesday's opponents, Manchester City, allow the other team fewer active minutes in possession than Brighton's 21.5.

Brighton's pressing intensity also means it is not that much of a surprise that they lead the league in counterattacking goals. As they do in goals from corners. As they do in higher-value chances where the shot is worth 0.1 expected goals or higher. As they do too in shots from outside the box. It all looks great, but then the sample size is still only eight games. That might be enough to form the outline of a conclusion in normal circumstances, but Brighton are one of only two teams in the league to have had a man advantage in two games so far this season. It should be said that both Aston Villa and Coventry looked like beaten teams when their player saw red, but we have to take the data set with a pinch of salt when over 10% of it involves Brighton having one more player. (There was also an impressive 33 minutes with 10 men against Sunderland, in which they held on to and ultimately added to a 1-0 lead.) So we should take some of their headline numbers under advisement. Drill deeper and there might be more factors to consider. Brighton lead the league in scoring and are second in xG, but there is a big gap between their 16.2 xG and 23 goals. This is a year in which Brighton's goal-of-the-season contest might be a reasonable proxy for the Premier League's as a whole (Lewis Dunk leads the way for me, Clive). Their shooting form was typified by that 3-0 win over Arsenal. They at least matched the champions in the first half, but they led 2-0 because both Gross and Kostoulas walloped shots in from range. You're not building a title challenge on that. Nor are you necessarily doing the same when you look porous at the other end. It isn't just that Brighton have allowed 11.4 xG to their opponents and are riding a run of shot-stopping that seems unlikely to continue even for a goalkeeper of Bart Verbruggen's quality. Hurzeler's side are also allowing the third-highest xG per shot of any team in the division. Much of that is a function of a worrying set-piece defense, but they are not much better from open play either, allowing 0.117 xG per shot, 10% above the Premier League average. When a team breaks their press like Chelsea did early in the season, that's when they end up in trouble. You don't compete for titles when you are giving up what Brighton are giving up defensively, but then that is a ludicrous conceit in the first place. What is clearly no longer ludicrous is the idea that this team might regularly beat Man City in a one-off match, whether that be the rotated outfit Enzo Maresca is due to field in the EFL Cup on Wednesday or the full-strength outfit that will presumably welcome them back to the Etihad on Saturday afternoon. Indeed, in the reasonably likely event that a sanction obliterates City's standing in this season's Premier League, Brighton could comfortably find themselves among the four or five Champions League qualifiers. The likes of Bournemouth, Nottingham Forest and Brentford are at best performing around Brighton's level so far this season in xG terms but have not picked up anywhere near as many points. Maybe the quality of Liverpool shows down the stretch. Perhaps Xabi Alonso simplifies things at Chelsea. Even then, that probably leaves a fifth spot for an English team to advance to the top tier. There is no question now that Brighton look better placed than anyone else to claim it, propelling themselves into a new class of club. If the experience of the last 10 seasons is anything to go on, this club tends to establish itself quite firmly when it moves up in the world.

#1243. 2026 Nobel Prize winner Anne Carson: Where to start reading

The works of this year's Nobel Prize-winning poet and essayist Anne Carson can feel slightly daunting. Here are some keys to understanding her universe.

This quote is from the long, lyrical poem "The Glass Essay" published in Anne Carson's 1995 collection "Glass, Irony and God" — an entry point into the works of the 2026 Nobel Prize in literature laureate.

In the poem, the narrator explores the burden of memory and obsessive desire after a failed love affair, all while regularly reflecting on Emily Brontë — an author renowned for her intense literary depiction of destructive and passionate love in "Wuthering Heights."

The poem brings several of Carson's recurring obsessions together into one work. She has repeatedly written about desire, abandonment and jealousy, and has often used other literary figures as emotional doubles, as historical anchor points to her ideas.

In a way, "The Glass Essay" encapsulates Carson's method; the Canadian poet, essayist, translator and classicist has often intellectualized emotional themes by intertwining her personal reflections with analysis, etymology, translation, literary history and philosophical thought.

Another trademark of her work is the genre fluidity found in "The Glass Essay," which — as the title indicates — is partly a literary criticism essay, even though it is also a poem due to its form.

"Almost all her literary production has centered upon the intersection between the philologist's obsession with words and the poet's desire for new meaning," noted Anders Olsson, chair of the Nobel Committee, in his description of the Nobel laureate on October 8.

Born in the Canadian city of Toronto, Carson first developed her fascination for ancient Greek myths as a teenager. She told literary journal The Brick that she spotted a bilingual edition of "Sappho" by Willis Barnstone in the display of a bookstore of a shopping mall in Ontario, and that had led her to ask a high school Latin teacher to teach her ancient Greek.

She went on to publish her doctoral thesis in Classics, entitled "Odi et Amo Ergo Sum" (I hate and I love, therefore I am).

Carson's first book of criticism, "Eros the Bittersweet," was published in 1986. It lays the foundation of her approach, as she draws on ancient Greek writers such as Sappho and Plato to examine how desire — and the obstacles between the lover and the beloved — creates emotional tension.

The book suggests that the ache of wanting is not separate from love; it is one of the things that makes desire so powerful.

Because "Eros the Bittersweet" moves between Greek poetry, philosophy and literary criticism and personal interpretations, it is not considered a conventionally easy read. A more immediately engaging work and good starting point to discover Carson is the verse novel "Autobiography of Red," published in 1998.

"Autobiography of Red" was inspired by the ancient Greek myth of Herakles (or Hercules) and the red-winged monster Geryon, which the hero kills as his 10th task in his series of 12 monumental labors.

An otherwise minor figure from mythology, Geryon is turned into Herakles' lover in Carson's book. She reimagines the myth as a modern, queer coming-of-age story, with the monster experiencing love, jealousy, sexuality and heartbreak.

"We all feel we're monsters most of the time," explained Carson.

The work is accessible, funny and moving, and no deep knowledge of Greek mythology is required to enjoy it.

The key to reading Carson is not to expect every connection to be immediately clear. Her books reward curiosity rather than certainty, and her sprawling, non-linear web of knowledge can be compared to going down a hyperlinked rabbit hole of narrative ideas.

"Men in the Off Hours" (2000) is another intellectually playful collection of poems. Here Carson collides the modern with the ancient, with references to figures as diverse as Beethoven, Virginia Woolf, Emily Dickinson, Jean-Luc Godard, Sigmund Freud, Homer and Hokusai.

The poems bring together fragments of history, mythology and ordinary life, allowing unexpected emotional and intellectual connections to emerge.

In the spoken and sung performance piece "Norma Jeane Baker of Troy" (2019), Carson similarly brings together classical and pop culture, reimagining the story of Helen of Troy alongside the life and cultural image of Marilyn Monroe.

How do people become the victims of desires they cannot control? This is a core theme Carson explores in "The Beauty of the Husband: A Fictional Essay in 29 Tangos," published in 2001.

It features the Canadian author's wry humor in a powerful and moving way, with erotic, painful and heartbreaking scenes from a doomed marriage: a 30-year obsession with a pathological liar whose singular redeeming quality is his sheer physical radiance.

The collection of poetry, which won her the T.S. Eliot Prize, is dedicated to the English Romantic poet John Keats, challenging his famous aphorism, "Beauty is truth."

As Chelsea and Liverpool meet in the EFL Cup, it's a good time to take a look at the beginning of the Xabi Alonso era at the club. #1240. Harry Kane is 'still processing' his Ballon d'Or win, so he went back to the only thing he knows

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

MUNICH – Less than an hour into a casual second-round cup match, a pocket of Bayern Munich fans in one corner of the Allianz Arena had moved on from reveling over Michael Olise's brace against second-division side Magdeburg. Their attention was instead on the group of substitutes who were warming up behind the opponent's goal and one person in particular.

It was a likely place for Harry Kane to spend a Wednesday evening, no matter the circumstances. Considering Bayern's relative strengths, the coaching staff had already hoped to give Kane the night off, especially with Borussia Dortmund awaiting this weekend and a trip to Atletico Madrid in the UEFA Champions League coming up on Tuesday. This was no ordinary midweek cup game, though, the pre-match guard of honor from his teammates as clear a sign as any of the occasion. It was Kane's first time back since winning the Ballon d'Or on Monday, doing so in his hometown of London.

The warm-ups were the only glimpse the crowd got of him on Wednesday, Bayern getting business done swiftly with a 6-1 win. Yet, Kane's appearance on the sidelines alone was celebratory, both after becoming the first Englishman to win the individual accolade in 25 years and the first player from the Bundesliga to do it since Matthias Sammer accomplished the feat in 1996. It was the type of thing that required an afterparty that allegedly stretched long after a delayed, bloated ceremony came to an end at around 11 p.m. local time, though Kane insisted he "didn't party too hard." It also allowed him to follow up a crowning achievement the only way he knows how – "straight back to work."

Kane trained on Tuesday and would have been ready to play if called upon on Wednesday, and is expected to prepare as usual for Saturday's clash with Dortmund. It comes as little surprise for a player who has rarely chased individual accolades. He has repeatedly insisted that his goal every four years is to win the World Cup with England, not the golden boot and left boyhood club Tottenham Hotspur for greater collective opportunities with Bayern in 2023 despite being just 47 goals behind Alan Shearer's Premier League goalscoring record at the age of 30. The spotlight has followed Kane for much of his career but he has always chosen to share it. There is no flexibility with the attention the Ballon d'Or carries, though; only one person can win it, no matter how team-oriented that person happens to be.

"It's strange," Kane said. "It's not my normal thing to enjoy. Even the guys, when I was walking out to warm up and they're all there clapping. I don't know. I get quite, maybe, embarrassed by it, but I know this is a big deal and I felt that obviously in the event, I felt that since with the reception and how much messages I've got from not just friends and family but people sending my number to other coaches and people just that have known me or know of me and they all wanted to just say well done. I think I'm still processing everything, to be honest, but look, I know it's a really big deal so I appreciate everyone, and you know, even on Saturday, I know we're going to do something before the game and all this, and it's important to do because it's a big celebration as well."

Even in his hometown on Monday, surrounded both by loved ones and his Bayern teammates who chanted his name in the London Palladium as Ronaldo revealed he had won the sport's ultimate individual prize, Kane felt out of place.

"A lot of nerves and just different emotions compared to a football match or anything like that and a lot of waiting around and just trying to picture what it'd be like if I did win but honestly, just really special," he said. "The support I've had from friends, family, fans, text messages, social media has just been overwhelming almost."

There is a lot Kane has not considered about life post-Ballon d'Or, either, like where the trophy might rest or what will come of the gold-flaked schnitzel that was made by a Bavarian restaurant and delivered to his home.

"I didn't actually eat it yesterday," he said. "With the match being today, I have a routine of what I eat and stuff but now, obviously, I appreciate it. It's a nice tradition that we have so to have a gold one, let's just keep them coming."

True to form, Kane has found the most comfort in a busy week in a return to his familiar routine.

"I think just being back to football," he said. "It feels like the Freiburg game [on Sunday] was six weeks ago. So much has happened in 48 hours. It was nice just to be back. A bit of normality, seeing the fans, getting a reception before the game, obviously, and then honestly just being back with the boys and just watching football and watching the boys play again so it's been a whirlwind of a 48 hours, and it's nice to just kind of be here and feel at home again."

He admitted he needs to add a new item to the routine at home, though – protecting the Ballon d'Or from his four children, aged nine to three.

"My wife and kids are still in London right now," he noted. "They get back on Friday so I haven't actually seen my kids since I won. I spoke to them, obviously, on FaceTime and stuff so I'm excited to see them and show them the trophy. I know they'll be trying to play with it and pick it up and it's quite heavy and so I might have to keep an eye on it this time but normally, the two boys, especially, just smash the ball around and then whoever wins picks up the trophy that I bring home but I'll have to explain it's a little bit more precious, so we'll have to keep an eye on it."

#1239. Finland, the world's happiest nation, faces a glum winter

Finns have many reasons to feel content, but the country's pile of debt is not one of them. Russia's war in Ukraine has added to the fiscal burden. Can the Nordic nation absorb another shock?

There's an uneasy mood in Finland, the country that's ranked the world's happiest for nine consecutive years. A colder-than-usual winter is on the way and so is the toughest austerity budget in years.

With an election due in April, the argument is no longer how much to cut, but which services, benefits and pensions will face the biggest cuts.

Finland's debt and deficit levels are in their worst state since the 1990s, when a banking crash and the collapse of the Soviet Union — a key export partner — pushed the Nordic nation into its own Great Depression.

Last month, Finland's national statistical institution confirmed that the national debt had reached 90.3% of gross domestic product (GDP) in the second quarter. Before the pandemic, that figure was around 65%.

Trouble to the east is, again, part of the reason. Finland ramped up defense spending after joining NATO a year after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Helsinki, which used to rely on Moscow for about a third of its energy, also faced much higher costs as it transitioned to other suppliers.

The Finnish government has spent more than it earns since the 2008/9 global financial crisis, partly due to an aging population and sluggish economic growth. Last month, the State Treasury projected the fiscal deficit would reach 4.2% of GDP in 2026.

Brussels has piled pressure on Helsinki to bring down the borrowing gap, as European Union rules require member states to stay below 3% of GDP. In January, the European Council opened an excessive deficit procedure and gave Finland until the end of 2028 to reach the desired target.

Prime Minister Petteri Orpo's government, which took office in June 2023, said it would aim to save about €9 billion ($10.1 billion) during this parliamentary term. But whoever wins the next election will have to cut much deeper, economists warn.

"The amounts currently estimated range from €8 to €11 billion," Jarkko Kivisto, an advisor to the Bank of Finland's monetary policy and research department, told DW.

Earlier this year, all but one political party agreed to support a debt brake, where the next government commits to tightening the country's deficit to about 2% of GDP by 2031.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

To date, Orpo's center-right National Coalition is the only party to promise a further €9 billion in cuts if he wins a second term. As well as further savings from health, social care and welfare, Orpo also plans to target workplace pensions, without reducing current payouts.

While the Social Democrats plan to split the reforms between spending cuts and tax hikes, Orpo plans to achieve his target without raising taxes — meaning public services will bear the brunt.

Kivisto, however, cautioned: "The deficit is so large that it would need a package that includes tax increases and expenditure cuts."

While Finland's at-risk-of-poverty rate is lower than the EU average, unemployment is higher than anywhere else in the bloc. In August, Finland's jobless total stood at 10.3%, just above Spain's 10%, according to Eurostat, the bloc's statistics agency. Youth unemployment reached 23.3%, against an EU average of 15.4%.

With household spending already falling, Lauri Holappa, director of the Finnish Centre for New Economic Analysis, warned that a new round of austerity would be a hard blow for the domestic economy.

"More than a quarter of the population works in the public sector, so if those workers face the threat of being sacked, the savings rate will rise and private spending will drop again," Holappa told DW.

Successive pressures ranging from the COVID-19 pandemic, higher interest rates and the global financial impact of two current wars have hurt efforts to cut the growing gap between income and borrowing. The 2027 budget proposal still counts on a spending gap of €12.4 billion.

Before the Ukraine war, Finland had already committed to buying 64 F-35A fighter jets from the United States, in a deal worth about €8.4 billion.

During more than four years of Russia's war in Ukraine, the Nordic nation raised military spending from $4.5 billion to over $8 billion per year, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI).

In April, the government said it would further increase defense spending to 3.2% of GDP, close to NATO's 3.5% target.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

With oil prices remaining close to $100 a barrel due to the Iran war, the government has so far resisted pressure to increase fuel subsidies. That's despite the Bank of Finland recording a 50% rise in the cost of imported energy in the early months of the Iran war.

While Finland’s shift to renewables, along with the opening of the Olkiluoto 3 nuclear power plant in 2023, has helped avoid a worse energy crisis, the central bank warned this summer that sustained high oil and gas prices would mean "lower economic growth and higher inflation" next year.

On another positive note, parts of Finland's export sector are booming, thanks to strong metal and shipbuilding orders, which Holappa described as strong as "the boom years of Nokia," when the once market-leading phone maker carried Finnish economic growth.

"There is a possibility that the export sector can steer us out of this recession," he told DW, as long as demand from the rest of Europe remains strong.

Despite the multiple roadblocks to bringing down the deficit, market reaction to Finland's debt woes has, so far, been muted. Rating agencies have kept the country's outlook stable, apart from S&P, which turned negative in April without cutting the rating.

On October 6, the premium the Finnish government pays over Germany to borrow for 10 years was 38 basis points. That compares to 128 for France and 107 for Italy. In other words, investors still treat Finnish debt as among the safest in Europe.

That is, as long as the next shock is not another extended oil-price spike, a fresh escalation from Russia, or a Europe-wide debt crisis centered on France.

Next March, Finland could still be named the planet's happiest nation for the 10th year in a row. How long the smiles last, once the bill for decades of borrowing arrives a month later, is anyone's guess.

#1237. World Cup 2034: Does Saudi Arabia shelving Neom Stadium spell trouble?

Since winning the right to hold the 2034 World Cup unopposed, Saudi Arabia has been pulling away from sport. With reports that its most ambitious stadium project will be abandoned, what does this mean for the World Cup?

It was billed as "the most unique stadium in the world," a key pillar of Saudi Arabia's World Cup 2034 plans. But now Neom Stadium, part of the kingdom's ambitious aims to build a 170-kilometer-long (111-mile) city in the desert known as The Line, looks set to be scrapped, with the broader project scaled back significantly.

A recent Reuters report said the stadium, which according to the country's bid book was going to be "350 meters (1,148 feet) above ground" and have "stunning vistas, and a roof created from the city itself," would no longer be built for the tournament, where it was to host a quarterfinal and several other games.

Observers of the gulf country saw this coming.

"When I was in Saudi Arabia in December there were already plenty of signals that the whole Neom project was being put on the back burner, if not abandoned altogether," F. Gregory Gause III, a regional expert from the Middle East Institute think tank in Washington D.C., told DW.

"I see it as part of a general reevaluation of their fiscal situation, both in light of the oil market before the current war and in light of the damage that the war is doing. The drawback from sports commitments is just part of a more general reassessment of priorities in the current, more straitened, situation."

Saudi Arabia's sports splurge that saw players like Cristiano Ronaldo join the country's football league and the kingdom invest in all sorts of sports in myriad ways has slowed dramatically. The country pulled funding for the multibillion dollar LIV Golf as well as events in snooker, tennis and rugby and also withdrew from ambitious plans to host the 2029 Asian Winter Games in Neom.

Sports had formed a key part of Saudi Arabia's Project 2030, which aimed to diversify the country's economy away from oil and increase its soft power. But Yasir Al-Rumayyan, the governor of the Saudi-government operated Public Investment Fund (PIF), which also owns Premier League football club Newcastle United, said earlier this year that the PIF was "reassessing its priorities" amid war in the region.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"The impact of the war has not only made the economic rationalization more important, but it's also accelerated the desire to rethink some of these projects in the sense that Neom is now being repurposed as an industrial center on the Red Sea, which has obviously assumed much greater urgency since the Strait of Hormuz was effectively blocked," Kristian Coates Ulrichsen, author of "Kingdom of Football: Saudi Arabia and the Remaking of World Soccer," told DW.

There are, Coates Ulrichsen continued, clear parallels with the 2022 World Cup in Qatar, where plans to build 12 stadiums resulted in only eight being used at the tournament. The Arab Spring uprising arrived shortly after the bid was accepted by FIFA and, though it didn't impact the country directly, it destabilized the region both politically and economically.

Neither Saudi Arabia's World Cup organizing authority or Sports Ministry has responded to questions from DW about whether we may again see fewer stadiums than the planned 15 for the 2034 World Cup, which could feature 64 teams.

"We're seeing the same obviously with Saudi Arabia now," said Coates Ulrichsen, who is also a fellow for the Middle East at Rice University in the US.

"[FIFA President] Gianni Infantino announced Saudi would be the only bidder on the 4th of October 2023. Three days later was October 7th, so within three days, the region was effectively in flames," he said.

Since then, there has been the Israel-US war against Iran, while Houthi attacks continue to hit Saudi Arabia as part of the conflict in Yemen, meaning that: "This whole hosting cycle is taking place against a backdrop of considerable uncertainty and kind of real tension."

But though the scope and cost of it may be reduced, Saudi Arabia's softening commitment to sport will not likely apply so firmly to the biggest sporting event in the world, said Gause.

"I think it continues to be a major priority, because of its global importance and because the Saudis will want to do at least as well, if not outshine, Qatar's hosting earlier."

Relations between Saudi Arabia and Qatar have improved since an agreement in 2021 but the pair remain regional rivals, something Coates Ulrichsen agrees will spur the 2034 hosts on.

As such, the 2034 tournament will still likely be a high-end affair, with Saudi Arabia building most stadiums from scratch. But, said Coates Ulrichsen, it may look somewhat different to what was planned.

"The fact that at least the Saudis were able to host a big event with 60,000 people in the stadiums, full stadiums without any security concerns [the Gulf Cup football final which they won this week] is a good sign," he said.

The regional expert thinks more matches could end up being hosted in the two biggest Saudi cities, Riyadh and Jeddah. This may be at the expense of some venues nearer the east coast such as Al Khobar or Al Ahsa. These are separated from Iran by the Persian Gulf, which includes the Strait of Hormuz, and could be reconsidered depending on the state of political affairs.

Saudi Arabia host football's Asian Cup in January, which Coates Ulrichsen thinks will be an "early test of whether that is viable to have a weeks-long major tournament under these conditions."

With nearly eight years until the World Cup, the political and economic situation in the country is difficult to predict. While the supposed shelving of Neom Stadium and general Saudi sporting withdrawal poses questions of commitment more broadly, it appears the World Cup show will go on. But probably not quite as billed.
